text: But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?
insight: Solomon's temple-dedication prayer admits the temple's inadequacy in advance. Reformed worship knows: no space contains God; even the holiest place is condescension.

text: And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word.
insight: Elijah's prosecutorial question — and the people answer with silence. Reformed conviction: the gospel forces decision; eternal hesitation is a vote against.

text: And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.
insight: After the wind and earthquake and fire — the still small voice. Reformed pastoral theology cherishes the verse: God's primary speech is not spectacle but Word.

text: And he answered, Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.
insight: Elisha to the trembling servant: more with us than with them. The verse is unseen reality reordering the seen — Reformed eschatology in OT form.

text: Turn again, and tell Hezekiah the captain of my people, Thus saith the LORD, the God of David thy father, I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will heal thee: on the third day thou shalt go up unto the house of the LORD.
insight: Hezekiah's deathbed prayer answered before the prophet leaves. The Lord 'hears' and 'sees' — Reformed pastoral theology says prayer is heard in real time, even when answers tarry.

text: Seek the LORD and his strength, seek his face continually.
insight: David's psalm at the ark's installation. The doubled 'seek' — strength and face — is the Reformed posture for the believer: continually after both.

text: If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.
insight: The covenant invitation to a divided people. Four verbs of returning — humble, pray, seek, turn — and the promise of healing. Reformed revival theology never tires of this verse.

text: For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments.
insight: Ezra's threefold rule for the teacher: to seek, to do, to teach. Reformed exegesis follows this order — study informs life before it informs sermon.

text: O Lord, I beseech thee, let now thine ear be attentive to the prayer of thy servant, and to the prayer of thy servants, who desire to fear thy name: and prosper, I pray thee, thy servant this day, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man. For I was the king's cupbearer.
insight: Nehemiah's intercession before his Persian assignment. The Reformed pastor prays before strategizing — and asks for ears before he asks for outcomes.

text: Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
insight: Ezra reads the law; the people weep; Nehemiah corrects them — joy in the Lord is your strength. Reformed worship learns: confession leads to celebration, not to permanent grief.

text: For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?
insight: Mordecai's challenge to Esther. The Reformed reading: providence appoints, but the appointed are still asked to act. Both true; the verse holds them together.

text: Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and my maidens will fast likewise; and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.
insight: Esther's resolve before approaching the king. The verse models faith that proceeds without guarantees — Reformed courage acts because the King is sovereign, not because the outcome is known.

text: And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
insight: Job's first response to catastrophe. The Reformed read this verse as the gold standard for grief — orthodox, theocentric, blessing-shaped. The Lord gives; the Lord takes; both are praised.

text: But he said unto her, Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips.
insight: Job rebukes his wife's counsel of curse-and-die. Reformed theodicy admits that good and evil both come from God's hand, refusing the dualism that would protect God from involvement.

text: Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him.
insight: The most famous verse of trust under duress. Job will trust even what he cannot understand — the Reformed posture against every fair-weather faith.

text: But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.
insight: Job's confidence in the refining work. The verse refuses to evaluate suffering by its present heat — gold comes out, but only after the fire has done its full work.

text: And unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding.
insight: The wisdom interlude lands here: fear of the Lord is wisdom. After all of Job's debate, the answer is Proverbs 1:7 — and the Reformed catechism agrees.

text: Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.
insight: God's interrogation begins. Reformed theology proper appeals to Job 38-41 against every modern attempt to question God in the dock — the Creator asks the questions.

text: I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee.
insight: Job's first confession from the dust: omnipotence and omniscience together. The Reformed read this as Job catching up to the doctrine Job has always held.

text: I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes.
insight: Job's repentance after the whirlwind. Hearing becomes seeing; theology becomes encounter. Reformed mysticism (if there is such a thing) lives in this transition.

text: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.
insight: The book's thesis. Vanity (hevel) is breath, vapor, mist — not 'worthless' but 'wisp-like.' The Preacher's whole project is teaching how to live in fog without losing the way.

text: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
insight: The famous verse on seasons. Reformed providence reads this not as fatalism but as ordered time — God assigns the moments, and the believer learns to recognize each.

text: For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not.
insight: The Preacher's anthropology. Total depravity proven in two lines — there is none who does good without sinning. Romans 3 will quote a similar conclusion.

text: Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;
insight: The Preacher's pastoral counsel to the young. The Reformed catechism includes this verse: youth should remember the Creator before the years rebel.

text: He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love.
insight: The shepherd's love-banner over the beloved. Read mystically by the Puritans (Owen, Sibbes) as Christ's covenanted affection for the soul.

text: I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine: he feedeth among the lilies.
insight: The mutual possession formula. Reformed expositors (Spurgeon especially) hear this as the believer's confession of union with Christ — owned and owning.

text: Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
insight: God's invitation to negotiate forgiveness. The colour transformation — scarlet to snow — is the chemistry of justification: dyed-in cleansed-out. Reformed proclamation borrows this verse for evangelistic invitation.

text: Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
insight: The Immanuel sign Matthew quotes for the virgin birth (Matt 1:23). The name itself — God with us — is the gospel in noun form.

text: Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the LORD JEHOVAH is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation.
insight: Isaiah's confidence in the day of salvation. The triple — salvation, strength, song — names the believer's daily posture. Reformed worship sings because the Lord has become both verb and noun of rescue.

text: For thus saith the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel; In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not.
insight: Four nouns of salvation — returning, rest, quietness, confidence — that Israel refused. Reformed pastoral counsel hears every age of the church refusing these same gifts.

text: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
insight: The verse on the durability of God's word. Reformed homiletics finds in this verse permission to preach with confidence — what is fading is not what is being preached.

text: All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.
insight: The atonement verse Reformed theology returns to. The 'all' of human sin meets the 'him' of divine substitution; the burden has been transferred.

text: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
insight: The gospel call extends to those who can pay nothing. Reformed proclamation reads this verse as the universal offer — without money and without price.

text: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
insight: The word's productivity. Reformed preaching trusts this verse — what is sown will accomplish what God sent it for, regardless of immediate evidence.

text: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;
insight: Jesus reads this passage in Nazareth (Luke 4:18). The Spirit-anointing mission has its OT scripture; Reformed missiology cites both verses together.

text: Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.
insight: God's election precedes the womb. Reformed soteriology cites this verse not only for vocational calling but for the priority of grace in every life.

text: Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches: But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD.
insight: The three glories denied — wisdom, might, riches — and the one glory permitted: understanding the Lord. Reformed theology's first principle is recognizable here.

text: O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the LORD. Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel.
insight: The potter and clay image. Romans 9 will repurpose this — Paul's strongest defense of sovereignty has its OT root here.

text: Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? saith the LORD. Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the LORD.
insight: Omnipresence stated as God's own question. Reformed theology proper hears this verse against every account of God's limitation; nowhere is unobserved.

text: But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.
insight: The new covenant promise — law internalized, not merely posted. Hebrews 8 will quote this as the Christian covenant's character; the Spirit's work has its prophetic charter here.

text: Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things, which thou knowest not.
insight: God's invitation to inquire. Reformed prayer is bold because the Inviter has issued the call — 'great and mighty things' are offered to those who ask.

text: The LORD is good unto them that wait for him, to the soul that seeketh him.
insight: Lamentations' refrain on waiting. After the destruction of Jerusalem, the verse insists the Lord is good to those who wait — a Reformed pastoral comfort in the worst weeks.

text: But though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies. For he doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men.
insight: God grieves; God shows compassion. The verse insists divine sorrow over judgment is real — Reformed theology refuses to flatten the divine pathos.

text: Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old.
insight: The Lamentation prayer for restoration. Reformed monergism reads it directly — only God can turn the hearts he has scattered; the verse is the asking.

text: Now when I passed by thee, and looked upon thee, behold, thy time was the time of love; and I spread my skirt over thee, and covered thy nakedness: yea, I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine.
insight: Covenant as marriage. Reformed federal theology reads this verse as God's nuptial commitment — the OT covenants prefigure the Bridegroom Lamb of Revelation.

text: Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD: and not that he should return from his ways, and live?
insight: God's stated reluctance toward judgment. Reformed exegesis takes seriously the divine 'no pleasure' in wickedness — judgment is just but not preferred.

text: And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them.
insight: The Spirit's promised work in the new covenant. Reformed sanctification reads obedience as Spirit-enabled walking, not just morality coached from outside.

text: Thus saith the Lord GOD unto these bones; Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live:
insight: The dry bones vision's central verse. Reformed soteriology — only the Spirit's breath makes the dead live — has its picture here. Regeneration is resurrection language.

text: And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding:
insight: Daniel's response to mystery revealed: God reigns over times and kingdoms. Reformed political theology never tires of this verse — empires are subordinate, not ultimate.

text: And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?
insight: Nebuchadnezzar's restored confession. The Reformed doctrine of God's sole rule has this verse — and the pagan king becomes its mouthpiece.

text: I saw in the night visions, and, behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
insight: Daniel's vision of the Son of Man — Jesus's favorite self-designation. Reformed Christology runs from this verse through the Gospels to Hebrews.

text: And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.
insight: The promise to the wise — they shall shine like stars. Reformed eschatology honors the verse: humble faithfulness will be conspicuous in the age to come.

text: And I will sow her unto me in the earth; and I will have mercy upon her that had not obtained mercy; and I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people; and they shall say, Thou art my God.
insight: The covenant reversal: not-my-people becomes my-people. Peter and Paul both quote this verse (Rom 9:25, 1 Pet 2:10) to ground Gentile inclusion. Reformed federal theology hears Gentile incorporation foreseen.

text: Take with you words, and turn to the LORD: say unto him, Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously: so will we render the calves of our lips.
insight: Hosea's altar call. 'Take with you words' is the verse for those who can offer nothing else — repentance has no requirement but bringing the words God has given.

text: And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you.
insight: The Lord restores what locusts have eaten — Reformed pastoral theology cherishes this as the verse for those whose decades feel devoured. Restoration is in God's vocabulary.

text: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:
insight: The Pentecost prophecy Peter quotes (Acts 2:17). The Spirit's outpouring on 'all flesh' is the OT root of the Reformed catholic vision: barriers of gender, age, status fall before the Spirit.

text: And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered: for in mount Zion and in Jerusalem shall be deliverance, as the LORD hath said, and in the remnant whom the LORD shall call.
insight: The verse Paul cites in Romans 10:13 — 'whosoever shall call.' The universal offer of salvation has its OT charter; the gospel name to invoke is the Lord's.

text: Therefore thus will I do unto thee, O Israel: and because I will do this unto thee, prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.
insight: The repeated 'yet have ye not returned' (4:6-11) lands here. The verse the Reformed conscience hears in every season of unrepented sin — prepare to meet the One who summons.

text: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:
insight: The worst famine — not bread, but the word. Reformed homiletics reads this verse as a warning to a Western church that has plenty of books and few hearings.

text: Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.
insight: God reveals his counsel to his prophets. Reformed doctrine of revelation hears here both the priority of God's initiative and the role of human messengers.

text: And saviours shall come up on mount Zion to judge the mount of Esau; and the kingdom shall be the LORD's.
insight: The kingdom shall be the Lord's. Reformed eschatology cites this verse — the smallest book in the OT closes with the largest claim.

text: And he said unto them, I am an Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land.
insight: Jonah's witness in transit. Even the fleeing prophet confesses the right doctrine — and the sailors believe before he repents. The verse mocks the messenger and honors the message.

text: And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?
insight: The book's last verse — a question, not a resolution. God's mercy reaches even ignorance and animals; Jonah is left to decide whether he can stomach a wider God.

text: But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.
insight: The Bethlehem prophecy. Matthew 2 will quote it; the Magi will follow it. The Reformed read this as proof of providential precision — even the village is foretold.

text: Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy.
insight: Micah's astonishment at God's pardoning. The verse is the Reformed doxology of forgiveness — there is no God like ours, and the proof is mercy.

text: The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.
insight: Two attributes balanced — slow to anger, great in power. Reformed theology proper refuses to let either eclipse the other; the patience and the wrath are both real.

text: Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith.
insight: 'The just shall live by his faith' — the Reformation's text in its original setting, a prophet told to wait for a vision that tarries. The New Testament quotes it three times (Rom 1:17, Gal 3:11, Heb 10:38), and Luther's whole theology grew from it.

text: For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.
insight: The promise that knowledge of God's glory will saturate the earth as the waters cover the sea. Reformed missiology rests on this verse — the consummation is universal recognition.

text: The great day of the LORD is near, it is near, and hasteth greatly, even the voice of the day of the LORD: the mighty man shall cry there bitterly.
insight: The day of the Lord — near and hastening. Reformed eschatology takes seriously both the imminence and the inevitability; the verse refuses to let the church be casual about it.

text: For then will I turn to the people a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the LORD, to serve him with one consent.
insight: The reversal of Babel — pure language given to all peoples. Reformed missiology reads this verse as gospel undoing Genesis 11; the Lord re-unifies what sin scattered.

text: Now therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts; Consider your ways.
insight: Haggai's refrain after seventy years of distracted building. 'Consider your ways' — the Reformed examination of conscience has this verse as its prompt.

text: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass.
insight: Palm Sunday's prophecy. Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey to fulfill this verse precisely — Reformed Christology never tires of pointing out the literal correspondence.

text: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn.
insight: The pierced One looked upon. John 19:37 cites this verse at the crucifixion. Reformed Christology reads it as Trinitarian — they pierced me (YHWH speaking), and he is the One pierced.

text: For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense shall be offered unto my name, and a pure offering: for my name shall be great among the heathen, saith the LORD of hosts.
insight: From sunrise to sunset, the Lord's name shall be great among the nations. Reformed missiology cites this verse — even before the New Covenant, the geographical scope was global.

text: Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.
insight: The Lord's invitation to test him in tithing. Reformed stewardship reads this verse — generous return is the believer's reasoned response to a giving God.

text: But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall.
insight: The Sun of righteousness rising with healing in his wings. Reformed Christology hears Christ's coming announced in solar terms; Zechariah's song picks up the image when it greets 'the dayspring from on high' (Luke 1:78).

ref: Homilies on the First Epistle of John, VII.8
text: Love, and do what you will. If you keep silence, keep silence with love; if you cry out, cry out with love; if you correct, correct with love; if you spare, spare with love. Let the root of love be within you, and from that root nothing but good can spring.
insight: Often shortened to 'love and do what you will' and misused as license. Augustine's full sentence makes love a root that disciplines its own branches — the freedom is grounded in the rule of love, not its absence.

text: I heard a voice from the neighbouring house, as of a boy or girl, I know not which, chanting and oft repeating, 'Take up and read; take up and read.' I rose, interpreting it to be no other than a command from God to open the book and read the first chapter I should find.
insight: The Tolle, lege conversion. Augustine opens Romans, reads 13:13-14, and the long resistance breaks. The Reformed know this pattern — Scripture reaches the heart that has been long under conviction.

text: If you understand, it is not God.
insight: Augustine's principle of theological humility — comprehension would make God a creature. Reformed theology takes the apophatic side of doctrine seriously here; God exceeds what minds can contain.

text: I desire to know God and the soul. Nothing more? Nothing whatever.
insight: Augustine's intellectual program in a single exchange. The early Reformed catechists adopted this as their own discipline — knowing God deeply, knowing oneself honestly, both at once.

text: Two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self.
insight: The hinge of City of God. Augustine reads history through two loves — and the Reformed instinct against worldly accommodation hears here the original analysis.

text: He was not, as might be imagined, circumscribed in the body; nor, while He was in the body, was He absent from elsewhere... He was at once everywhere.
insight: Athanasius on what later Reformed theologians called the extra Calvinisticum: the Word fills the universe even while incarnate. Reformed Christology has read this passage with delight.

text: It was unfitting that creatures made by God should be brought to nothing through the deceit wrought upon man by the devil; and supremely unfitting that the work of God in mankind should disappear.
insight: Athanasius gives the metaphysical reason for the incarnation: God's goodness will not let his work perish. Reformed soteriology hears in this the priority of divine love over creaturely failure.

text: These are the springs of salvation, that he who thirsts may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone the doctrine of godliness is proclaimed. Let no one add to these; let no one take away from them.
insight: The earliest catalogue of the 27 New Testament books — Athanasius lists what the church will recognize as canon. Reformed bibliology cites his Festal Letter for the canon's reception.

text: It was necessary for man's salvation that there should be a knowledge revealed by God besides philosophical science... For man is directed to God as to an end that surpasses the grasp of his reason.
insight: The opening question of the Summa: why revealed theology is needed in addition to natural reason. The Reformed instinct against rationalist sufficiency hears Aquinas here, even as the traditions differ on natural theology's reach.

text: I mean by charity that affection of the mind which aims at the enjoyment of God for His own sake, and the enjoyment of one's self and one's neighbor in subordination to God; by lust I mean that affection of the mind which aims at enjoying one's self and one's neighbor, and other corporeal things, without reference to God.
insight: Augustine's rule for reading Scripture: whatever does not build up this love of God for his own sake is being misread. The line between charity and lust is not the object loved but whether God is the end or left out.

text: I devoutly adore you, hidden Deity, truly hidden beneath these appearances. My whole heart submits to you, for in contemplating you, it surrenders itself completely.
insight: The Eucharistic hymn Aquinas wrote in 1264. Reformed readers can affirm the adoration of the hidden Christ even as they differ on the elements' theology — the longing to behold him is shared.

text: From this, that is also clear by way of induction, which was proved above by rational arguments, namely, that man's ultimate felicity consists only in the contemplation of God.
insight: Aquinas closes a long elimination: happiness is not in wealth, body, pleasure, moral action, art or prudence. Only the vision of God is an end and not a means, which is why the catechism can say 'enjoy him for ever'.

ref: The Bondage of the Will (1525), Part II, Sect. XXIV (Cole trans.; WA 18:635)
text: Thus the human will is, as it were, a beast between the two. If God sit thereon, it wills and goes where God will: as the Psalm saith, "I am become as it were a beast before thee, and I am continually with thee." (Ps. lxxiii. 22-23.) If Satan sit thereon, it wills and goes as Satan will.
insight: Luther's metaphor for the bondage of the will against Erasmus. Reformed monergism cites this passage to anchor the necessity of divine initiative — neither rider chooses the mount.

text: A theologian of glory calls evil good and good evil. A theologian of the cross calls the thing what it actually is.
insight: Luther's theology of the cross against medieval glory-theology. Reformed preaching learns from this thesis to start where God starts — at the cross, not at the spectacular.

text: Of this article one cannot yield or surrender any part... On this article rests all that we teach and practice against the pope, the devil, and the world.
insight: Luther's resolve on justification by faith. Reformed confessionalism agrees — there is no negotiable doctrine if this one falls.

text: He found in me no right mind and no good will. But the good Lord had mercy upon me. Out of pure kindness He loved me, loved me so that He gave Himself for me, that I should be free from the Law, from sin, devil, and death.
insight: Luther putting Paul's 'who loved me and gave himself for me' into the first person. Christ began, not we: the love came before there was anything in the sinner to love, and it set him free from everything that had a claim on him.

ref: The Freedom of a Christian (1520), opening theses
text: A Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none. A Christian is a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all.
insight: Luther's paradox of Christian freedom. Reformed sanctification holds both poles — free from condemnation, bound to serve in love, simultaneously and without contradiction.

ref: Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott (1529)
text: Did we in our own strength confide, our striving would be losing; were not the right Man on our side, the Man of God's own choosing. Dost ask who that may be? Christ Jesus, it is he.
insight: Luther's hymn translates Psalm 46 into Reformation theology. The 'right Man' is Christ, chosen by God for the battle — Reformed worship still sings what Luther wrote.

text: Faith is a firm and certain knowledge of God's benevolence toward us, founded upon the truth of the freely given promise in Christ, both revealed to our minds and sealed upon our hearts through the Holy Spirit.
insight: Calvin's definition of faith in three motions: knowledge (firm), promise (in Christ), Spirit (sealing). Reformed catechism has not improved on this triple structure.

text: Prayer is an intercourse of men with God, by which, having entered the heavenly sanctuary, they appeal to him in person concerning his promises.
insight: Calvin reads prayer as conversation — intercourse, not transaction. Reformed prayer theology owes this passage the relational frame.

text: Let us learn from her single title of mother how useful, indeed how necessary, the knowledge of her is, since there is no other means of entering into life unless she conceive us in her womb, give us birth, nourish us at her breast.
insight: Calvin's strong ecclesiology, quoting Cyprian. Reformed federal theology takes seriously the church's instrumental role: salvation is personal, not solitary.

text: The same Spirit who has spoken through the mouths of the prophets must penetrate into our hearts to persuade us that they faithfully proclaimed what had been divinely commanded.
insight: Calvin's internal testimony of the Spirit (testimonium internum Spiritus Sancti). Reformed bibliology rests its assurance of Scripture not on argument alone but on the Spirit's persuasion.

text: Justification is the principal hinge by which religion is supported.
insight: Calvin names justification the hinge on which religion turns (praecipuum cardinem). Luther had said much the same in the Smalcald Articles (1537), a year after the first Institutes; the Reformers did not tire of it.

text: There is no people so barbarous, no nation so brutal, as not to be imbued with the conviction that there is a God.
insight: Calvin's sensus divinitatis — the seed of religion sown in every person. Reformed apologetics rests on this universal sense; atheism is a position requiring effort.

text: Set faith at work on Christ for the killing of thy sin. His blood is the great sovereign remedy for sin-sick souls.
insight: Owen's pastoral counsel in the trenches of sin. Reformed sanctification has its method here: faith applied to Christ specifically for mortification, not in general for forgiveness only.

witness.quote: Set faith at work on Christ for the killing of thy sin.

text: Let us assure ourselves there is no better way for our healing and deliverance, yea, no other way but this alone, -- namely, the obtaining a fresh view of the glory of Christ by faith, and a steady abiding therein.
insight: Owen prescribing for spiritual decay: coldness, deadness, an unreadiness for grace. The remedy is not more effort but a fresh sight of Christ, since the beholding itself does the transforming (2 Cor 3:18).

text: Whatsoever is required for a complete and perfect saving of his peculiar people from their sins was intended by his coming. To say that he did but in part or in some regard effect the work of salvation, is of ill report to Christian ears.
insight: Owen on 'he shall save his people from their sins'. The cross was not a door left ajar for those who might walk through; it was the saving of a people, and any account that leaves the outcome uncertain has misread the intention.

text: To be spiritually minded is the great distinguishing character of true believers from all unregenerate persons.
insight: Owen's first remark on Romans 8:6. The frame of the mind is not a mood but a mark: those who are carnally minded are, on the apostle's terms, unregenerate, and the inward bent of the thoughts is itself a moral state.

text: Indwelling sin always abides whilst we are in this world; therefore it is always to be mortified.
insight: Owen's premise: sin's residence is permanent; mortification's labor must be too. Reformed sanctification is not eradication but constant warfare — and Romans 8:13 grounds the campaign.

ref: Communion with God (1657), Part II, ch. 3, Digression 1
text: Consider, hence, his eternal, free, unchangeable love. Were the love of Christ unto us but the love of a mere man, though never so excellent, innocent, and glorious, it must have a beginning, it must have an ending, and perhaps be fruitless.
insight: Owen's argument for the deity of Christ from the kind of love we need: a merely human love, however excellent, has a beginning and an ending. Christ's love is fixed by what he is, not by how we feel about ourselves.

text: It appears that all that is ever spoken of in the Scripture as an ultimate end of God's works, is included in that one phrase, 'the glory of God.'
insight: Edwards's account of God's purpose in creation: glory radiating outward. Reformed teleology has not improved on this — God's chief end and ours overlap (cf. WSC Q.1).

text: The affections are no other than the more vigorous and sensible exercises of the inclination and will of the soul.
insight: Edwards on affections — not feelings in the sentimental sense, but vigorous motions of the will. Reformed psychology treats the affections seriously because Edwards taught us to.

text: Christian practice or a holy life is a great and distinguishing sign of true and saving grace.
insight: Edwards on the most important sign of true conversion: holy practice. Reformed examination of conscience reads with Edwards — feelings can deceive; sustained obedience is harder to fake.

text: And this renders heaven a world of love; for God is the fountain of love, as the sun is the fountain of light. And therefore the glorious presence of God in heaven, fills heaven with love, as the sun, placed in the midst of the visible heavens in a clear day, fills the world with light.
insight: Heaven is not lovely because its inhabitants are; it is lovely because God is there, and love pours from him the way light pours from the sun. Whatever else eternity holds, it holds that.

text: The first instance, that I remember, of that sort of inward, sweet delight in God and divine things, that I have lived much in since, was on reading those words, 1 Tim. i. 17. ... As I read the words, there came into my soul, and was as it were diffused through it, a sense of the glory of the Divine Being.
insight: Edwards records his own conversion-experience triggered by a single text. Reformed pastoral theology reads conversion narratives because the Word's work is always personal.

insight: Edwards does not rank love among the virtues; he says the saving virtues are all love wearing different clothes. Where love is absent, the rest is performance.

text: There is an admirable conjunction of diverse excellencies in Jesus Christ. ... There do meet in Jesus Christ infinite highness and infinite condescension. Christ, as he is God, is infinitely great and high above all.
insight: Edwards's sermon on Revelation 5:5-6. Reformed Christology stretches between attributes that seem opposite — Edwards taught the church to see them as harmony, not paradox.

witness.quote: There is an admirable conjunction of diverse excellencies in Jesus Christ.

text: The Calvinist in a word is the man who sees God; he has caught sight of the ineffable Vision, and he will not let it fade a moment from his eyes. God in nature, God in history, God in grace; everywhere he sees God in his mighty stepping, everywhere he feels the working of his mighty arm, the throbbing of his mighty heart.
insight: Warfield's compact summary of the Reformed instinct. To see God truly is to see oneself rightly — and the Calvinist's preoccupation with God's sovereignty flows from that prior seeing.

insight: Three marks, and the third carries the weight: grace alone, with self excluded from the whole of salvation. Warfield ties the doctrine of grace to the posture of prayer.

insight: Vos's thesis on Paul: eschatology is not one locus among many but the structural frame of Pauline thought. Reformed biblical theology took this insight and rebuilt its curriculum.

witness.work: Is There a Meaning in This Text?
witness.quote: I now wish to define the text as a communicative act of a communicative agent

text: Doctrine proceeds from an authoritative script and gives direction as to how individuals and the church can participate fittingly in the drama of redemption.
insight: Vanhoozer's thesis sentence. Scripture is the script, doctrine is the stage direction, and the church is the company that has to perform; doctrine that is never enacted has stopped one step short of its purpose.

witness.quote: Doctrine proceeds from an authoritative script and gives direction

text: Mere Protestant Christianity uses the resources of the solas and the priesthood of all believers to express the unity-in-diversity that local churches have in Christ.
insight: Vanhoozer's defence of Protestantism against the charge that sola scriptura only breeds division. The five solas and the priesthood of believers are the resources for a unity that does not require uniformity, which is what the New Testament churches already had.

witness.quote: Mere Protestant Christianity uses the resources of the solas

text: Yet Christianity is not primarily about lifestyle change; it is about knowing God.
insight: Reeves recentering the Christian religion on its object. Ethics and doctrine are downstream; the thing itself is knowing the Father, Son and Spirit, and a Christianity that skips to behaviour has skipped the point.

witness.quote: Christianity is not primarily about lifestyle change; it is about knowing God

text: This book, then, aims for something deeper than a new technique or a call to action: to consider Christ, that he might become more central for you, that you might know him better, treasure him more and enter into his joy.
insight: Reeves stating his aim in the introduction titled 'Christianity Is Christ'. Most Christian books offer a technique; this one offers a Person, on the theory that beholding Christ is what actually changes people.

witness.quote: to consider Christ, that he might become more central for you

text: The closer one looks, the clearer it becomes: the Reformation was not, principally, a negative movement, about moving away from Rome; it was a positive movement, about moving towards the gospel.
insight: Reeves reframing the Reformation's positive aim. Reformed self-understanding with Reeves reads our heritage not in oppositional terms but in recovered ones — Christ found, not Rome rejected, was the main event.

witness.quote: the Reformation was not, principally, a negative movement

text: And when Jesus tells us what animates him most deeply, what is most true of him—when he exposes the innermost recesses of his being—what we find there is: gentle and lowly.
insight: Ortlund's premise from Matthew 11:29, the one place Jesus describes his own heart. What he says about himself outweighs what we project onto him, and what he says is not severe but gentle.

witness.quote: what we find there is: gentle and lowly

text: Time and again it is the morally disgusting, the socially reviled, the inexcusable and undeserving, who do not simply receive Christ's mercy but to whom Christ most naturally gravitates.
insight: Ortlund reading the Gospels for where Jesus actually goes. His mercy is not a reluctant concession to the worst people; they are the ones he moves toward, which is bad news for the respectable and very good news for everyone who knows what they are.

witness.quote: Time and again it is the morally disgusting, the socially reviled

text: Growing in Christ is not centrally improving or adding or experiencing but deepening.
insight: Ortlund on the geometry of sanctification. Reformed soteriology with Ortlund reads spiritual progress as descent into what is already given, not accumulation of what was missing.

witness.quote: in Christ is not centrally improving or adding or experiencing but deepening

text: In the matter of reforming things, as distinct from deforming them, there is one plain and simple principle; a principle which will probably be called a paradox. There exists in such a case a certain institution or law; let us say, for the sake of simplicity, a fence or gate erected across a road.
insight: Chesterton's fence — the principle of conservative humility. Reformed reform with Chesterton refuses iconoclasm for its own sake: before tearing down, understand what was being protected.

witness.quote: In the matter of reforming things, as distinct from deforming them, there

ref: What's Wrong with the World (1910), Part I, ch. 5
text: The Christian ideal has not been tried and found wanting. It has been found difficult; and left untried.
insight: Chesterton's diagnostic for cultural Christianity. Reformed self-criticism reads with Chesterton — most modern dismissals of Christianity are dismissals of a Christianity never actually attempted.

witness.quote: The Christian ideal has not been tried and found wanting. It has

ref: The God Who Is There (1968), ch. 1
text: The present chasm between the generations has been brought about almost entirely by a change in the concept of truth.
insight: The opening sentence of Schaeffer's first book, and still his most useful diagnosis. Before arguing about God with anyone, ask what they mean by 'true'; if truth has become a feeling, no amount of evidence will land.

witness.quote: The present chasm between the generations has been brought about

ref: He Is There and He Is Not Silent (1972), Introduction
text: The infinite-personal God is there, but also he is not silent; that changes the whole world.
insight: Schaeffer's whole title in one clause. A God who exists but never speaks leaves us guessing about everything that matters; a God who has spoken means metaphysics, morals and knowledge all have a floor under them.

witness.work: He Is There and He Is Not Silent
witness.quote: The infinite-personal God is there, but also he is not silent

ref: The Mark of the Christian (1970), closing section
text: Love—and the unity it attests to—is the mark Christ gave Christians to wear before the world. Only with this mark may the world know that Christians are indeed Christians and that Jesus was sent by the Father.
insight: Schaeffer's reading of John 13:35 and 17:21: Jesus handed the world the right to judge our claims by our love for one another. Doctrinal precision without visible love does not merely look bad; it forfeits the apologetic Christ himself appointed.

witness.quote: is the mark Christ gave Christians to wear before the world

text: The Christian life, true spirituality, can never have a mechanical solution. The real solution is being cast up into the moment-by-moment communion, personal communion, with God himself, and letting Christ's truth flow through me through the agency of the Holy Spirit.
insight: Schaeffer wrote this after a crisis in which technique had failed him. Sanctification is not a procedure to run but a Person to stay in communion with, moment by moment, and the Spirit does the flowing.

witness.quote: The Christian life, true spirituality, can never have a mechanical solution

text: The essence of sin is man substituting himself for God, while the essence of salvation is God substituting himself for man.
insight: Stott's chiasmus on substitution. Reformed atonement with Stott reads the cross as the precise inverse of the fall — man's substitution undone by God's, with mathematical symmetry.

witness.quote: essence of sin is man substituting himself for God

text: Essentially Christianity is Christ. The person and work of Christ are the rock upon which the Christian religion is built.
insight: Stott's catechetical compression. Reformed proclamation with Stott centers Christology — without the Person, the religion has lost its rock.

witness.quote: The person and work of Christ are the rock upon which the Christian religion is built

text: A true sermon bridges the gulf between the biblical and the modern worlds, and must be equally earthed in both.
insight: Stott's homiletical metaphor. Reformed preaching with Stott refuses the false binary — neither marooned in the ancient world nor adrift in the contemporary one; the bridge spans both.

witness.quote: A true sermon bridges the gulf between the biblical and the modern worlds

text: For the church lies at the very centre of the eternal purpose of God. It is not a divine afterthought. It is not an accident of history.
insight: Stott's lifelong conviction, set down at eighty-six. Low views of the church usually come from treating it as a means to individual salvation; Scripture treats it as the goal God had in mind before history began.

witness.quote: For the church lies at the very centre of the eternal purpose of God

ref: The Knowledge of the Holy (1961), ch. 1
text: What comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us.
insight: Tozer's opening sentence — the inverse of every secular anthropology. Reformed theology proper with Tozer reads our God-thoughts as the diagnostic of who we are.

witness.quote: What comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us

ref: The Divine Conquest (1950; reissued as God's Pursuit of Man), ch. 1
text: It is well that we accept the hard truth now: the man who would know God must give time to Him.
insight: Tozer's pastoral arithmetic. Reformed devotion with Tozer reads relational depth as time-bound — knowing God is no different from any other knowing, in that it cannot be rushed.

witness.quote: the man who would know God must give time to Him

text: He waits to be wanted. Too bad that with many of us He waits so long, so very long, in vain.
insight: Tozer's diagnosis of a cold church is not bad doctrine but absent desire. God manifests himself to those who want him, and complacency is the one thing that keeps him waiting; the cure is to start wanting.

witness.quote: He waits to be wanted

ref: The Root of the Righteous (1955), 'Praise God for the Furnace'
text: It is doubtful whether God can bless a man greatly until He has hurt him deeply.
insight: Tozer's hard pastoral observation. Reformed providence with Tozer reads wounding as preparation — not punitive, but emptying, so that grace has somewhere to go.

witness.quote: It is doubtful whether God can bless a man greatly until He has hurt him deeply

text: Faith does not eliminate questions. But faith knows where to take them.
insight: Elliot, writing Amy Carmichael's life, on what faith does with the unanswerable. It is not the absence of questions but the habit of carrying them to God rather than away from him, which is what Job and the psalmists did.

witness.quote: Faith does not eliminate questions. But faith knows where to take them

text: If I belittle those whom I am called to serve, talk of their weak points in contrast perhaps with what I think of as my strong points... then I know nothing of Calvary love.
insight: Carmichael's diagnostic for missionary pride. Reformed sanctification reads with Carmichael — knowing Calvary love is incompatible with treating others as less; the cross levels the field.

witness.quote: then I know nothing of Calvary love

text: Do not be discouraged; He is not discouraged. He Who has begun a good work in us will go on to perfect it.
insight: Carmichael's note to her Dohnavur family on the moment self is noticed again. Discouragement over our slowness assumes the work depends on us; Philippians 1:6 says the one who started it will finish it, and he has not lost heart.

witness.quote: Do not be discouraged; He is not discouraged

ref: The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life (1875), ch. 4
text: To sum up, then: in order to enter into this blessed interior life of rest and triumph, you have two steps to take: first, entire abandonment; and second, absolute faith.
insight: Two steps, and neither is a technique: give yourself up, and believe God. Smith's whole book is an argument that the second is as much a duty as the first.

witness.work: The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life
witness.quote: To sum up, then: in order to enter into this blessed interior

ref: The God of All Comfort (1906), ch. 17
text: The last and greatest lesson that the soul has to learn is the fact that God, and God alone, is enough for all its needs. This is the lesson that all His dealings with us are meant to teach; and this is the crowning discovery of our whole Christian life. God is enough!
insight: Smith ends her book where the psalmist begins: God alone. Every providence, kind or hard, is teaching the same one sentence, and it is the last lesson because it is the hardest to believe.

witness.quote: The last and greatest lesson that the soul has to learn is

text: Trying to do the Lord's work in your own strength is the most confusing, exhausting, and tedious of all work.
insight: Ten Boom on misplaced effort. Reformed vocational theology reads with her — there is a Christian fatigue that is not faithful but evidence of self-reliance; the cure is the Person, not more effort.

witness.quote: Lord's work in your own strength is the most confusing

ref: Letter to John Wesley, 8 June 1725 (in Adam Clarke, Memoirs of the Wesley Family)
text: Whatever weakens your reason, impairs the tenderness of your conscience, obscures your sense of God, or takes off the relish of spiritual things; in short, whatever increases the strength and authority of your body over your mind, that thing is sin to you, however innocent it may be in itself.
insight: Susanna's pastoral letter to her son. Reformed catechesis reads sin functionally with Susanna — anything that dulls the soul's God-ward instincts is sin, regardless of cultural permission.

witness.quote: Whatever weakens your reason, impairs the tenderness of your conscience, obscures your

ref: When God Weeps (1997, with Steve Estes), Part 2
text: God permits what he hates to achieve what he loves.
insight: The sentence Steve Estes first gave Joni at nineteen, when she was newly paralysed, and which she and Estes later wrote into this book. Permission is real, so God is not the author of evil; purpose is real, so nothing he permits is pointless.

witness.quote: God permits what he hates to achieve what he loves

ref: A Step Further (1978, with Steve Estes), Part 2
text: Christians are to pray for healing, but they are not necessarily to think something is wrong if God refuses the request.
insight: Joni wrote this a decade after praying for healing that did not come. The command to ask is real and so is God's freedom to say no; a refused request is not evidence of weak faith or hidden sin, as Paul learned with his thorn.

witness.quote: Christians are to pray for healing, but they are not necessarily

text: Q. What is the chief end of man? A. Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever.
insight: Man's chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy him for ever: one end with two sides, and neither is the lesser. Whatever else fills your hours, you were made to give him glory and to find your gladness in him.

text: Q. What rule hath God given to direct us how we may glorify and enjoy him? A. The Word of God, which is contained in the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, is the only rule to direct us how we may glorify and enjoy him.
insight: Carpenters keep one true rule on the bench so every cut can be checked against it. Scripture is named the only rule for glorifying and enjoying God, so when your gut and the page disagree, measure your gut by the page.

text: Q. What do the Scriptures principally teach? A. The Scriptures principally teach what man is to believe concerning God, and what duty God requires of man.
insight: Which half do you lean on: what to believe about God, or what duty he requires? Scripture principally teaches both, and a faith that never obeys or an obedience that never trusts is missing half of what you were given to read.

text: Q. What is God? A. God is a Spirit, infinite, eternal, and unchangeable in his being, wisdom, power, holiness, justice, goodness, and truth.
insight: Definitions usually shrink what they describe, yet this one grows: every perfection of God, from wisdom to truth, is infinite, eternal, and unchangeable. The God who meets you in the school pickup line is the same God, undiminished, who has always been.

text: Q. Are there more Gods than one? A. There is but one only, the living and true God.
insight: Canaan was crowded with gods of rain, harvest, and war when Israel learned there is but one only, the living and true God. Your neighborhood keeps its own crowded shelf, and every rival on it is lifeless beside the God who hears you.

text: Q. How many persons are there in the Godhead? A. There are three persons in the Godhead; the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost; and these three are one God, the same in substance, equal in power and glory.
insight: Notice 'equal in power and glory': the Son and the Spirit are never junior partners in the Godhead. When you pray to the Father through the Son by the Spirit, you are addressing one God, fully present in each person.

text: Q. What are the decrees of God? A. The decrees of God are, his eternal purpose, according to the counsel of his will, whereby, for his own glory, he hath foreordained whatsoever comes to pass.
insight: God's decrees are his eternal purpose, by which he foreordained whatsoever comes to pass, according to the counsel of his will and for his own glory. If a diagnosis or a layoff has come to you, it came within the purpose of a wise and holy God, and you can ask him for grace to glorify him in it.

text: Q. How doth God execute his decrees? A. God executeth his decrees in the works of creation and providence.
insight: What God purposed in eternity he carries out in time, by making the world and by governing it. His plan does not sit apart from the ordinary events of your life; it is worked out through them, so look for his wisdom in what he has made and in what he does.

text: Q. What is the work of creation? A. The work of creation is, God's making all things of nothing, by the word of his power, in the space of six days, and all very good.
insight: Imagine nothing at all, and then a word, and then light, land, and living things, every one of them very good. The world you walk through this afternoon was spoken out of nothing, so thank its Maker for its goodness even where sin has scarred it.

text: Q. How did God create man? A. God created man male and female, after his own image, in knowledge, righteousness, and holiness, with dominion over the creatures.
insight: Productivity is how most of us price a person, but God made man male and female after his own image before either had done a day's work. Your worth came with the image, and so did the worth of the coworker you find hardest to like.

text: Q. What are God's works of providence? A. God's works of providence are, his most holy, wise, and powerful preserving and governing all his creatures, and all their actions.
insight: Sparrows, stock markets, and the stranger who merges in front of you are all among the creatures and actions God preserves and governs. Nothing that reaches you wanders in from outside his most holy, wise, and powerful care.

text: Q. What special act of providence did God exercise toward man in the estate wherein he was created? A. When God had created man, he entered into a covenant of life with him, upon condition of perfect obedience; forbidding him to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, upon pain of death.
insight: Before Adam had sinned, God made a covenant of life with him on condition of perfect obedience, with death threatened for eating from one forbidden tree. Adam broke those terms, and only Christ has fulfilled them, so look to him who obeyed perfectly and bore the penalty for all who trust him.

text: Q. Did our first parents continue in the estate wherein they were created? A. Our first parents, being left to the freedom of their own will, fell from the estate wherein they were created, by sinning against God.
insight: Confidence in your own willpower feels safe until the night it fails. Our first parents, left to the freedom of their own will, fell from a sinless state, so ask God for grace before temptation comes knocking on your door.

text: Q. What is sin? A. Sin is any want of conformity unto, or transgression of, the law of God.
insight: Two failures fit inside one definition: falling short of God's law and stepping across it. You may cross no bright line for days on end, yet the kindness you withheld counts all the same, which is why you need a Savior more than a better scorecard.

text: Q. What was the sin whereby our first parents fell from the estate wherein they were created? A. The sin whereby our first parents fell from the estate wherein they were created, was their eating the forbidden fruit.
insight: Eating what was forbidden sounds almost ordinary, but underneath it lay a deeper unbelief: doubting God's word before ever reaching for the fruit. Your smaller disobediences carry that same root, so ask what you disbelieved before you ask what you did.

text: Q. Did all mankind fall in Adam's first transgression? A. The covenant being made with Adam, not only for himself, but for his posterity; all mankind, descending from him by ordinary generation, sinned in him, and fell with him, in his first transgression.
insight: Consider 'not only for himself, but for his posterity': Adam stood as a covenant head, and you fell with him before you had a name. That same logic of representation is how Christ's obedience can be counted as yours.

text: Q. Into what estate did the fall bring mankind? A. The fall brought mankind into an estate of sin and misery.
insight: Grief can make you wonder what you did to deserve it. Adam's fall brought all mankind into an estate of sin and misery, so your sorrow belongs to a broken world as a whole, and you can bring it to Christ without first tracing it to one sin of your own.

text: Q. Wherein consists the sinfulness of that estate whereinto man fell? A. The sinfulness of that estate whereinto man fell, consists in the guilt of Adam's first sin, the want of original righteousness, and the corruption of his whole nature, which is commonly called original sin; together with all actual transgressions which proceed from it.
insight: Roots decide the fruit long before the first bud shows, and original sin names three roots at once: Adam's guilt, lost righteousness, and a corrupted nature. When you pray about your worst habit, pray about the root too.

text: Q. What is the misery of that estate whereinto man fell? A. All mankind by their fall lost communion with God, are under his wrath and curse, and so made liable to all miseries in this life, to death itself, and to the pains of hell for ever.
insight: The first misery named is lost communion with God, ahead of wrath, curse, death, and hell, and the other miseries follow from it. The deepest remedy offered to you is the one Christ brings: peace with God and access to him again.

text: Q. Did God leave all mankind to perish in the estate of sin and misery? A. God having, out of his mere good pleasure, from all eternity, elected some to everlasting life did enter into a covenant of grace, to deliver them out of the estate of sin and misery, and to bring them into an estate of salvation by a Redeemer.
insight: Nothing in you prompted it: 'out of his mere good pleasure' God elected some to everlasting life and made a covenant to deliver them. When you doubt he could want you, remember that his choice never rested on what he saw in you first.

text: Q. Who is the Redeemer of God's elect? A. The only Redeemer of God's elect is the Lord Jesus Christ, who, being the eternal Son of God, became man and so was, and continueth to be, God and man in two distinct natures, and one person, forever.
insight: Could a Redeemer who was only God die in your place if you trust him, or one who was only man carry the weight of your sin? The only Redeemer is both, two natures in one person forever, so you pray to someone who has felt your weakness and has power over it.

text: Q. How did Christ, being the Son of God, become man? A. Christ, the Son of God, became man, by taking to himself a true body, and a reasonable soul, being conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost, in the womb of the virgin Mary, and born of her yet without sin.
insight: Picture Mary holding a newborn with a true body and a reasonable soul, as human as any child in the room and without sin. When your body tires or your mind clouds, you are cared for by a Savior who took both on and kept them pure.

text: Q. What offices doth Christ execute as our Redeemer? A. Christ, as our Redeemer, executeth the offices of a prophet, of a priest, and of a king, both in his estate of humiliation and exaltation.
insight: Confused, guilty, and afraid are three ways you can wake up on any given morning, and Christ meets each one: as prophet he tells you the truth, as priest he answers for your guilt, and as king he rules and defends you.

text: Q. How doth Christ execute the office of a prophet? A. Christ executeth the office of a prophet, in revealing to us, by his Word and Spirit the will of God for our salvation.
insight: Information alone never saved anyone; Christ reveals the will of God by his Word and Spirit together, so the truth reaches the heart as well as the head. Open your Bible asking the Spirit to make its words land on you.

text: Q. How doth Christ execute the office of a priest? A. Christ executeth the office of a priest, in his once offering up of himself a sacrifice to satisfy divine justice, and reconcile us to God; and in making continual intercession for us.
insight: Who is speaking for you right now? Christ offered himself once to satisfy divine justice and makes continual intercession for you, so on your worst prayer day an advocate is already pleading your case before the Father.

text: Q. How doth Christ execute the office of a king? A. Christ executeth the office of a king, in subduing us to himself, in ruling and defending us, and in restraining and conquering all his and our enemies.
insight: Bring your fiercest temptation to Christ as to a King who subdues, rules, defends, restrains, and conquers. Those verbs belong to someone fighting on your side, and the enemies he conquers include the ones living in your own heart.

text: Q. Wherein did Christ's humiliation consist? A. Christ's humiliation consisted in his being born, and that in a low condition, made under the law, undergoing the miseries of this life, the wrath of God, and the cursed death of the cross; in being buried, and continuing under the power of death for a time.
insight: Manger to tomb, Christ walked every step of humiliation: a low birth, the law's demands, the miseries of this life, God's wrath, the curse of the cross, and burial. Whatever low place you have come to, he has been lower, and he went there for sinners like you.

text: Q. Wherein consisteth Christ's exaltation? A. Christ's exaltation consisteth in his rising again from the dead on the third day, in ascending up into heaven, in sitting at the right hand of God the Father, and in coming to judge the world at the last day.
insight: Discouragement tells you the world has no one in charge. Christ rose on the third day, ascended, and sits at the Father's right hand, and he is coming to judge; you can face a hard week knowing the throne is occupied.

text: Q. How are we made partakers of the redemption purchased by Christ? A. We are made partakers of the redemption purchased by Christ, by the effectual application of it to us by his Holy Spirit.
insight: Accomplished at the cross and applied by the Spirit: redemption purchased by Christ reaches you through the Spirit's effectual work. If you believe, thank the Spirit who brought Christ's finished work home to you, and pray for friends who have yet to receive it.

text: Q. How doth the Spirit apply to us the redemption purchased by Christ? A. The Spirit applieth to us the redemption purchased by Christ, by working faith in us, and thereby uniting us to Christ in our effectual calling.
insight: Effort feels like the way into Christ, but the Spirit applies redemption by working faith in you and so uniting you to him. When your grip on Christ feels weak, you can rest in the Spirit who does the joining.

text: Q. What is effectual calling? A. Effectual calling is the work of God's Spirit, whereby, convincing us of our sin and misery, enlightening our minds in the knowledge of Christ, and renewing our wills, he doth persuade and enable us to embrace Jesus Christ, freely offered to us in the gospel.
insight: Effectual calling is the Spirit's work from start to finish: he convinces of sin and misery, enlightens the mind in the knowledge of Christ, and renews the will until a sinner embraces him. If you have embraced Christ, credit the Spirit, and if you have not, the Christ you hesitate over is freely offered to you in the gospel.

text: Q. What benefits do they that are effectually called partake of in this life? A. They that are effectually called do in this life partake of justification, adoption, and sanctification, and the several benefits which in this life do either accompany or flow from them.
insight: Gifts sometimes come in one box: justification, adoption, and sanctification belong to everyone effectually called, with their benefits flowing after. You cannot keep the pardon and send back the holiness, and you never have to earn the family.

text: Q. What is justification? A. Justification is an act of God's free grace, wherein he pardoneth all our sins, and accepteth us as righteous in his sight, only for the righteousness of Christ imputed to us, and received by faith alone.
insight: Pardon and acceptance are the two halves of justification: God not only cancels the charge against you but credits you with a righteousness that was never your own doing. Faith receives this gift; it does not earn a fraction of it.

text: Q. What is adoption? A. Adoption is an act of God's free grace, whereby we are received into the number, and have a right to all the privileges, of the sons of God.
insight: Orphans who are adopted get a name, a room, and a seat at the table; adoption by God's free grace gives a right to all the privileges of his sons. If you are in Christ, pray to him the way a child walks into a kitchen, expecting to be welcomed.

text: Q. What is sanctification? A. Sanctification is the work of God's free grace, whereby we are renewed in the whole man after the image of God, and are enabled more and more to die unto sin, and live unto righteousness.
insight: Frustration at your slow progress is common, and the wording helps: you are enabled 'more and more' to die unto sin. God renews the whole man by degrees, so measure your growth in years and keep asking him for the next step.

text: Q. What are the benefits which in this life do accompany or flow from justification, adoption, and sanctification? A. The benefits which in this life do accompany or flow from justification, adoption, and sanctification, are, assurance of God's love, peace of conscience, joy in the Holy Ghost, increase of grace, and perseverance therein to the end.
insight: Where do assurance, peace of conscience, and joy in the Holy Ghost come from? They flow from justification, adoption, and sanctification, so on a day when you feel none of them, look back to the pardon and sonship they grow from.

text: Q. What benefits do believers receive from Christ at death? A. The souls of believers are at their death made perfect in holiness, and do immediately pass into glory; and their bodies, being still united to Christ, do rest in their graves till the resurrection.
insight: Mourning a believer is real sorrow, and you need not hide it. Their soul has passed immediately into glory, and their body remains united to Christ in the grave until the resurrection, so you grieve with hope.

text: Q. What benefits do believers receive from Christ at the resurrection? A. At the resurrection, believers being raised up in glory, shall be openly acknowledged and acquitted in the day of judgment, and made perfectly blessed in the full enjoying of God to all eternity.
insight: Believers raised at the resurrection will be openly acknowledged and acquitted in the day of judgment, before everyone, and made perfectly blessed in the full enjoying of God. If you are in Christ, the verdict that matters most will be spoken aloud in your favor, and you can live toward that day with hope.

text: Q. What is the duty which God requireth of man? A. The duty which God requireth of man, is obedience to his revealed will.
insight: Guessing at God's secret plan can paralyze you, but the duty he requires is obedience to his revealed will. You can know what to do this week by reading what he has said, and leave the hidden things with him.

text: Q. What did God at first reveal to man for the rule of his obedience? A. The rule which God at first revealed to man for his obedience, was the moral law.
insight: Adam knew the moral law before Sinai put it on tablets of stone; it was the rule God revealed to man at first. When you feel its weight in your conscience, you are meeting a law as old as humanity and as current as your next conversation.

text: Q. Wherein is the moral law summarily comprehended? A. The moral law is summarily comprehended in the ten commandments.
insight: Compact and complete, the ten commandments are a summary of the whole moral law, short enough to learn by heart. Know them well enough to recite in a waiting room, and you will carry a map of everything you owe God and your neighbor.

text: Q. What is the sum of the ten commandments? A. The sum of the ten commandments is, To love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul, with all our strength, and with all our mind; and our neighbour as ourselves.
insight: The ten commandments sum up as love for God with all your heart, soul, strength, and mind, and love for your neighbor as yourself. That sum exposes every duty done coldly, so ask whether your obedience has engaged your heart or only your calendar.

text: Q. What is the preface to the ten commandments? A. The preface to the ten commandments is in these words, I am the Lord thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.
insight: Israel heard 'I am the Lord thy God, which have brought thee out' before a single command, while the memory of Egypt was fresh. You also obey as someone already rescued, and that order keeps your duty from souring into a bargain.

text: Q. What doth the preface to the ten commandments teach us? A. The preface to the ten commandments teacheth us, That because God is the Lord, and our God, and Redeemer, therefore we are bound to keep all his commandments.
insight: The preface grounds obedience in three titles: God is the Lord, he is our God, and he is our Redeemer. Duty grows out of who he is and what he has done, so when a commandment feels heavy, look at the God who gave it before you weigh what it costs.

text: Q. Which is the first commandment? A. The first commandment is, Thou shalt have no other gods before me.
insight: Name the thing that most often outranks God in your thoughts, and hold it up against 'no other gods before me.' God does not ask for first place among many; he claims the only place, and he is kind to claim it.

text: Q. What is required in the first commandment? A. The first commandment requireth us to know and acknowledge God to be the only true God, and our God; and to worship and glorify him accordingly.
insight: Emptying your life of idols is only half the first commandment; it also requires you 'to know and acknowledge God' and to worship and glorify him accordingly. Fill the space you clear with prayer and praise offered to him by name.

text: Q. What is forbidden in the first commandment? A. The first commandment forbiddeth the denying, or not worshipping and glorifying the true God as God, and our God; and the giving of that worship and glory to any other, which is due to him alone.
insight: Pressure reveals who gets your worship, because fear pushes you to hand God's glory to whoever seems able to save you. The first commandment forbids giving that worship to any other, so when fear presses on you, run to him before anyone else.

text: Q. What are we specially taught by these words, 'before me', in the first commandment? A. These words, before me, in the first commandment teach us, that God, who seeth all things, taketh notice of, and is much displeased with, the sin of having any other God.
insight: The words 'before me' teach that God, who sees all things, takes notice of any other god and is much displeased with it. No rival you keep is hidden from him, so name what competes with him in your heart and confess it to him plainly.

text: Q. Which is the second commandment? A. The second commandment is, Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth: thou shalt not bow down thy self to them, nor serve them: for I the Lord thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me; and showing mercy unto thousands of them that love me, and keep my commandments.
insight: The second commandment forbids making images to bow down to, and God backs it with his jealousy: he visits iniquity on those who hate him and shows mercy to thousands who love him. He guards his own honor in how he is worshiped, so come to him on his terms and take both the warning and the mercy seriously.

text: Q. What is required in the second commandment? A. The second commandment requireth the receiving, observing, and keeping pure and entire, all such religious worship and ordinances as God hath appointed in his Word.
insight: Ask of Sunday's service what the second commandment asks: whether it receives, observes, and keeps pure the worship God appointed in his Word. You do not have to invent ways to please God; he has already told you how he wants to be met.

text: Q. What is forbidden in the second commandment? A. The second commandment forbiddeth the worshipping of God by images, or any other way not appointed in his Word.
