insight: The ban reaches past images to 'any other way not appointed in his Word,' so worship can be heartfelt and wrong in its form. Ask of any practice you bring to God whether Scripture appointed it, because a warm heart does not make an unappointed way acceptable.

text: Q. What are the reasons annexed to the second commandment? A. The reasons annexed to the second commandment are, God's sovereignty over us, his propriety in us, and the zeal he hath to his own worship.
insight: Whose are you? The reasons annexed to the second commandment answer with God's sovereignty over you, his propriety in you, and his zeal for his worship: three ways of saying you belong to him and he cares how you come.

text: Q. Which is the third commandment? A. The third commandment is, Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain; for the Lord will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.
insight: Careless talk about God can feel harmless when everyone around you does it, and the Lord says he will not hold such a speaker guiltless. Weigh your words about him the way you would weigh an oath in court.

text: Q. What is required in the third commandment? A. The third commandment requireth the holy and reverend use of God's names, titles, attributes, ordinances, Word, and works.
insight: Respect for God covers more than his name: his titles, attributes, ordinances, Word, and works all call for holy and reverend use. Familiarity with church talk can make you casual, so handle Scripture and worship like someone standing in his presence.

text: Q. What is forbidden in the third commandment? A. The third commandment forbiddeth all profaning or abusing of anything whereby God maketh himself known.
insight: The ban covers profaning or abusing anything by which God makes himself known, and that includes using his Word or his worship for your own ends. Quoting Scripture to win an argument or to look devout can abuse it as surely as mockery does, so watch the motives behind your religious words.

text: Q. What is the reason annexed to the third commandment? A. The reason annexed to the third commandment is, that however the breakers of this commandment may escape punishment from men, yet the Lord our God will not suffer them to escape his righteous judgment.
insight: Envy flares when someone breaks every rule and seems to pay nothing. Those who profane God's name may escape punishment from men, yet God will not let them escape his righteous judgment, so you can leave justice to him and guard your own tongue.

text: Q. Which is the fourth commandment? A. The fourth commandment is, Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labor, and do all thy work; but the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the Lord blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it.
insight: Sinai gave Israel the fourth commandment in writing, yet its reason reaches back to creation: in six days the Lord made heaven and earth and rested the seventh. Your weekly rest follows a rhythm God set in the world's first week, long before any tablet of stone.

text: Q. What is required in the fourth commandment? A. The fourth commandment requireth the keeping holy to God such set times as he hath appointed in his Word; expressly one whole day in seven, to be a holy sabbath to himself.
insight: God requires keeping holy the set times he has appointed in his Word, expressly one whole day in seven, to be a holy sabbath to himself. That day belongs to him before it belongs to your rest, so ask how its hours can be given to him in worship.

text: Q. Which day of the seven hath God appointed to be the weekly sabbath? A. From the beginning of the world to the resurrection of Christ, God appointed the seventh day of the week to be the weekly sabbath; and the first day of the week ever since, to continue to the end of the world, which is the Christian sabbath.
insight: God appointed the seventh day as the sabbath from creation to Christ's resurrection, and from then on the first day of the week, to continue to the end of the world. The change came by his appointment, so when you keep the Lord's Day you honor both a finished creation and a risen Redeemer.

text: Q. How is the sabbath to be sanctified? A. The sabbath is to be sanctified by a holy resting all that day, even from such worldly employments and recreations as are lawful on other days; and spending the whole time in the public and private exercises of God's worship, except so much as is to be taken up in the works of necessity and mercy.
insight: Sanctifying the sabbath means laying down even lawful weekday work and recreation to spend the day in worship, with room made only for real necessity and mercy. Plan your Saturday chores early enough that Sunday can stay free for worship and for helping whoever truly needs it.

text: Q. What is forbidden in the fourth commandment? A. The fourth commandment forbiddeth the omission or careless performance of the duties required, and the profaning the day by idleness, or doing that which is in itself sinful, or by unnecessary thoughts, words, or works, about our worldly employments or recreations.
insight: Boredom on a Sunday afternoon can pass for rest, yet idleness profanes the day as surely as worldly busyness does. Plan something that feeds you: a psalm read aloud, a visit to someone lonely, a long talk about the sermon, and you will keep the day holy.

text: Q. What are the reasons annexed to the fourth commandment? A. The reasons annexed to the fourth commandment are, God's allowing us six days of the week for our own employments, his challenging a special propriety in the seventh, his own example, and his blessing the sabbath day.
insight: The fourth commandment comes with four reasons: six days allowed for your own work, a special claim on the seventh, God's own example in resting, and his blessing on the sabbath day. A God who gives six days and blesses the seventh is no grudging master, so receive his day as a gift he has blessed.

text: Q. Which is the fifth commandment? A. The fifth commandment is, Honour thy father and thy mother; that thy days may be long upon the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee.
insight: The fifth commandment carries a promise, 'that thy days may be long upon the land,' and Paul calls it the first commandment with a promise in Ephesians 6. God has attached good to honoring father and mother, so you can honor yours trusting that he blesses the obedience, even when it costs you.

text: Q. What is required in the fifth commandment? A. The fifth commandment requireth the preserving the honor, and performing the duties, belonging to everyone in their several places and relations, as superiors, inferiors, or equals.
insight: Whom do you owe honor to besides your parents? The fifth commandment reaches superiors, inferiors, and equals alike, so the intern, the boss, and the friend down the hall each hold a place you are called to respect.

text: Q. What is forbidden in the fifth commandment? A. The fifth commandment forbiddeth the neglecting of, or doing anything against, the honor and duty which belongeth to everyone in their several places and relations.
insight: Indifference feels safer than conflict, yet neglecting the honor due to someone breaks the fifth commandment as surely as insulting them. If you have gone quiet toward an aging parent or a struggling colleague, you can reach out and give them the honor their place deserves.

text: Q. What is the reason annexed to the fifth commandment? A. The reason annexed to the fifth commandment is, a promise of long life and prosperity (as far as it shall serve for God's glory and their own good) to all such as keep this commandment.
insight: Parentheses carry the weight: long life and prosperity are promised '(as far as it shall serve for God's glory and their own good).' If you honor your parents and face a short or hard road, you may trust that God kept the promise in the form that served you best.

text: Q. Which is the sixth commandment? A. The sixth commandment is, Thou shalt not kill.
insight: Faces on the subway, in the checkout line, and at your dinner table all bear God's image, and that is why he says, Thou shalt not kill. Every person you pass carries a life God guards, so treat each one as someone worth protecting.

text: Q. What is required in the sixth commandment? A. The sixth commandment requireth all lawful endeavors to preserve our own life, and the life of others.
insight: Check on the neighbor who has gone silent, wear the seatbelt, take the medicine: the sixth commandment requires all lawful endeavors to preserve your own life and the lives of others. You obey it in small acts of care long before you are tempted to harm anyone.

text: Q. What is forbidden in the sixth commandment? A. The sixth commandment forbiddeth the taking away of our own life, or the life of our neighbour, unjustly, or whatsoever tendeth thereunto.
insight: The sixth commandment forbids taking our own life or a neighbour's unjustly, and also whatsoever tends that way, so neglect, rage, and reckless endangerment fall under it as well. Ask where anger or carelessness in you is moving toward harm, and deal with it while it is small.

text: Q. Which is the seventh commandment? A. The seventh commandment is, Thou shalt not commit adultery.
insight: The seventh commandment guards the marriage bed, and Jesus carried it into the heart when he said that looking with lust is adultery already committed. Married or single, you keep it in small choices about where your eyes, your words, and your time go.

text: Q. What is required in the seventh commandment? A. The seventh commandment requireth the preservation of our own and our neighbour's chastity, in heart, speech, and behavior.
insight: Mind, mouth, and body all fall under this commandment's positive demand, which means chastity is never only about what you do with your body. Guard your imagination and your words as carefully as you guard your actions.

text: Q. What is forbidden in the seventh commandment? A. The seventh commandment forbiddeth all unchaste thoughts, words, and actions.
insight: Unchaste thoughts head the list, beside words and actions, as things forbidden in themselves. A fantasy you never act on is already a breach of the seventh commandment, and you may confess it and seek cleansing in Christ's blood the moment you notice it.

text: Q. Which is the eighth commandment? A. The eighth commandment is, Thou shalt not steal.
insight: Four words, Thou shalt not steal, stand guard over what God has entrusted to each of your neighbors. Before you take anything, from a shop shelf to an employer's hours, ask whether it is truly yours to take.

text: Q. What is required in the eighth commandment? A. The eighth commandment requireth the lawful procuring and furthering the wealth and outward estate of ourselves and others.
insight: Two small words at the end, “and others,” keep God's concern for honest earning from stopping at your own paycheck. When you work, bargain, or budget this week, count your neighbor's flourishing as part of the job.

text: Q. What is forbidden in the eighth commandment? A. The eighth commandment forbiddeth whatsoever doth, or may, unjustly hinder our own, or our neighbour's, wealth or outward estate.
insight: Fraud, a broken promise on a debt, and every scheme that quietly drains a neighbor's estate fall under the same commandment as outright theft. Guard someone else's resources as carefully as you guard your own.

text: Q. Which is the ninth commandment? A. The ninth commandment is, Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
insight: Words spoken about someone else's character carry real weight, and the ninth commandment treats a lie about your neighbor as an assault on him. Speak of others the way you would want spoken of you.

text: Q. What is required in the ninth commandment? A. The ninth commandment requireth the maintaining and promoting of truth between man and man, and of our own and our neighbour's good name, especially in witness bearing.
insight: Fear of an awkward moment keeps many of us quiet when a friend's name is being picked apart over lunch. God asks you to promote your neighbor's good name, so speak up for the absent person, especially when your testimony carries weight.

text: Q. What is forbidden in the ninth commandment? A. The ninth commandment forbiddeth whatsoever is prejudicial to truth, or injurious to our own, or our neighbour's, good name.
insight: Gossip, exaggeration, and silence when the truth would help a neighbor's name all fall under what this commandment forbids. Ask whether your words build a name up or quietly wear it down.

text: Q. Which is the tenth commandment? A. The tenth commandment is, Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor anything that is thy neighbour's.
insight: Scroll past a friend's new kitchen or easy marriage and the old list comes alive: house, wife, ox, anything that is his. God names your wanting before it ever reaches your hands, so bring that ache to him the moment you feel it.

text: Q. What is required in the tenth commandment? A. The tenth commandment requireth full contentment with our own condition, with a right and charitable frame of spirit toward our neighbour, and all that is his.
insight: Godly contentment is a settled gladness in the portion God has handed you, joined to a warm heart toward whatever he has handed your neighbor. The two belong together; you cannot resent his lot and rest in your own.

text: Q. What is forbidden in the tenth commandment? A. The tenth commandment forbiddeth all discontentment with our own estate, envying or grieving at the good of our neighbour, and all inordinate motions and affections to anything that is his.
insight: When a coworker gets the promotion and something in you sours, that grief at another's good is named as sin to confess. Bring it to God quickly, and ask him for the harder grace of rejoicing with the one who rejoices.

text: Q. Is any man able perfectly to keep the commandments of God? A. No mere man, since the fall, is able in this life perfectly to keep the commandments of God, but doth daily break them in thought, word, and deed.
insight: Which did you break first this morning: a thought, a word, or a deed? Naming those three spheres makes confession concrete, so walk back through your day with them and bring each specific failure to the Christ who kept the law for you.

text: Q. Are all transgressions of the law equally heinous? A. Some sins in themselves, and by reason of several aggravations, are more heinous in the sight of God than others.
insight: Flattening all sins into one gray pile can feel humble, yet it blurs what God sees clearly: some sins, by their aggravations, weigh more in his sight. Ask which of yours carry that extra weight, and repent of those by name.

text: Q. What doth every sin deserve? A. Every sin deserveth God's wrath and curse, both in this life, and that which is to come.
insight: Every sin deserves God's wrath and curse, both in this life and in the life to come, so no sin is too small to matter. Let the size of the debt teach you the size of the mercy, and bring even the sins you shrug off to Christ.

text: Q. What doth God require of us, that we may escape his wrath and curse, due to us for sin? A. To escape the wrath and curse of God, due to us for sin, God requireth of us faith in Jesus Christ, repentance unto life, with the diligent use of all the outward means whereby Christ communicateth to us the benefits of redemption.
insight: Keep showing up to the plain things: the sermon, the table, the prayers before bed. Alongside faith and repentance, God calls you to “the diligent use” of outward means, because that is where Christ hands you the benefits of his redemption.

text: Q. What is faith in Jesus Christ? A. Faith in Jesus Christ is a saving grace, whereby we receive and rest upon him alone for salvation, as he is offered to us in the gospel.
insight: Picture a tired swimmer who stops thrashing and lets the lifeguard carry him to shore. To “receive and rest upon” Christ is that kind of surrender, and you can practice it every time guilt tempts you to start swimming for yourself again.

text: Q. What is repentance unto life? A. Repentance unto life is a saving grace, whereby a sinner, out of a true sense of his sin, and apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ, doth, with grief and hatred of his sin, turn from it unto God, with full purpose of, and endeavour after, new obedience.
insight: Genuine repentance has four moving parts: seeing your sin truly, grasping God's mercy in Christ, grieving over and hating the sin, and turning to God with a real purpose of new obedience. If you only feel bad, ask him for the rest.

text: Q. What are the outward and ordinary means whereby Christ communicateth to us the benefits of redemption? A. The outward and ordinary means whereby Christ communicateth to us the benefits of redemption are, his ordinances, especially the Word, sacraments, and prayer; all which are made effectual to the elect for salvation.
insight: Word, sacraments, and prayer are the ordinary channels of Christ's benefits, and he makes them effectual to the elect for salvation. Come to them asking him to do that work in you, since the power lies with him and no sermon or prayer saves by its own force.

text: Q. How is the Word made effectual to salvation? A. The Spirit of God maketh the reading, but especially the preaching of the Word, an effectual means of convincing and converting sinners, and of building them up in holiness and comfort, through faith, unto salvation.
insight: Boredom in the pew is a real temptation when the sermon seems plain and the preacher unremarkable. The Spirit makes preaching effectual for convicting, converting, and building up, so come to next Sunday's sermon asking him to do that work in you.

text: Q. How is the Word to be read and heard, that it may become effectual to salvation? A. That the Word may become effectual to salvation, we must attend thereunto with diligence, preparation, and prayer; receive it with faith and love, lay it up in our hearts, and practice it in our lives.
insight: Three verbs trail after the reading: receive it with faith and love, “lay it up in our hearts,” and practice it. Before you close your Bible, choose one line to carry into the afternoon and one way to obey it before dinner.

text: Q. How do the sacraments become effectual means of salvation? A. The sacraments become effectual means of salvation, not from any virtue in them, or in him that doth administer them; but only by the blessing of Christ, and the working of his Spirit in them that by faith receive them.
insight: A sacrament's power lies in Christ's blessing and his Spirit working in those who receive by faith, so a minister's gifts or failings neither add to it nor take from it. Receive it from a lawfully called minister without fretting over his eloquence, and look past the man to the Lord.

text: Q. What is a sacrament? A. A sacrament is an holy ordinance instituted by Christ; wherein, by sensible signs, Christ, and the benefits of the new covenant, are represented, sealed, and applied to believers.
insight: Water, bread, and wine are “sensible signs,” things your senses can grasp, because God knows you believe more readily with something to see and taste. They represent, seal, and apply Christ to you, so receive them as his tangible promise.

text: Q. Which are the sacraments of the New Testament? A. The sacraments of the New Testament are, Baptism, and the Lord's Supper.
insight: Only two ordinances of the New Testament bear the name of sacrament, baptism and the Lord's Supper, because these alone were instituted by Christ as signs and seals of his covenant. Be wary of any rite that claims to add to what he appointed, and prize the two he gave.

text: Q. What is Baptism? A. Baptism is a sacrament, wherein the washing with water in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, doth signify and seal our ingrafting into Christ, and partaking of the benefits of the covenant of grace, and our engagement to be the Lord's.
insight: Think of a branch bound into a new tree, its old sap giving way to new life. Baptism signs and seals that ingrafting into Christ and marks you as the Lord's, so when you doubt whose you are, remember the water once put on you.

text: Q. To whom is Baptism to be administered? A. Baptism is not to be administered to any that are out of the visible church, till they profess their faith in Christ, and obedience to him; but the infants of such as are members of the visible church are to be baptized.
insight: Covenant children receive baptism because God's promise has always run “to you and to your children,” while an outsider waits until he professes faith. If you are a parent in the church, raise your children as ones who already bear the Lord's name.

text: Q. What is the Lord's Supper? A. The Lord's Supper is a sacrament, wherein, by giving and receiving bread and wine, according to Christ's appointment, his death is showed forth; and the worthy receivers are, not after a corporal and carnal manner, but by faith, made partakers of his body and blood, with all his benefits, to their spiritual nourishment, and growth in grace.
insight: Hungry, weary believers are the very guests this meal was set for. By faith you truly feed on Christ's body and blood, with all his benefits, so bring your spiritual exhaustion to the table and expect to be nourished for the week ahead.

text: Q. What is required for the worthy receiving of the Lord's Supper? A. It is required of them that would worthily partake of the Lord's Supper, that they examine themselves of their knowledge to discern the Lord's body, of their faith to feed upon him, of their repentance, love, and new obedience; lest, coming unworthily, they eat and drink judgment to themselves.
insight: Before the Supper, examine five things: your knowledge to discern the Lord's body, your faith to feed on him, and your repentance, love, and new obedience. The warning about eating and drinking judgment is meant in earnest, so if those questions trouble you, talk with a pastor before you come.

text: Q. What is prayer? A. Prayer is an offering up of our desires unto God, for things agreeable to his will, in the name of Christ, with confession of our sins, and thankful acknowledgement of his mercies.
insight: Offer God what you truly want, shaped to his will and brought in Christ's name, and fold in confession of sins and thanks for mercies. When your prayers go stiff and formal, begin with one honest desire and one specific thanks.

text: Q. What rule hath God given for our direction in prayer? A. The whole Word of God is of use to direct us in prayer; but the special rule of direction is that form of prayer which Christ taught his disciples, commonly called The Lord's Prayer.
insight: That single prayer Jesus taught becomes the pattern for every other prayer, so when you don't know what to ask, you already have a template. Pray it slowly instead of reciting it quickly.

text: Q. What doth the preface of the Lord's Prayer teach us? A. The preface of the Lord's Prayer, which is, Our Father which art in heaven, teacheth us to draw near to God with all holy reverence and confidence, as children to a father, able and ready to help us; and that we should pray with and for others.
insight: Before a single request, Jesus puts “Our Father” in your mouth. “Our” pulls your neighbors into the prayer, and “Father” gives you a child's confidence that he is able and ready to help, so pray with both in view.

text: Q. What do we pray for in the first petition? A. In the first petition, which is, Hallowed be thy name, we pray, that God would enable us, and others, to glorify him in all that whereby he maketh himself known; and that he would dispose all things to his own glory.
insight: Hallowing God's name means asking him to enable you and others to glorify him in all by which he makes himself known, and to order all things to his own glory. When you read Scripture or look at what he has made, pray to honor what he shows you of himself.

text: Q. What do we pray for in the second petition? A. In the second petition, which is, Thy kingdom come, we pray, that Satan's kingdom may be destroyed; and that the kingdom of grace may be advanced, ourselves and others brought into it, and kept in it; and that the kingdom of glory may be hastened.
insight: The second petition moves in three steps: Satan's kingdom destroyed, the kingdom of grace advanced with ourselves and others brought into it and kept in it, and the kingdom of glory hastened. Pray by name for someone outside the faith to be brought in, and for yourself to be kept.

text: Q. What do we pray for in the third petition? A. In the third petition, which is, Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven, we pray, that God, by his grace, would make us able and willing to know, obey, and submit to his will in all things, as the angels do in heaven.
insight: Imagine the angels around God's throne, who never drag their feet or argue terms. You pray to be made “able and willing” to obey as they do, so ask for the willing part too when the next hard instruction from Scripture lands in front of you.

text: Q. What do we pray for in the fourth petition? A. In the fourth petition, which is, Give us this day our daily bread, we pray that of God's free gift we may receive a competent portion of the good things of this life, and enjoy his blessing with them.
insight: Thank God at your next ordinary lunch for both the food and the pleasure of eating it. Daily bread asks for a sufficient portion of this life's good things from his free gift, along with his blessing to enjoy them.

text: Q. What do we pray for in the fifth petition? A. In the fifth petition, which is, And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors, we pray that God, for Christ's sake, would freely pardon all our sins; which we are the rather encouraged to ask, because by his grace we are enabled from the heart to forgive others.
insight: Resentment toward someone who wronged you sits awkwardly beside this petition, because the grace that pardons you also enables you to forgive from the heart. Name that person before God, and ask for the mercy you have received to flow out toward them.

text: Q. What do we pray for in the sixth petition? A. In the sixth petition, which is, And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil, we pray, that God would either keep us from being tempted to sin, or support and deliver us when we are tempted.
insight: Do you pray about temptation before it arrives, or only after you have fallen? You may ask God to keep you from being tempted at all, and when temptation comes anyway, to hold you up and bring you safely through.

text: Q. What doth the conclusion of the Lord's Prayer teach us? A. The conclusion of the Lord's Prayer, which is, For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever, Amen. teacheth us to take our encouragement in prayer from God only, and in our prayers to praise him, ascribing kingdom, power, and glory to him; and, in testimony of our desire, and assurance to be heard, we say, Amen.
insight: The conclusion of the prayer teaches that our encouragement to pray comes from God alone, and that praise belongs in prayer, ascribing kingdom, power, and glory to him. Close your own prayers the same way, and let your Amen voice both your desire and your confidence that he hears.

text: Q. What is your only comfort in life and death? A. That I am not my own, but belong with body and soul, both in life and in death, to my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ. He has fully paid for all my sins with His precious blood, and has set me free from all the power of the devil. He also preserves me in such a way that without the will of my heavenly Father not a hair can fall from my head; indeed, all things must work together for my salvation. Therefore, by His Holy Spirit He also assures me of eternal life and makes me heartily willing and ready from now on to live for Him.
insight: The only comfort named in the first answer is belonging, body and soul, in life and in death, to a faithful Savior who paid for sin and keeps his own. If you are in Christ, carry your fears to the One who owns you; if you are unsure, his invitation to come and belong is open to you.

text: Q. What do you need to know in order to live and die in the joy of this comfort? A. First, how great my sins and misery are; second, how I am delivered from all my sins and misery; third, how I am to be thankful to God for such deliverance.
insight: Guilt, grace, and gratitude is the familiar shorthand for the three things you need to know to live and die in this comfort. Each opens the next, so when thankfulness runs dry, go back and look again at how great a rescue you received.

text: Q. From where do you know your sins and misery? A. From the law of God.
insight: Mirrors tell the truth that friends are too kind to mention, and God's law works like one, showing you your sin and misery. When comparing yourself to others makes you feel fine, open the law and look again.

text: Q. What does God's law require of us? A. Christ teaches us this in a summary in Matthew 22: You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment. And a second is like it, You shall love your neighbour as yourself. On these two commandments depend all the law and the prophets.
insight: Did you love God with all your heart, soul, and mind since you woke up, and your neighbor as yourself? Jesus' summary makes the law short enough to memorize and deep enough to expose every hour, which is why you need his grace.

text: Q. Can you keep all this perfectly? A. No, I am inclined by nature to hate God and my neighbour.
insight: Does “inclined by nature to hate God and my neighbour” sound too harsh? Watch your reactions the next time God crosses your plans or a neighbor crosses your path, and you may find the diagnosis fits, and that grace is far more welcome.

text: Q. Did God, then, create man so wicked and perverse? A. No, on the contrary, God created man good and in His image, that is, in true righteousness and holiness, so that he might rightly know God His Creator, heartily love Him, and live with Him in eternal blessedness to praise and glorify Him.
insight: Blaming the Creator for human wickedness gets the story backward, since he made man good and in his image, in true righteousness and holiness, to know and love him. You were made for that blessedness, and in Christ he means to restore you to it.

text: Q. From where, then, did man's depraved nature come? A. From the fall and disobedience of our first parents, Adam and Eve, in Paradise, for there our nature became so corrupt that we are all conceived and born in sin.
insight: Poison in the headwaters reaches every stream below, and the fall of our first parents in Paradise corrupted the nature you were born with. Expect sin to show up in you uninvited, and run to Christ, the new head who makes his people clean.

text: Q. But are we so corrupt that we are totally unable to do any good and inclined to all evil? A. Yes, unless we are regenerated by the Spirit of God.
insight: Everything turns on the hinge of “unless we are regenerated by the Spirit of God.” Without that clause the verdict of total inability would crush you; with it, you can pray for the Spirit's renewing work in yourself and in the people you love.

text: Q. Is God, then, not unjust by requiring in His law what man cannot do? A. No, for God so created man that he was able to do it. But man, at the instigation of the devil, in deliberate disobedience robbed himself and all his descendants of these gifts.
insight: God is not unjust in requiring what man cannot do, because he created man able to keep his law, and man, prompted by the devil, deliberately threw that ability away for himself and his descendants. When God's demands feel unfair, remember the loss was ours, and ask him for mercy.

text: Q. Will God allow such disobedience and apostasy to go unpunished? A. Certainly not. He is terribly displeased with our original sin as well as our actual sins. Therefore He will punish them by a just judgment both now and eternally, as He has declared: Cursed be every one who does not abide by all things written in the book of the law, and do them (Galatians 3:10).
insight: Justice in God means real displeasure at both the sin you were born with and the sins you choose, answered by a righteous judgment now and eternally. Taking that seriously will make you less casual about sin and far more grateful for the cross.

text: Q. But is God not also merciful? A. God is indeed merciful, but He is also just. His justice requires that sin committed against the most high majesty of God also be punished with the most severe, that is, with everlasting, punishment of body and soul.
insight: How can God be merciful without ceasing to be just? Only a substitute who bears the punishment that sin against his majesty deserves resolves it, and when you look at the cross you see mercy and justice both kept whole.

text: Q. Since, according to God's righteous judgment we deserve temporal and eternal punishment, how can we escape this punishment and be again received into favour? A. God demands that His justice be satisfied. Therefore full payment must be made either by ourselves or by another.
insight: Full payment for sin must be made, either by ourselves or by another, because God will have his justice satisfied. No sinner can pay his own way, so stop trying to square the account yourself and bring the whole debt to Christ, who bears it for all who come to him.

text: Q. Can we ourselves make this payment? A. Certainly not. On the contrary, we daily increase our debt.
insight: Every day of our lives adds to the debt of sin, so no effort of ours can bring the balance down to zero. Give up hoping to pay God back by self-improvement, and look to Christ, who can pay what you owe in full.

text: Q. Can any mere creature pay for us? A. No. In the first place, God will not punish another creature for the sin which man has committed. Furthermore, no mere creature can sustain the burden of God's eternal wrath against sin and deliver others from it.
insight: Two reasons shut out every mere creature: God will not punish another kind of creature for the sin man committed, and none could bear his eternal wrath against sin and deliver others from it. Look for rescue from no angel or saint, and bring your guilt to the Mediator God has provided.

text: Q. What kind of mediator and deliverer must we seek? A. One who is a true and righteous man, and yet more powerful than all creatures; that is, one who is at the same time true God.
insight: Both “a true and righteous man” and “true God” are required, since only a man can stand in your place if you come to him in faith, and only God can carry the load. When you pray, you come through someone who fully understands you and is fully able to help.

text: Q. Why must He be a true and righteous man? A. He must be a true man because the justice of God requires that the same human nature which has sinned should pay for sin. He must be a righteous man because one who himself is a sinner cannot pay for others.
insight: Human nature sinned, so human nature must pay, but only a righteous man can pay for someone else instead of merely for himself. See how carefully this rules out every sinner, including you, as your own rescuer.

text: Q. Why must He at the same time be true God? A. He must be true God so that by the power of His divine nature He might bear in His human nature the burden of God's wrath, and might obtain for us and restore to us righteousness and life.
insight: Christ had to be true God so that, by the power of his divine nature, he could bear the burden of God's wrath in his human nature, and could win righteousness and life and restore them to us. Look to him for both halves of that work, the wrath carried and the life given.

text: Q. But who is that Mediator who at the same time is true God and a true and righteous man? A. Our Lord Jesus Christ, whom God made our wisdom, our righteousness and sanctification and redemption (I Corinthians 1:30).
insight: Bring your need for wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and rescue to one address, Jesus Christ, whom God made all four for you. Whatever you lack as you face the next decision, look to him first and ask him to supply it.

text: Q. From where do you know this? A. From the holy gospel, which God Himself first revealed in Paradise. Later, He had it proclaimed by the patriarchs and prophets, and foreshadowed by the sacrifices and other ceremonies of the law. Finally, He had it fulfilled through His only Son.
insight: Starting as a whisper in Paradise, the gospel grew louder through patriarchs and prophets, took shape in the sacrifices, and came to full voice in the Son. Open the Old Testament expecting to hear that same promise of Jesus spoken to you.

text: Q. Are all men, then, saved by Christ just as they perished through Adam? A. No. Only those are saved who by a true faith are grafted into Christ and accept all His benefits.
insight: Have you received Christ yourself, or only grown up near people who did? Everyone perished in Adam, but only those grafted into Christ by true faith share his benefits, and that grafting cannot be inherited from your parents.

text: Q. What is true faith? A. True faith is a sure knowledge whereby I accept as true all that God has revealed to us in His Word. At the same time it is a firm confidence that not only to others, but also to me, God has granted forgiveness of sins, everlasting righteousness, and salvation, out of mere grace, only for the sake of Christ's merits. This faith the Holy Spirit works in my heart by the gospel.
insight: Beyond agreeing that God's Word is true, faith makes a personal claim: “not only to others, but also to me” God has granted forgiveness. Say those words about yourself when doubt whispers that grace is meant for other people.

text: Q. What, then, must a Christian believe? A. All that is promised us in the Gospel, which the articles of our catholic and undoubted Christian faith teach us in a summary.
insight: Centuries of Christians have confessed the gospel's promises in the Apostles' Creed, the summary Heidelberg walks through line by line in the questions that follow. When you say it on Sunday, you join a very old chorus and need not invent a faith of your own.

text: Q. How are these articles divided? A. Into three parts: the first is about God the Father and our creation; the second about God the Son and our redemption; the third about God the Holy Spirit and our sanctification.
insight: The creed's articles fall into three parts, each joining a divine person to a work: the Father to creation, the Son to redemption, the Spirit to sanctification. When you recite it, let each part become prayer: thanks for your life, trust in the Son for rescue, and a plea for holiness.

text: Q. Since there is only one God, why do you speak of three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? A. Because God has so revealed Himself in His Word that these three distinct persons are the one, true, eternal God.
insight: Kneeling before three persons who are one God, you are not asked to master the arithmetic first. The answer rests the doctrine on revelation, 'God has so revealed Himself in His Word,' and your worship may begin at the edge of your explanations.

text: Q. What do you believe when you say: I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth? A. That the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who out of nothing created heaven and earth and all that is in them, and who still upholds and governs them by His eternal counsel and providence, is, for the sake of Christ His Son, my God and my Father. In Him I trust so completely as to have no doubt that He will provide me with all things necessary for body and soul, and will also turn to my good whatever adversity He sends me in this life of sorrow. He is able to do so as almighty God, and willing also as a faithful Father.
insight: The Father who made heaven and earth from nothing and governs them by his providence is, for Christ's sake, the one a believer calls my God and my Father. Trusting him means expecting him to provide for body and soul and to turn adversity to good, so bring him the need that weighs on you.

text: Q. What do you understand by the providence of God? A. God's providence is His almighty and ever present power, whereby, as with His hand, He still upholds heaven and earth and all creatures, and so governs them that leaf and blade, rain and drought, fruitful and barren years, food and drink, health and sickness, riches and poverty, indeed, all things, come not by chance but by His fatherly hand.
insight: Nothing is too small for the list: “leaf and blade, rain and drought,” food and drink, health and sickness. Because every item comes to you by God's fatherly hand, you can meet a canceled flight or a good report without calling it luck.

text: Q. What does it benefit us to know that God has created all things and still upholds them by His providence? A. We can be patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity, and with a view to the future we can have a firm confidence in our faithful God and Father that no creature shall separate us from His love; for all creatures are so completely in His hand that without His will they cannot so much as move.
insight: Match your response to the season you are in: patience when things go badly, thanks when they go well, and confidence about tomorrow, because no creature can separate you from your Father's love.

text: Q. Why is the Son of God called Jesus, that is, Saviour? A. Because He saves us from all our sins, and because salvation is not to be sought or found in anyone else.
insight: The name Jesus means Savior, and he bears it because he saves from all sins and salvation is found in no one else. When you catch yourself trusting a good reputation, religious habits, or willpower to make you right with God, turn that trust to him alone.

text: Q. Do those believe in the only Saviour Jesus who seek their salvation and well-being from saints, in themselves, or anywhere else? A. No. Though they boast of Him in words, they in fact deny the only Saviour Jesus. For one of two things must be true: either Jesus is not a complete Saviour, or those who by true faith accept this Saviour must find in Him all that is necessary for their salvation.
insight: Lip service to Jesus can sit alongside quiet trust in saints, in yourself, or in something else, and that divided trust denies him as the only Savior. Either he is complete or he is not, so look honestly at where your hope rests when life shakes you.

text: Q. Why is He called Christ, that is, Anointed? A. Because He has been ordained by God the Father, and anointed with the Holy Spirit, to be our chief Prophet and Teacher, who has fully revealed to us the secret counsel and will of God concerning our redemption; our only High Priest, who by the one sacrifice of His body has redeemed us, and who continually intercedes for us before the Father; and our eternal King, who governs us by His Word and Spirit, and who defends and preserves us in the redemption obtained for us.
insight: Messiah means Anointed One, and Christ was anointed to be your chief Prophet who reveals God's will, your only High Priest who offered himself and intercedes, and your eternal King who rules and guards you. Bring each office a matching need.

text: Q. Why are you called a Christian? A. Because I am a member of Christ by faith and thus share in His anointing, so that I may as prophet confess His Name, as priest present myself a living sacrifice of thankfulness to Him, and as king fight with a free and good conscience against sin and the devil in this life, and hereafter reign with Him eternally over all creatures.
insight: Oil once poured on prophets, priests, and kings now runs down onto you through faith in Christ. You get to confess his name, offer yourself as a living sacrifice of thanks, and fight sin with a free conscience at the desk, the sink, or the steering wheel.

text: Q. Why is He called God's only begotten Son, since we also are children of God? A. Because Christ alone is the eternal, natural Son of God. We, however, are children of God by adoption, through grace, for Christ's sake.
insight: Christ alone is the eternal, natural Son of God, and all others called children of God are so by adoption, through grace, for Christ's sake. If you long to belong to God's family, the way in is his grace in Christ, so come to him and receive the place he gives.

text: Q. Why do you call Him our Lord? A. Because He has ransomed us, body and soul, from all our sins, not with silver or gold but with His precious blood, and has freed us from all the power of the devil to make us His own possession.
insight: Bought “not with silver or gold but with His precious blood,” you are now Christ's own possession, freed from the devil's power. When an old habit claims ownership over you, answer that the price was paid and you belong to someone else.

text: Q. What do you confess when you say: He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary? A. The eternal Son of God, who is and remains true and eternal God, took upon Himself true human nature from the flesh and blood of the virgin Mary, through the working of the Holy Spirit. Thus He is also the true seed of David, and like His brothers in every respect, yet without sin.
insight: The eternal Son took true human nature from the flesh and blood of Mary by the Spirit's working, and he remained true and eternal God as he did it. Since he is like his brothers in every respect except sin, bring him your weakness, knowing he shares your nature.

text: Q. What benefit do you receive from the holy conception and birth of Christ? A. He is our Mediator, and with His innocence and perfect holiness covers, in the sight of God, my sin, in which I was conceived and born.
insight: Christ's innocence and perfect holiness cover, in God's sight, the sin in which his people were conceived and born, a corrupt nature present before any deed. Since your sin reaches back to your conception, look to the Mediator whose holy conception answers it at the root.

text: Q. What do you confess when you say that He suffered? A. During all the time He lived on earth, but especially at the end, Christ bore in body and soul the wrath of God against the sin of the whole human race. Thus, by His suffering, as the only atoning sacrifice, He has redeemed our body and soul from everlasting damnation, and obtained for us the grace of God, righteousness, and eternal life.
insight: Christ bore God's wrath in body and soul through his whole life on earth, and most of all at the end, and by that suffering, the only atoning sacrifice, he redeemed your body and soul from everlasting damnation, if you trust him. When your past rises up at night, you can answer that grace, righteousness, and eternal life were obtained for you at that cost.

text: Q. Why did He suffer under Pontius Pilate as judge? A. Though innocent, Christ was condemned by an earthly judge, and so He freed us from the severe judgment of God that was to fall on us.
insight: Though innocent, Jesus was condemned by an earthly judge, and so he freed us from the severe judgment of God that was headed our way. If you are in Christ, no court of opinion you fear can hand down a sentence heavier than the one he has already borne for you.

text: Q. Does it have a special meaning that Christ was crucified and did not die in a different way? A. Yes. Thereby I am assured that He took upon Himself the curse which lay on me, for a crucified one was cursed by God.
insight: Deuteronomy pronounced a hanged man cursed, and Paul applies that to the cross in Galatians 3, which is why the words "a crucified one was cursed" matter so much. When guilt says you live under a curse, point to the manner of his death: he took the one lying on you.

text: Q. Why was it necessary for Christ to humble Himself even unto death? A. Because of the justice and truth of God satisfaction for our sins could be made in no other way than by the death of the Son of God.
insight: God's justice and truth required a satisfaction for your sins that nothing short of the death of his own Son could make. If you suspect your sins are too heavy for grace, remember that the highest possible price has already been paid for them.

text: Q. Why was he buried? A. His burial testified that He had really died.
insight: Christ's burial testified that he had really died, and his was a true death laid in a true grave. When grief makes the resurrection feel like a story about someone else, remember that the one who rose had first gone all the way into the death you mourn.

text: Q. Since Christ has died for us, why do we still have to die? A. Our death is not a payment for our sins, but it puts an end to sin and is an entrance into eternal life.
insight: Many assume a believer's death must be some final installment on sin's bill. Heidelberg answers that death pays nothing; it puts an end to sin and becomes the entrance into eternal life, so you may face your own mortality as a doorway you will walk through.

text: Q. What further benefit do we receive from Christ's sacrifice and death on the cross? A. Through Christ's death our old nature is crucified, put to death, and buried with Him, so that the evil desires of the flesh may no longer reign in us, but that we may offer ourselves to Him as a sacrifice of thankfulness.
insight: Which desire of the flesh do you keep obeying as though it reigned over you? Through Christ's death your old nature was crucified and buried with him, so you are free to offer yourself to him as a sacrifice of thankfulness.

text: Q. Why is there added: He descended into hell? A. In my greatest sorrows and temptations I may be assured and comforted that my Lord Jesus Christ, by His unspeakable anguish, pain, terror, and agony, which He endured throughout all His sufferings but especially on the cross, has delivered me from the anguish and torment of hell.
insight: Nights of sorrow and temptation are exactly where this comfort is aimed: Christ endured unspeakable anguish, pain, and terror, especially on the cross, to deliver you from the anguish of hell. When fear feels bottomless, you may know he went lower first.

text: Q. How does Christ's resurrection benefit us? A. First, by His resurrection He has overcome death, so that He could make us share in the righteousness which He had obtained for us by His death. Second, by His power we too are raised up to a new life. Third, Christ's resurrection is to us a sure pledge of our glorious resurrection.
insight: Imagine an empty tomb with three doors opening out of it: righteousness shared with you now, new life raised in you by his power, and a sure pledge of your own glorious resurrection. Walk through all three when you feel stuck in who you used to be.

text: Q. What do you confess when you say, He ascended into heaven? A. That Christ, before the eyes of His disciples, was taken up from the earth into heaven, and that He is there for our benefit until He comes again to judge the living and the dead.
insight: Pray as someone whose advocate is seated in the room where every decision is made. The disciples watched Christ taken up bodily into heaven, and he remains there for your benefit until he comes again to judge the living and the dead.

text: Q. Is Christ, then, not with us until the end of the world, as He has promised us? A. Christ is true man and true God. With respect to His human nature He is no longer on earth, but with respect to His divinity, majesty, grace, and Spirit He is never absent from us.
insight: Loneliness can make you wonder whether the promise to be with you always has lapsed. In his human nature Christ is no longer on earth, but in his divinity, majesty, grace, and Spirit he is never absent from you, even in an empty kitchen at midnight.

text: Q. But are the two natures in Christ not separated from each other if His human nature is not present wherever His divinity is? A. Not at all, for His divinity has no limits and is present everywhere. So it must follow that His divinity is indeed beyond the human nature which He has taken on and nevertheless is within this human nature and remains personally united with it.
insight: Some have argued that if Christ's human nature is not present everywhere his divinity is, the two natures must be separated. His divinity has no limits, so it is beyond the humanity he took on and yet within it, personally united to it, and you can trust that the Christ near you by his Spirit is the same person whose body is in heaven.

text: Q. How does Christ's ascension into heaven benefit us? A. First, He is our Advocate in heaven before His Father. Second, we have our flesh in heaven as a sure pledge that He, our Head, will also take us, His members, up to Himself. Third, He sends us His Spirit as a counter-pledge, by whose power we seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God, and not the things that are on earth.
insight: Christ keeps our flesh in heaven as a sure pledge that he, our Head, will take his members up to himself, and he sends his Spirit down to us as the counter-pledge. When errands pin your thoughts to the ground, that Spirit gives you power to seek the things above, where Christ is seated at God's right hand.

text: Q. Why is it added, And sits at the right hand of God? A. Christ ascended into heaven to manifest Himself there as Head of His Church, through whom the Father governs all things.
insight: Sitting at God's right hand means Christ holds the office of Head over his church, the one through whom the Father governs all things. Whatever lands on your desk or in your inbox comes to you under his rule, so you can take up the work in front of you without fearing it has slipped out of his hands.

text: Q. How does the glory of Christ, our Head, benefit us? A. First, by His Holy Spirit He pours out heavenly gifts upon us, His members. Second, by His power He defends and preserves us against all enemies.
insight: Think of a head that pours strength down into every limb and guards the whole body from attack. That is the shape of Christ's glory: by his Spirit he gives you heavenly gifts, and by his power he defends and preserves you against every enemy.

text: Q. What comfort is it to you that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead? A. In all my sorrow and persecution I lift up my head and eagerly await as judge from heaven the very same person who before has submitted Himself to the judgment of God for my sake, and has removed all the curse from me. He will cast all His and my enemies into everlasting condemnation, but He will take me and all His chosen ones to Himself into heavenly joy and glory.
insight: Dread of the final judgment is met with a surprising posture: lift up your head. The judge you will face is the very person who first submitted himself to God's judgment for your sake and removed every curse from you.

text: Q. What do you believe concerning the Holy Spirit? A. First, He is, together with the Father and the Son, true and eternal God. Second, He is also given to me, to make me by true faith share in Christ and all His benefits, to comfort me, and to remain with me forever.
insight: The Holy Spirit is true and eternal God together with the Father and the Son, and he is also given to you, to make you share in Christ and all his benefits by true faith and to comfort you. He will remain with you forever, so on a lonely evening you are never without the company of God himself.

text: Q. What do you believe concerning the holy catholic Christian church? A. I believe that the Son of God, out of the whole human race, from the beginning of the world to its end, gathers, defends, and preserves for Himself, by His Spirit and Word, in the unity of the true faith, a church chosen to everlasting life. And I believe that I am and forever shall remain a living member of it.
insight: The Son of God gathers, defends, and preserves a church chosen to everlasting life out of the whole human race, from the beginning of the world to its end. If you trust Christ, you may say with the catechism's closing words that you are and forever shall remain a living member of it, because he is the one who keeps his members.

text: Q. What do you understand by the communion of saints? A. First, that believers, all and everyone, as members of Christ have communion with Him and share in all His treasures and gifts. Second, that everyone is duty-bound to use his gifts readily and cheerfully for the benefit and well-being of the other members.
insight: Every believer shares in all of Christ's treasures and gifts as a member of him, and every member is bound to spend their own gifts readily and cheerfully for the good of the others. If you belong to Christ, whatever he has given you was meant to be handed on to someone in your congregation.

text: Q. What do you believe concerning the forgiveness of sins? A. I believe that God, because of Christ's satisfaction, will no more remember my sins, nor my sinful nature, against which I have to struggle all my life, but He will graciously grant me the righteousness of Christ, that I may never come into condemnation.
insight: Somewhere a record of your sins was kept, and God has chosen, because of Christ's satisfaction, never to remember it against you. You will fight your sinful nature all your life, yet the file you dread has been replaced with Christ's righteousness.

text: Q. What comfort does the resurrection of the body offer you? A. Not only shall my soul after this life immediately be taken up to Christ, my Head, but also this my flesh, raised by the power of Christ, shall be reunited with my soul and made like Christ's glorious body.
insight: Aching knees and a failing memory can make your body feel like a loss you are merely enduring. This very flesh, raised by Christ's power, will be reunited with your soul and made like his glorious body, so you may grieve its weakness with hope.

text: Q. What comfort do you receive from the article about the life everlasting? A. Since I now already feel in my heart the beginning of eternal joy, I shall after this life possess perfect blessedness, such as no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man conceived-- a blessedness in which to praise God forever.
insight: The joy a believer "now already" feels in the heart is the beginning of the eternal joy of praising God, a first share in a blessedness no eye has seen. Seek that joy in God himself, and when your feelings run low, remember that the perfect blessedness to come rests on his promise and does not rise or fall with your mood.

text: Q. But what does it help you now that you believe all this? A. In Christ I am righteous before God and heir to life everlasting.
insight: The benefit of believing all this is that in Christ a believer is righteous before God and an heir to life everlasting. If you trust Christ, no errand, failure, or diagnosis can revise that standing or cancel that inheritance, so you can face an ordinary afternoon knowing what waits for you.

text: Q. How are you righteous before God? A. Only by true faith in Jesus Christ. Although my conscience accuses me that I have grievously sinned against all God's commandments, have never kept any of them, and am still inclined to all evil, yet God, without any merit of my own, out of mere grace, imputes to me the perfect satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness of Christ. He grants these to me as if I had never had nor committed any sin, and as if I myself had accomplished all the obedience which Christ has rendered for me, if only I accept this gift with a believing heart.
insight: Your conscience may accuse you of breaking every commandment and keeping none, and God answers it by crediting Christ's perfect satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness to you out of mere grace, through true faith alone. On a morning when your record condemns you, admit the charge and receive that gift again "with a believing heart."

text: Q. Why do you say that you are righteous only by faith? A. Not that I am acceptable to God on account of the worthiness of my faith, for only the satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness of Christ is my righteousness before God. I can receive this righteousness and make it mine my own by faith only.
insight: Weak believers often fear their faith is too thin to count. Faith was never the worthiness God accepts; Christ's satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness are, and faith is only the hand by which you receive them and make them your own.

text: Q. But why can our good works not be our righteousness before God, or at least a part of it? A. Because the righteousness which can stand before God's judgment must be absolutely perfect and in complete agreement with the law of God, whereas even our best works in this life are all imperfect and defiled with sin.
insight: Bring even your best day before God's judgment and you will find it imperfect and stained with sin, because the righteousness that stands there must be absolutely perfect. Rest your case on Christ's, and you can stop grading your good works.

text: Q. But do our good works earn nothing, even though God promises to reward them in this life and the next? A. This reward is not earned; it is a gift of grace.
insight: Parents know the pleasure of rewarding a child for a drawing made with crayons they bought themselves. God rewards your good works in this life and the next, and every reward is a gift of grace, so you can serve without keeping a ledger.

text: Q. Does this teaching not make people careless and wicked? A. No. It is impossible that those grafted into Christ by true faith should not bring forth fruits of thankfulness.
insight: Orchard language, "grafted into Christ," answers the fear that free grace breeds careless living: a living graft cannot help bearing fruit. Look for thankfulness budding in you as the sign that the graft has taken.

text: Q. Since then faith alone makes us share in Christ and all His benefits, where does this faith come from? A. From the Holy Spirit, who works it in our hearts by the preaching of the gospel, and strengthens it by the use of the sacraments.
insight: Sit under faithful preaching and come to the sacraments expecting the Holy Spirit to work, since he works faith in your heart by the preaching of the gospel and strengthens it by the sacraments. You receive faith before you ever exercise it.

text: Q. What are the sacraments? A. The sacraments are holy, visible signs and seals. They were instituted by God so that by their use He might the more fully declare and seal to us the promise of the gospel. And this is the promise: that God graciously grants us forgiveness of sins and everlasting life because of the one sacrifice of Christ accomplished on the cross.
insight: Kings once pressed a signet into wax so that a letter could be trusted. Sacraments are God's seals of that kind, set on the gospel promise of forgiveness and everlasting life, so that you may grasp that promise more fully.

text: Q. Are both the Word and the sacraments then intended to focus our faith on the sacrifice of Jesus Christ on the cross as the only ground of our salvation? A. Yes, indeed. The Holy Spirit teaches us in the gospel and assures us by the sacraments that our entire salvation rests on Christ's one sacrifice for us on the cross.
insight: The preaching of the gospel and the sacraments are both meant to fix your faith on Christ's one sacrifice on the cross as the only ground of salvation for those who trust him, the Spirit teaching through the one and assuring through the other. When a sermon ends or the bread is passed, ask whether your eyes have been turned back to the cross.

text: Q. How many sacraments has Christ instituted in the new covenant? A. Two: holy baptism and the holy supper.
insight: Medieval Rome counted seven sacraments; Heidelberg names two, holy baptism and the holy supper, because only these did Christ institute in the new covenant. You need no extra rituals to be sure grace has reached you.

text: Q. How does holy baptism signify and seal to you that the one sacrifice of Christ on the cross benefits you? A. In this way: Christ instituted this outward washing and with it gave the promise that, as surely as water washes away the dirt from the body, so certainly His blood and Spirit wash away the impurity of my soul, that is, all my sins.
insight: Muddy hands after an afternoon in the garden come clean under the tap, and Christ promised that his blood and Spirit wash away your soul's pollution just as surely. When you doubt your forgiveness, return to your baptism as the promise attached to that washing.

text: Q. What does it mean to be washed with Christ's blood and Spirit? A. To be washed with Christ's blood means to receive forgiveness of sins from God, through grace, because of Christ's blood, poured out for us in His sacrifice on the cross. To be washed with His Spirit means to be renewed by the Holy Spirit and sanctified to be members of Christ, so that more and more we become dead to sin and lead a holy and blameless life.
insight: Pardon and renewal are the two things this washing means: Christ's blood brings forgiveness of sins, and his Spirit renews and sanctifies you as a member of Christ. Ask God for both, so that you want a changed life along with a clean record.

text: Q. Where has Christ promised that He will wash us with His blood and Spirit as surely as we are washed with the water of baptism? A. In the institution of baptism, where He says: Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. He who believes and is baptized will be saved, but he who does not believe will be condemned. This promise is repeated where Scripture calls baptism the washing of regeneration and the washing away of sins.
insight: Christ's promise to wash you with his blood and Spirit stands in his own command to baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, joined to the words "He who believes and is baptized will be saved." That promise is received by faith, so let your baptism send you to believe what Christ said about it.

text: Q. Does this outward washing with water itself wash away sins? A. No, only the blood of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit cleanse us from all sins.
insight: Superstition treats the font as if the water itself did the cleansing. Only the blood of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit cleanse you from all sin, so cherish the sign while resting your hope on the One it points to.

text: Q. Why then does the Holy Spirit call baptism the washing of regeneration and the washing away of sins? A. God speaks in this way for a good reason. He wants to teach us that the blood and Spirit of Christ remove our sins just as water takes away dirt from the body. But, even more important, He wants to assure us by this divine pledge and sign that we are as truly cleansed from our sins spiritually as we are bodily washed with water.
insight: Why would the Spirit call baptism the washing away of sins if water cannot do it? Because God wants to teach you, and even more to assure you by this divine pledge, that you are washed spiritually as truly as your body is washed with water.

text: Q. Should infants, too, be baptized? A. Yes. Infants as well as adults belong to God's covenant and congregation. Through Christ's blood the redemption from sin and the Holy Spirit, who works faith, are promised to them no less than to adults. Therefore, by baptism, as sign of the covenant, they must be grafted into the Christian church and distinguished from the children of unbelievers. This was done in the old covenant by circumcision, in place of which baptism was instituted in the new covenant.
insight: Remember, if you were baptized as an infant, that God's covenant promise was spoken over you before you could speak at all. Children belong to his covenant and congregation, and the sign they receive calls them, and you, toward the faith it announced.

text: Q. What does it mean to eat the crucified body of Christ and to drink His shed blood? A. First, to accept with a believing heart all the suffering and the death of Christ, and so receive forgiveness of sins and life eternal. Second, to be united more and more to His sacred body through the Holy Spirit, who lives both in Christ and in us. Therefore, although Christ is in heaven and we are on earth, yet we are flesh of His flesh and bone of His bones, and we forever live and are governed by one Spirit, as the members of our body are by one soul.
insight: To eat Christ's body is to accept his suffering and death with a believing heart and to be united more and more to him by the Holy Spirit, who lives both in Christ and in you. Christ is in heaven and you are on earth, yet at the Supper you can trust that his one Spirit binds you to him as flesh of his flesh.

text: Q. Are then the bread and wine changed into the real body and blood of Christ? A. No. Just as the water of baptism is not changed into the blood of Christ and is not the washing away of sins itself but is simply God's sign and pledge, so also the bread in the Lord's supper does not become the body of Christ itself, although it is called Christ's body in keeping with the nature and usage of sacraments.
insight: Sixteenth-century Europe was divided over whether the bread becomes Christ's body, and Heidelberg answered that it does not, any more than baptismal water turns into his blood. Come to the table expecting Christ to feed your faith through signs that remain bread and wine.

text: Q. Who are to come to the table of the Lord? A. Those who are truly displeased with themselves because of their sins and yet trust that these are forgiven them and that their remaining weakness is covered by the suffering and death of Christ, and who also desire more and more to strengthen their faith and amend their life. But hypocrites and those who do not repent eat and drink judgment upon themselves.
insight: The Lord's table is for those truly displeased with themselves because of their sins who yet trust that Christ's death forgives them and covers their remaining weakness, and who long to grow in faith and amend their lives. Hypocrites and the unrepentant eat judgment on themselves, so ask honestly whether sorrow for sin and trust in Christ are both in you.

text: Q. Are those also to be admitted to the Lord's supper who by their confession and life show that they are unbelieving and ungodly? A. No, for then the covenant of God would be profaned and His wrath kindled against the whole congregation. Therefore, according to the command of Christ and His apostles, the Christian church is duty-bound to exclude such persons by the keys of the kingdom of heaven, until they amend their lives.
insight: Exclusion from the Lord's supper can look harsh, yet it guards God's covenant from being profaned and spares the whole congregation his wrath. Examine yourself before you eat, and receive the church's watchfulness as care for your soul.

text: Q. What are the keys of the kingdom of heaven? A. The preaching of the holy gospel and church discipline. By these two the kingdom of heaven is opened to believers and closed to unbelievers.
insight: The keys of the kingdom are two, the preaching of the gospel and church discipline, and by both of them heaven is opened to believers and closed to unbelievers. When you hear the gospel preached or see the church's discipline exercised, receive each as Christ's own word of welcome to faith and of warning to unbelief.

text: Q. How is the kingdom of heaven opened and closed by the preaching of the gospel? A. According to the command of Christ, the kingdom of heaven is opened when it is proclaimed and publicly testified to each and every believer that God has really forgiven all their sins for the sake of Christ's merits, as often as they by true faith accept the promise of the gospel. The kingdom of heaven is closed when it is proclaimed and testified to all unbelievers and hypocrites that the wrath of God and eternal condemnation rest on them as long as they do not repent. According to this testimony of the gospel, God will judge both in this life and in the life to come.
insight: Listen to a faithful sermon as a declaration from Christ: to every believer it publicly testifies that God has really forgiven all their sins, and to the unrepentant it announces his wrath. Receive the pardon meant for you as spoken by God himself.

text: Q. How is the kingdom of heaven closed and opened by church discipline? A. According to the command of Christ, people who call themselves Christians but show themselves to be unchristian in doctrine or life are first repeatedly admonished in a brotherly manner. If they do not give up their errors or wickedness, they are reported to the church, that is, to the elders. If they do not heed also their admonitions, they are forbidden the use of the sacraments, and they are excluded by the elders from the Christian congregation, and by God Himself from the kingdom of Christ. They are again received as members of Christ and of the church when they promise and show real amendment.
insight: Stages matter in Christ's pattern of discipline: repeated brotherly admonition first, then the elders, then exclusion from the sacraments, and full restoration as soon as real amendment appears. Welcome a friend's gentle correction early, when your road back is short.

text: Q. Since we have been delivered from our misery by grace alone through Christ, without any merit of our own, why must we yet do good works? A. Because Christ, having redeemed us by His blood, also renews us by His Holy Spirit to be His image, so that with our whole life we may show ourselves thankful to God for His benefits, and He may be praised by us. Further, that we ourselves may be assured of our faith by its fruits, and that by our godly walk of life we may win our neighbours for Christ.
insight: Gratitude or fear: which one gets you out of bed toward obedience? Christ redeemed you by his blood and renews you by his Spirit into his image, so that your whole life can show thankfulness and praise him.

text: Q. Can those be saved who do not turn to God from their ungrateful and impenitent walk of life? A. By no means. Scripture says that no unchaste person, idolater, adulterer, thief, greedy person, drunkard, slanderer, robber, or the like shall inherit the kingdom of God.
insight: Struggling Christians sometimes read this list of the unchaste, greedy, and slanderous and assume it names them. It targets an impenitent walk that refuses to turn to God, so answer its warning by turning again, as often as you need to.

text: Q. What is the true repentance or conversion of man? A. It is the dying of the old nature and the coming to life of the new.
insight: Turning to God has two halves: the dying of the old nature and the coming to life of the new. If you look only for relief, you will miss the dying, and if you look only for sorrow, you will miss the joy of coming alive.

text: Q. What is the dying of the old nature? A. It is to grieve with heartfelt sorrow that we have offended God by our sin, and more and more to hate it and flee from it.
insight: Regret that only makes you miserable for an afternoon falls short of dying to sin, which is heartfelt sorrow that you have offended God, growing into hatred of the sin and flight from it. Ask God for that kind of grief, the kind that moves your feet.

text: Q. What is the coming to life of the new nature? A. It is a heartfelt joy in God through Christ, and a love and delight to live according to the will of God in all good works.
insight: The coming to life of the new nature is heartfelt joy in God through Christ, joined with a love and delight to live by his will in all good works. When obedience feels like drudgery, ask God for that joy in him, since the new life he gives delights in his will as well as doing it.

text: Q. But what are good works? A. Only those which are done out of true faith, in accordance with the law of God, and to His glory, and not those based on our own opinion or on precepts of men.
insight: Three tests sit inside the definition of good works: "out of true faith," "in accordance with the law of God," and "to His glory." Before you call a project good, ask all three, since works built on your own opinion or on human precepts fail them.

text: Q. How are these commandments divided? A. Into two parts. The first teaches us how to live in relation to God; the second, what duties we owe our neighbour.
insight: Moses brought the law down the mountain on two tablets, and Heidelberg divides its commandments into two parts: how you live toward God and what you owe your neighbor. Your kindness to a coworker is meant to grow from the first part, never to replace it.

text: Q. What does the LORD require in the first commandment? A. That for the sake of my very salvation I avoid and flee all idolatry, witchcraft, superstition, and prayer to saints or to other creatures. Further, that I rightly come to know the only true God. trust in Him alone, submit to Him with all humility and patience, expect all good from Him only, and love, fear, and honour Him with all my heart. In short, that I forsake all creatures rather than do the least thing against His will.
insight: The first commandment asks you to flee all idolatry and superstition, including prayer to saints or other creatures, and to know the only true God rightly, trust him alone, and expect all good from him only. Name the thing you would reach for first in a crisis, and give that trust back to the God who asks for all of it.

text: Q. What is idolatry? A. Idolatry is having or inventing something in which to put our trust instead of, or in addition to, the only true God who has revealed Himself in His Word.
insight: Anything you trust instead of the true God, or merely in addition to him, qualifies as idolatry. Most idols ask only for a little extra confidence alongside God, so watch what you reach for when you are anxious.

text: Q. What does God require in the second commandment? A. We are not to make an image of God in any way, nor to worship Him in any other manner than He has commanded in His Word.
insight: Approach God the way he has asked to be approached, since the second commandment forbids making any image of him or worshiping him in any manner he has not commanded in his Word. You are freed from inventing a worship that merely pleases you.

text: Q. May we then not make any image at all? A. God cannot and may not be visibly portrayed in any way. Creatures may be portrayed, but God forbids us to make or have any images of them in order to worship them or to serve God through them.
