text: All persons throughout the world, professing the faith of the Gospel, and obedience unto God by Christ, according unto it; not destroying their own profession by any Errors everting the foundation, or unholyness of conversation, are and may be called visible Saints; and of such ought all particular Congregations to be constituted.
insight: Visible saints are all who profess the gospel and obey God through Christ without overturning the foundation by error or unholy living, and local churches are to be made of such people. Welcome the struggling believer in your pew as a saint, for a credible profession of Christ marks one out.

witness.voice: Andrew Gifford, Benjamin Keach, Charles Archer et al.

text: The purest Churches under heaven are subject to mixture, and error; and som have so degenerated as to become no Churches of Christ, but Synagogues of Satan; nevertheless Christ always hath had, and ever shall have a Kingdome in this world, to the end thereof, of such as believe in him, and make profession of his Name.
insight: Even the purest churches under heaven are subject to mixture and error, and some have degenerated past being churches at all, yet Christ always has had and ever shall have a kingdom of believers in this world. Keep serving your imperfect congregation with hope in its King.

witness.voice: Andrew Gifford, Benjamin Keach, Charles Archer et al.

text: The Lord Jesus Christ is the Head of the Church, in whom by the appointment of the Father, all power for the calling, institution, order, or Government of the Church, is invested in a supream & soveraigne manner, neither can the Pope of Rome in any sense be head thereof, but is that Antichrist, that Man of sin, and Son of perdition, that exalteth himself in the Church against Christ, and all that is called God; whom the Lord shall destroy with the brightness of his coming.
insight: All power "for the calling, institution, order, or Government of the Church" rests in Christ by the Father's appointment, "in a supream & soveraigne manner," so no human head can claim it. Whoever leads your congregation holds a charge from Christ, and you follow them as they follow his word.

witness.voice: Andrew Gifford, Benjamin Keach, Charles Archer et al.

text: In the execution of this power wherewith he is so intrusted, the Lord Jesus calleth out of the World unto himself, through the Ministry of his word, by his Spirit, those that are given unto him by his Father; that they may walk before him in all the ways of obedience, which he prescribeth to them in his Word. Those thus called he commandeth to walk together in particular societies, or Churches, for their mutual edification; and the due performance of that publick worship, which he requireth of them in the World.
insight: Christ calls his people out of the world through his Word and Spirit, and then commands those he calls to walk together in particular churches for mutual edification and public worship. If you have been following him alone, find a faithful congregation and join its common life.

witness.voice: Andrew Gifford, Benjamin Keach, Charles Archer et al.

text: The Members of these Churches are Saints by calling, visibly manifesting and evidencing (in and by their profession and walking) their obedience unto that call of Christ; and do willingly consent to walk together according to the appointment of Christ, giving up themselves, to the Lord & one to another by the will of God, in professed subjection to the Ordinances of the Gospel.
insight: Mark the double gift in "giving up themselves, to the Lord & one to another." Church membership starts with surrender to Christ and then becomes surrender to people. Ask whom in your congregation you have given yourself to in more than name.

witness.voice: Andrew Gifford, Benjamin Keach, Charles Archer et al.

text: To each of these Churches thus gathered, according to his mind, declared in his word, he hath given all that power and authority, which is any way needfull, for their carrying on that order in worship, and discipline, which he hath instituted for them to observe; with commands, and rules, for the due and right exerting, and executing of that power.
insight: Christ has given each gathered church all the authority it needs for the worship and discipline he instituted, along with rules for how that power is to be used. Pray that your congregation will exercise its authority by his word, neither looking for an outside hierarchy nor inventing rules of its own.

witness.voice: Andrew Gifford, Benjamin Keach, Charles Archer et al.

text: A particular Church gathered, and compleatly Organized, according to the mind of Christ, consists of Officers, and Members; And the Officers appointed by Christ to be chosen and set apart by the Church (so called and gathered) for the peculiar Administration of Ordinances, and Execution of Power, or Duty, which he intrusts them with, or calls them to, to be continued to the end of the World are Bishops or Elders and Deacons.
insight: A completely organized church, by Christ's appointment, consists of officers and members, and its officers to the end of the world are elders and deacons, chosen and set apart by the church. Thank your own elders and deacons by name, and pray for them as servants Christ has given you.

witness.voice: Andrew Gifford, Benjamin Keach, Charles Archer et al.

text: The way appointed by Christ for the Calling of any person, fitted, and gifted by the Holy Spirit, unto the Office of Bishop, or Elder, in a Church, is, that he be chosen thereunto by the common suffrage of the Church it self; and Solemnly set apart by Fasting and Prayer, with imposition of hands of the Eldership of the Church, if there be any before Constituted therein; And of a Deacon that he be chosen by the like suffrage, and set apart by Prayer, and the like Imposition of hands.
insight: Christ appointed two acts in calling an elder: the church chooses him "by the common suffrage of the Church it self," and he is then solemnly set apart by fasting and prayer with the laying on of hands. When your congregation calls a pastor, your vote and the church's prayer both belong to how Christ fills that office.

witness.voice: Andrew Gifford, Benjamin Keach, Charles Archer et al.

text: Although it be incumbent on the Bishops or Pastors of the Churches to be instant in Preaching the Word, by way of Office; yet the work of Preaching the Word, is not so peculiarly confined to them; but that others also gifted, and fitted by the Holy Spirit for it, and approved, and called by the Church, may and ought to perform it.
insight: Pastors are bound by office to preach the word, yet preaching is open to others who are gifted and fitted by the Spirit and approved and called by the church. If your church recognizes such a gift in you, you may take up the charge with humility and prepare as for a work Christ gives.

witness.voice: Andrew Gifford, Benjamin Keach, Charles Archer et al.

text: As all Believers are bound to joyn themselves to particular Churches, when and where they have opportunity so to do; So all that are admitted unto the priviledges of a Church, are also under the Censures and Government thereof, according to the Rule of Christ.
insight: Obligation and accountability travel together: all believers are "bound to joyn themselves" to a particular church when they have opportunity, and all who share its privileges come under its government according to the rule of Christ. Receive your church's correction as part of belonging to it.

witness.voice: Andrew Gifford, Benjamin Keach, Charles Archer et al.

text: No Church-members upon any offence taken by them, having performed their Duty required of them towards the person they are offended at, ought to disturb any Church order, or absent themselves from the Assemblies of the Church, or Administration of any Ordinances, upon the account of such offence at any of their fellow-members; but to wait upon Christ, in the further proceeding of the Church.
insight: A member who has done his duty toward someone who offended him should neither disturb church order nor absent himself from worship and the ordinances, but wait on Christ as the church proceeds. If a fellow member has hurt you, keep your place at worship and the Lord's Table, and trust Christ with what remains.

witness.voice: Andrew Gifford, Benjamin Keach, Charles Archer et al.

text: As each Church, and all the Members of it are bound to pray continually, for the good and prosperity of all the Churches of Christ, in all places; and upon all occasions to further it (every one within the bounds of their places, and callings, in the Exercise of their Gifts and Graces) so the Churches (when planted by the providence of God so as they may injoy opportunity and advantage for it) ought to hold communion amongst themselves for their peace, increase of love, and mutual edification.
insight: Every church and member is bound to pray continually for the good of all Christ's churches, and churches that have opportunity ought to hold communion with one another for peace, love, and mutual edification. Pray by name for a congregation across town from your own, and look for one way to help it.

witness.voice: Andrew Gifford, Benjamin Keach, Charles Archer et al.

ref: When I survey the wondrous cross (1707), st. 1
text:
When I survey the wondrous cross
On which the Prince of Glory dy'd,
My richest gain I count but loss,
And pour contempt on all my pride.
insight: Churches in Watts's England sang psalms almost exclusively, and he handed them a hymn in which the singer counts his richest gain as loss before a dying Prince of Glory. Bring whatever you are proudest of to the foot of that cross and let it be weighed against his love.

ref: When I survey the wondrous cross (1707), st. 3
text:
See from his head, his hands, his feet,
Sorrow and love flow mingled down;
Did e'er such love and sorrow meet?
Or thorns compose so rich a crown?
insight: Watts sees sorrow and love flow mingled down from Christ's head, hands, and feet, so the wounds that show what sin cost also show how much he loved. When you grieve your sin, grieve it at the cross, where the sorrow comes mixed with love.

ref: When I survey the wondrous cross (1707), st. 5
text:
Were the whole realm of nature mine,
That were a present far too small;
Love so amazing, so divine,
Demands my soul, my life, my all.
insight: Watts reckons that even the whole realm of nature would be a present far too small for love so amazing, so the only fitting answer is soul, life, and all. You cannot repay the cross and are never asked to; you are asked to give your whole self to the One whose love has claimed it.

ref: Alas! and did my Saviour bleed (1707), st. 1
text:
Alas! and did my Saviour bleed,
And did my Sovereign die?
Would he devote that sacred head
For such a worm as I?
insight: Modern ears flinch at "such a worm as I," yet Watts is measuring himself against a Sovereign who chose to bleed and devote his sacred head. If you feel small beside that love, you are seeing clearly, and the fitting reply is wonder.

ref: Alas! and did my Saviour bleed (1707), st. 6
text:
But drops of grief can ne'er repay
The debt of love I owe;
Here, Lord, I give myself away,
'Tis all that I can do.
insight: Watts owns a debt of love that no drops of grief can repay, and he answers it by giving himself away, the thanks of a sinner whose Saviour has already satisfied for his sin. When regret pushes you to pay God back in tears, give yourself to him in gratitude and rest your standing on what Christ has done.

ref: Come, we that love the Lord (1707), st. 1
text:
Come, we that love the Lord,
And let our joys be known;
Join in a song with sweet accord,
And thus surround the throne.
insight: Sing out on Sunday, even if your voice is thin, because Watts wrote these lines for a whole congregation making its joys known together around the throne. Your joy grows when others can hear it, and theirs grows when they hear yours.

ref: How sweet and awful is the place (1707), st. 1
text:
How sweet and awful is the place
With Christ within the doors,
While everlasting love displays
The choicest of her stores!
insight: Eighteenth-century English used "awful" for what fills you with awe, so Watts can call the place where Christ meets his people both sweet and fearful at once. Walk into worship this Sunday expecting delight and trembling in the same room.

ref: Join all the glorious names (1707), st. 1
text:
Join all the glorious names
Of wisdom, love, and power,
That ever mortals knew,
That angels ever bore:
All are too mean
To speak his worth,
Too mean to set
My Saviour forth.
insight: Frustration with your own words in prayer is an honest experience, and Watts shares it: every name mortals knew and angels bore is too mean to set the Saviour forth. When your praise feels thin, you have found out how great he is.

ref: Not all the blood of beasts (1709), st. 1
text:
Not all the blood of beasts
On Jewish altars slain
Could give the guilty conscience peace,
Or wash away the stain.
insight: Hebrews 10:4 says the blood of bulls and goats cannot take away sins, and Watts sets that verse to music. If you carry a conscience that ritual and effort have never quieted, you need the one sacrifice that reaches all the way down to the stain.

ref: Not all the blood of beasts (1709), st. 3
text:
My faith would lay her hand
On that dear head of thine,
While like a penitent I stand
And there confess my sin.
insight: Picture the worshiper under the old law pressing a hand on the animal's head while confessing sin over it; Watts puts his faith in that posture before Christ. Confession and trust make one motion for you as well: you name the sin while you lean on him.

ref: There is a land of pure delight (1707), st. 1
text:
There is a land of pure delight
Where saints immortal reign,
Infinite day excludes the night,
And pleasures banish pain.
insight: Critics call longing for heaven escapism, yet Watts sings of infinite day and pleasures that banish pain because Scripture promises exactly that country. Your homesickness for a land you have never seen is faith doing its proper work.

ref: Give me the wings of faith to rise (1709), st. 1
text:
Give me the wings of faith to rise
Within the veil, and see
The saints above, how great their joys,
How bright their glories be.
insight: Watts asks for the wings of faith to rise within the veil and see the saints above, because faith sees what the eye cannot and carries the heart into heaven's joy. When heaven feels distant and abstract, ask God for that same faith and let the joy of those who are with Christ draw your own heart toward him.

ref: Come, holy Spirit, heavenly Dove (1707), st. 1
text:
Come, holy Spirit, heavenly Dove,
With all thy quickening powers,
Kindle a flame of sacred love,
In these cold hearts of ours.
insight: Numbness in prayer is common, and Watts does not scold cold hearts into warmth; he asks the heavenly Dove to kindle a flame of sacred love. On the mornings you feel nothing, pray his line and ask for a love you cannot manufacture.

ref: Hark! from the tombs a doleful sound (1707), st. 1
text:
Hark! from the tombs a doleful sound,
My ears attend the cry,
"Ye living men, come view the ground
"Where you must shortly lie.
insight: Imagine walking past a churchyard and hearing the graves call out, "come view the ground where you must shortly lie." Watts wants that voice in your ears so that you number your days and spend this one on what will last.

ref: Nature with open volume stands (1707), st. 1
text:
Nature with open volume stands
To spread her Maker's praise abroad;
And every labour of his hands
Shews something worthy of a God.
insight: Step outside at dawn and you are reading the book Watts describes, with every labour of God's hands spread open like pages. You can turn an ordinary commute into praise by noticing whose handwriting covers the sky and the trees.

ref: Begin, my tongue, some heavenly theme (1707), st. 1
text:
Begin, my tongue, some heavenly theme,
And speak some boundless thing,
The mighty works, or mightier name
Of our eternal King.
insight: Talk to yourself the way Watts talks to his tongue, ordering it to begin some heavenly theme before any feeling arrives. On a flat morning you may start rehearsing the mighty works of God and find your heart catching up with your mouth.

ref: How condescending and how kind (1709), st. 1
text:
How condescending and how kind
Was God's eternal Son!
Our misery reach'd his heavenly mind,
And pity brought him down.
insight: Stooping down is the old sense of "condescending": the eternal Son crossing the whole distance from glory to our misery because pity moved him. When someone's need costs you pride or time, you are being invited to stoop the way he did.

ref: With joy we meditate the grace (1709), st. 1
text:
With joy we meditate the grace
Of our High Priest above;
His heart is made of tenderness,
His bowels melt with love.
insight: Watts uses the old language of Scripture, in which the bowels were the seat of compassion, to say that our High Priest above has a heart made of tenderness. Bring Christ the thing you are ashamed of, because Hebrews 4:15 says he is touched with the feeling of our infirmities.

ref: Why should we start and fear to die (1707), st. 1
text:
Why should we start and fear to die?
What timorous worms we mortals are!
Death is the gate of endless joy,
And yet we dread to enter there.
insight: Anxiety about dying can sit quietly under a busy week, and Watts names it plainly: timorous worms flinching at a gate that opens on endless joy. If you are afraid, bring the fear to Christ, who has walked through that gate ahead of you.

text:
The Lord Jehovah reigns
His throne is built on high;
The garments he assumes
Are light and majesty;
His glories shine
With beams so bright
No mortal eye
Can bear the sight.
insight: Watts echoes Psalm 93, where the Lord who reigns is clothed with majesty, and adds that his glories shine so bright no mortal eye can bear the sight. Come to prayer with reverence before a King you cannot look upon, and be glad that God has made his glory known in the face of Jesus Christ.

text:
I give immortal praise
To God the Father's love
For all my comforts here,
And better hopes above;
He sent his own
Eternal Son,
To die for sins
That man had done.
insight: Gratitude in Watts runs two directions at once, toward present comforts and "better hopes above," and both flow from the Father who sent his own Son to die. Thank him for tonight's supper and for your resurrection in the same breath.

ref: Salvation! O, the joyful sound (1707), st. 1
text:
Salvation! O, the joyful sound!
'Tis pleasure to our ears;
A sovereign balm for every wound,
A cordial for our fears.
insight: Apothecaries in Watts's day sold cordials to revive the faint, and he pairs one with a sovereign balm to describe what salvation does to fear. When anxiety drains you, take the gospel like medicine and expect it to lift your heart.

ref: When I can read my title clear (1707), st. 1
text:
When I can read my title clear
To mansions in the skies,
I bid farewell to every fear,
And wipe my weeping eyes.
insight: Watts begins with "When," admitting that a believer reads his title to the mansions in the skies more clearly at some times than at others, and that fear lifts when he can. If your assurance is clouded, keep looking to Christ's promises and ask God to make your title clear, since a believer's title does not change when his reading of it grows dim.

ref: Great God, how infinite art thou (1707), st. 1
text:
Great God, how infinite art thou!
What worthless worms are we!
Let the whole race of creatures bow
And pay their praise to thee.
insight: Watts sets the infinite God against the smallness of every creature and then calls the whole race of creatures to bow together in praise. When worship feels private or small, remember that you are joining a chorus that includes everything God has made.

ref: No more, my God, I boast no more (1709), st. 1
text:
No more, my God, I boast no more
Of all the duties I have done;
I quit the hopes I held before
To trust the merits of thy Son.
insight: Watts gives up boasting of all the duties he has done and quits the hopes he once held, so that he may trust the merits of the Son alone. If you have been building a case for God's approval out of your own record, you may set it down and rest your hope on what Christ has done.

text:
Amazing grace! (how sweet the sound)
That saved a wretch like me!
I once was lost, but now am found,
Was blind, but now I see.
insight: Newton kept working in the slave trade for several years after his conversion in 1748 and denounced it in print only decades later, so the man who wrote "was blind, but now I see" knew that sight can come slowly. Ask God for the same grace, which saves wretches and goes on opening their eyes to sins they once could not see.

text:
Through many dangers, toils and snares,
I have already come;
'Tis grace has brought me safe thus far,
And grace will lead me home.
insight: Look back over your own dangers, toils, and snares and count how many you walked out of without your own cleverness saving you. Newton does that and concludes that the grace which brought him safe thus far will lead him home; you may draw the same conclusion.

text:
The earth shall soon dissolve like snow,
The sun forbear to shine;
But GOD, who called me here below,
Will be for ever mine.
insight: Watch a spring snowbank shrink by noon and you have Newton's picture of the whole earth, with the sun itself on borrowed time. Everything you can see has an expiration date, and the God who called you will be yours for ever.

ref: How sweet the name of Jesus sounds (1779), st. 1
text:
How sweet the name of Jesus sounds
In a believer's ear?
It soothes his sorrows, heals his wounds,
And drives away his fear.
insight: Superstition treats the name of Jesus as a charm, but Newton locates its sweetness in a believer's ear, where faith hears the Person behind the syllables. Say his name in a hard hour as a prayer to him, and your sorrows meet a Friend.

ref: How sweet the name of Jesus sounds (1779), st. 3
text:
Dear name! the rock on which I build,
My shield and hiding place;
My never-failing treas'ry filled
With boundless stores of grace.
insight: Newton gathers four pictures of Christ's name into one stanza: a rock to build on, a shield, a hiding place, and a never-failing treasury filled with boundless stores of grace. Whatever trouble presses on you, you can run to Christ under the name that fits it, since he is all four at once.

ref: How sweet the name of Jesus sounds (1779), st. 5
text:
Jesus! my Shepherd, Husband, Friend,
My Prophet, Priest, and King;
My Lord, my Life, my Way, my End,
Accept the praise I bring.
insight: Newton fills three lines with ten names for Jesus, and the middle line gathers his three offices of Prophet, Priest, and King, while the rest speak of care, union, friendship, and journey's end. Before you bring him your praise, pray through the list slowly and let each name teach you what he has promised to be to his people.

ref: Glorious things of thee are spoken (1779), st. 1
text:
Glorious things of thee are spoken,
Zion, city of our God!
He, whose word cannot be broken,
Formed thee for his own abode:
On the rock of ages founded,
What can shake thy sure repose?
With salvation's walls surrounded
Thou may'st smile at all thy foes.
insight: Newton applies the glorious things of Psalm 87 to the church Christ founded on the rock of ages, his one people in every age, which no foe can overthrow. When the news makes you anxious for Christ's church, remember that its safety rests on a word that cannot be broken, and pray that your own congregation keeps to that rock.

ref: Glorious things of thee are spoken (1779), st. 2
text:
See! the streams of living waters
Springing from eternal love;
Well supply thy sons and daughters,
And all fear of want remove:
Who can faint while such a river
Ever flows their thirst t' assuage?
Grace, which like the LORD, the giver,
Never fails from age to age.
insight: Who can faint while such a river flows? Newton asks it as a dare, and on the day you feel spent you can answer it by drinking from a grace that, like the Lord who gives it, never fails from age to age.

text:
Begone unbelief,
My Savior is near,
And for my relief
Will surely appear:
By prayer let me wrestle,
And he wilt perform,
With CHRIST in the vessel,
I smile at the storm.
insight: Atlantic waves nearly sank Newton's ship in 1748, the storm in which he began to pray, so Christ in the vessel was no idle figure to him. When your own weather turns, wrestle in prayer until you can smile at what once terrified you.

text:
Though dark be my way,
Since he is my guide,
'Tis mine to obey,
'Tis his to provide;
Though cisterns be broken,
And creatures all fail,
The word he has spoken
Shall surely prevail.
insight: Newton divides the labour plainly, "'Tis mine to obey, 'tis his to provide," and he holds to it though his way is dark, the cisterns are broken, and every creature fails. When a friend or a plan gives way under you, do the next thing God has commanded and leave the providing to him, trusting the word he has spoken.

ref: One there is, above all others (1779), st. 1
text:
One there is, above all others,
Well deserves the name of friend;
His is love beyond a brother's,
Costly, free, and knows no end:
They who once his kindness prove,
Find it everlasting love!
insight: Loneliness has a way of convincing you that no one will stay, and Newton answers with a Friend whose love goes beyond a brother's and knows no end. Once you prove his kindness, you find it was everlasting love all along.

ref: Approach, my soul, the mercy-seat (1779), st. 1
text:
Approach, my soul, the mercy-seat
Where JESUS answers prayer;
There humbly fall before his feet,
For none can perish there.
insight: Under the old covenant only the high priest came near the mercy-seat, once a year and with blood, and Newton now coaxes his own soul to approach it freely. If prayer feels like a door you hesitate to open, speak to yourself as he does and go in.

ref: Approach, my soul, the mercy-seat (1779), st. 2
text:
Thy promise is my only plea,
With this I venture nigh;
Thou callest burdened souls to thee,
And such, O LORD, am I.
insight: Newton comes to the mercy-seat with one plea, God's own promise, and meets the call to burdened souls with a plain confession: "And such, O LORD, am I." When you pray under a heavy load, name the burden honestly and let what God has promised be your whole case.

ref: Let us love, and sing, and wonder (1779), st. 1
text:
Let us love, and sing, and wonder,
Let us praise the Savior's name!
He has hushed the Law's loud thunder,
He has quenched mount Sinai's flame:
He has washed us with his blood,
He has brought us nigh to God.
insight: Newton's "us" are those Christ has washed with his blood, and for them the thunder and flame of Sinai, the law's sentence on sin, have been hushed because he bore it. If you are trusting Christ, sing Newton's line as your own; if the law's thunder frightens you, let it drive you to the blood that alone can quiet it.

text:
Safely through another week,
GOD has brought us on our way,
Let us now a blessing seek
On th' approaching sabbath-day:
Day, of all the week, the best;
Emblem of eternal rest!
insight: Saturday night, with the week survived and Sunday ahead, is the hour these lines imagine. Before you sleep at the end of your week, thank God for bringing you through and ask a blessing on the day of rest that pictures the eternal one.

ref: In evil long I took delight (1779), st. 1
text:
In evil long I took delight,
Unawed by shame or fear;
Till a new object struck my sight,
And stopped my wild career.
insight: Embarrassment usually wants you to edit your testimony, yet Newton says flatly that he took delight in evil, unawed by shame or fear, until a new object stopped him. You can tell the truth about who you were, because the story is about who stopped you.

ref: In evil long I took delight (1779), st. 2
text:
I saw one hanging on a tree,
In agonies and blood;
Who fixed his languid eyes on me,
As near his cross I stood.
insight: Newton was never at Calvary, so the languid eyes that fixed on him as near the cross he stood describe the sight of faith, when the dying Christ became personal to him. When you read the Gospels' account of the crucifixion, stand near in your mind and ask what that suffering says about your sin and his mercy.

ref: I asked the LORD that I might grow (1779), st. 1
text:
I asked the LORD that I might grow
In faith, and love, and every grace;
Might more of his salvation know,
And seek, more earnestly, his face.
insight: Are you ready for how God might answer a prayer to grow in faith and love? Newton asked in earnest, and the rest of his hymn tells how the answer came through trouble; you can pray it anyway, trusting the One who answers.

text:
Though troubles assail
And dangers affright,
Though friends should all fail
And foes all unite;
Yet one thing secures us,
Whatever betide,
The scripture assures us,
The Lord will provide.
insight: Write down the troubles, the dangers, the friends who failed, and the foes who united, and then write one line under them: the Lord will provide. Newton weighs the whole list against that promise, and so can you.

ref: Why should I fear the darkest hour (1779), st. 1
text:
Why should I fear the darkest hour,
Or tremble at the tempter's pow'r?
Jesus vouchsafes to be my tow'r.
insight: Newton says Jesus vouchsafes to be his tower, an old word for granting something graciously, so the shelter he trusts in the darkest hour is a gift of Christ's own kindness. When temptation presses, run into that tower and let your courage rest on Christ's willingness to shelter you.

ref: Precious Bible! what a treasure (1779), st. 1
text:
Precious Bible! what a treasure
Does the word of God afford?
All I want for life or pleasure,
FOOD and MED'CINE, SHIELD and SWORD:
Let the world account me poor,
Having this I need no more.
insight: Reach for your Bible as Newton did, expecting food when you are empty, medicine when you are sick, a shield when you are accused, and a sword when you are tempted. If you read it only one way, you have not yet leaned on it hard enough.

ref: Quiet, Lord, my froward heart (1779), st. 1
text:
Quiet, LORD, my froward heart,
Make me teachable and mild,
Upright, simple, free from art,
Make me as a weaned child:
From distrust and envy free,
Pleased with all that pleases thee.
insight: "Froward" meant stubborn and contrary, and Newton asks for a heart like the weaned child of Psalm 131, content without crying for more. When envy and distrust flare, you can pray to be changed in your wanting before your circumstances change.

ref: Come, my soul, thy suit prepare (1779), st. 1
text:
Come, my soul, thy suit prepare,
Jesus loves to answer prayer,
He himself has bid thee pray,
Therefore will not say thee nay.
insight: Ask God for what you need with confidence, since Newton rests his whole case on one fact: Jesus himself has bid you pray and will not say you nay. Your permission to pray comes from his invitation, whatever your record looks like.

ref: Come, my soul, thy suit prepare (1779), st. 2
text:
Thou art coming to a King,
Large petitions with thee bring;
For his grace and pow'r are such,
None can ever ask too much.
insight: Timid prayers can pass for humility, yet Newton tells you that coming to a King means bringing large petitions, since none can ever ask too much. Your small asking may reflect a small picture of his grace and power.

ref: Physician of my sin-sick soul (1779), st. 1
text:
Physician of my sin-sick soul,
To thee I bring my case;
My raging malady control,
And heal me by thy grace.
insight: Doctors can only treat what the patient admits, and Newton brings his case as a raging malady instead of a minor complaint. Tell the Physician the real symptoms when you pray, and you will find his grace aimed at the actual disease.

ref: God moves in a mysterious way (1774), st. 1
text:
God moves in a mysterious way,
His wonders to perform;
He plants his footsteps in the sea,
And rides upon the storm.
insight: Cowper wrote through long bouts of severe depression, so his confidence that God plants his footsteps in the sea was hard-won and personal. When you cannot trace God's path through your own storm, you can trust that he is walking there.

ref: God moves in a mysterious way (1774), st. 2
text:
Deep in unfathomable mines
Of never failing skill
He treasures up his bright designs,
And works his sovereign will.
insight: Cowper pictures God treasuring up his bright designs in unfathomable mines of never failing skill, so his purposes are stored where no human search can reach them. When you cannot see what God is doing with your year, you can trust that his plans are safe in his own wisdom and that he is working his sovereign will.

ref: God moves in a mysterious way (1774), st. 3
text:
Ye fearful saints fresh courage take,
The clouds ye so much dread
Are big with mercy, and shall break
In blessings on your head.
insight: Worriers get their own verse: Cowper tells fearful saints that the clouds they dread are big with mercy and shall break in blessings on their heads. Your fear may have the storm right and the outcome wrong, so wait to see what breaks over you.

ref: God moves in a mysterious way (1774), st. 4
text:
Judge not the LORD by feeble sense,
But trust him for his grace;
Behind a frowning providence,
He hides a smiling face.
insight: First impressions of a hard providence tend to read God's face as a frown, and Cowper warns against judging by that feeble sense. When circumstances look hostile, you can suspend your verdict and trust the smiling face hidden behind them.

ref: God moves in a mysterious way (1774), st. 5
text:
His purposes will ripen fast,
Unfolding every hour;
The bud may have a bitter taste,
But sweet will be the flow'r.
insight: Gardeners never judge a flower by the taste of its bud, and Cowper asks you to give God's purposes the same patience. Whatever tastes bitter in your life this month may be a flower that has not opened yet.

ref: God moves in a mysterious way (1774), st. 6
text:
Blind unbelief is sure to err,
And scan his work in vain;
GOD is his own interpreter,
And he will make it plain.
insight: Interpretation belongs to God alone, Cowper says: "GOD is his own interpreter, and he will make it plain." When your doubts demand an explanation on their schedule, you can wait for his, since blind unbelief is sure to err.

ref: There is a fountain filled with blood (1772), st. 1
text:
There is a fountain filled with blood
Drawn from EMMANUEL'S veins;
And sinners, plunged beneath that flood,
Loose all their guilty stains.
insight: Readers sometimes wince at Cowper's physical picture of a fountain drawn from Emmanuel's veins, but he refuses to make guilt sound polite. Your cleansing rests on that blood, whether or not the image moves you on a given morning.

ref: There is a fountain filled with blood (1772), st. 2
text:
The dying thief rejoiced to see
That fountain in his day;
And there have I, as vile as he,
Washed all my sins away.
insight: Despair says you have gone too far, and Cowper answers by standing next to the dying thief, as vile as he, and washing in the same fountain. If grace reached a criminal in his last hours, it can reach whatever you are hiding.

ref: There is a fountain filled with blood (1772), st. 3
text:
Dear dying Lamb, thy precious blood
Shall never lose its pow'r;
Till all the ransomed church of God
Be saved, to sin no more.
insight: Cowper sings that the Lamb's blood will never lose its power until all the ransomed church of God is saved, so Christ's death will bring home every one it was shed to redeem. You can pray for the person who seems furthest away and urge them toward the fountain, knowing that no one who comes will find its power spent.

ref: There is a fountain filled with blood (1772), st. 4
text:
E'er since, by faith, I saw the stream
Thy flowing wounds supply:
Redeeming love has been my theme,
And shall be till I die.
insight: Cowper's "shall be till I die" is a vow that the theme of redeeming love will hold for the rest of his life. You can make the same vow this morning and return to that theme on your hardest days, because it rests on Christ's flowing wounds, which do not change with your moods.

ref: O! for a closer walk with God (1772), st. 1
text:
O! for a closer walk with God,
A calm and heav'nly frame;
A light to shine upon the road
That leads me to the Lamb!
insight: Cowper longs for a closer walk with God, a calm and heavenly frame, and a light on the road that leads him to the Lamb, so his prayer keeps Christ as the end of the journey. If you miss a nearness you once knew, pray his words and keep walking toward the Lamb, asking him to light the road.

ref: O! for a closer walk with God (1772), st. 4
text:
Return, O holy Dove, return,
Sweet messenger of rest;
I hate the sins that made thee mourn,
And drove thee from my breast.
insight: Cowper borrows the language of Ephesians 4:30, where the Spirit is grieved by a believer's sin, and he feels that grief as the Dove leaving his breast. The Spirit never abandons those he has sealed, yet sin can rob you of the sense of his comfort, so hate the sins that grieve him and pray for that comfort to return.

ref: O! for a closer walk with God (1772), st. 6
text:
So shall my walk be close with God,
Calm and serene my frame;
So purer light shall mark the road
That leads me to the Lamb.
insight: Nobody earns the calm frame of the final stanza; Cowper returns to it through the confession that comes before. When you feel far from God, the road back runs through honest repentance, and the Lamb waits at its end.

text:
Sometimes a light surprises
The christian while he sings;
It is the LORD who rises
With healing in his wings:
When comforts are declining,
He grants the soul again
A season of clear shining
To cheer it after rain.
insight: Malachi promised a sun of righteousness rising with healing in his wings, and Cowper has that sun break in on an ordinary Christian mid-song. Keep singing through your gray season, because clear shining after rain can surprise you.

text:
The vine, nor fig-tree neither,
Their wonted fruit should hear,
Though all the fields should wither,
Nor flocks, nor herds, be there:
Yet God the same abiding,
His praise shall tune my voice;
For while in him confiding,
I cannot but rejoice.
insight: If every vine, fig tree, field, and flock failed this year, what would you have left to rejoice in? Cowper, borrowing Habakkuk, answers with God the same abiding, and that answer can hold you when the fields are bare.

ref: Hark, my soul! it is the LORD (1768), st. 1
insight: Suppose Jesus asked you by name, as he asked Peter by the lake after the resurrection: do you love me? Cowper puts that question into every singer's mouth so you must answer it yourself, and a faltering, honest yes is the answer Peter gave too.

ref: Hark, my soul! it is the LORD (1768), st. 3
text:
Can a woman's tender care
Cease, towards the child she bare?
Yes, she may forgetful be,
Yet will I remember thee.
insight: Cowper takes up Isaiah 49:15, grants that even a mother 'may forgetful be', and then gives God's answer: 'Yet will I remember thee.' The promise rests on God's own faithfulness, so when the people who ought to remember you do not, you can hold on to his word that he has not forgotten you.

ref: Jesus, where'er thy people meet (1769), st. 1
text:
Jesus, where'er thy people meet,
There they behold thy mercy-seat;
Where'er they seek thee thou art found,
And every place is hallowed ground.
insight: Picture a rented school gym with folding chairs and a portable keyboard: Cowper would call it hallowed ground, because Christ is found wherever his people seek him. Walk into your next small gathering expecting a mercy-seat, and you will listen differently.

ref: Jesus, where'er thy people meet (1769), st. 2
text:
For thou, within no walls confined,
Inhabitest the humble mind;
Such ever bring thee, where they come,
And going, take thee to their home.
insight: Cowper says Christ, 'within no walls confined', dwells in the humble mind, and that such people bring him wherever they come and take him home when they go. Whatever room you walk into after worship, you can go humbly, knowing that you carry him with you.

ref: What various hindrances we meet (1779), st. 1
text:
What various hindrances we meet
In coming to a mercy-seat?
Yet who that knows the worth of prayer,
But wishes to be often there.
insight: Weariness at the thought of prayer is common enough that Cowper opens with it, admitting the various hindrances everyone meets on the way to the mercy-seat. If prayer feels like a chore you keep postponing, you are in honest company, and its worth is reason enough to go anyway.

ref: Ere God had built the mountains (1779), st. 1
text:
Ere God had built the mountains,
Or raised the fruitful hills;
Before he filled the fountains
That feed the running rills;
In me, from everlasting,
The wonderful I AM,
Found pleasures never wasting,
And Wisdom is my name.
insight: In Cowper's stanza Wisdom speaks, the Son of Proverbs 8, and says that from everlasting 'the wonderful I AM' found pleasures in him that never waste. Before any hill was raised the Father delighted in his Son, and if you belong to Christ, Jesus prays in John 17 that the same love may be in you.

ref: The billows swell the winds are high (1779), st. 1
text:
The billows swell the winds are high,
Clouds overcast my wintry sky;
Out of the depths to thee I call,
My fears are great, my strength is small.
insight: Afraid and short of strength, Cowper does what Psalm 130 does and calls out of the depths without tidying up the fear first. When your fears are great and your strength is small, you are free to pray exactly that sentence to God.

ref: To keep the lamp alive (1779), st. 1
text:
To keep the lamp alive
With oil we fill the bowl;
'Tis water makes the willow thrive,
And grace that feeds the soul.
insight: Cowper sets grace beside the oil in a lamp and the water at a willow's roots: the soul lives on what is given to it from outside itself. Keep returning to the ordinary means of Word, prayer and sacrament, and do not be ashamed that you need to be filled again.

ref: Far from the world, O Lord, I flee (1779), st. 1
text:
Far from the world, O Lord, I flee,
From strife and tumult far;
From scenes, where Satan wages still,
His most successful war.
insight: Know where you lose. Cowper flees the scenes where Satan wages his most successful war, and wisdom for you may be as plain as staying away from the room, the screen, or the company where you keep falling.

ref: O Lord, my best desire fulfill (1779), st. 1
text:
O Lord, my best desire fulfill
And help me to resign,
Life, health, and comfort to thy will,
And make thy pleasure mine.
insight: Cowper asks for help to resign life, health and comfort to God's will, and he pairs that with a harder request, 'make thy pleasure mine'. Ask God for the same change of desire, so that what you hand over to him is given willingly because you have come to want what he wants.

ref: O For a thousand tongues to sing (1739), st. 1
text:
O FOR a thousand tongues to sing
My great Redeemer's praise,
The glories of my God and King,
The triumphs of his grace!
insight: Charles Wesley wrote this hymn around the first anniversary of his conversion in May 1738, and a thousand tongues is a new believer's admission that one voice will not do. When gratitude outruns your words, borrow his and sing them anyway.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: O For a thousand tongues to sing (1739), st. 3
text:
Jesus! the name that charms our fears,
That bids our sorrows cease;
'Tis music in the sinner's ears,
'Tis life, and health, and peace.
insight: You may feel too guilty to sing this, and the stanza names exactly your kind of listener: to 'the sinner's ears' the name of Jesus is music, life, health, and peace. Say it aloud on the drive home and hear it as an offer made to you.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: O For a thousand tongues to sing (1739), st. 4
text:
He breaks the power of cancelled sin,
He sets the prisoner free;
His blood can make the foulest clean,
His blood availed for me.
insight: Debt language opens the line: cancelled sin is a closed account, and only after that does Wesley say the power of sin is broken. Your pardon comes first and your freedom follows it, so you can fight the next temptation as someone already forgiven.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: O For a thousand tongues to sing (1739), st. 5
text:
He speaks, and, listening to his voice,
New life the dead receive,
The mournful, broken hearts rejoice,
The humble poor believe.
insight: Self-help would turn this into advice, yet Wesley gives the dead nothing to do but receive: Christ speaks, and new life arrives. If you are waiting to feel alive enough to come to him, you have the order backwards, so listen to his voice first.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: Jesu, Lover of my soul (1740), st. 1
text:
JESU, Lover of my soul,
Let me to thy bosom fly,
While the nearer waters roll,
While the tempest still is high:
Hide me, O my Saviour, hide,
Till the storm of life be past!
Safe into the haven guide,
O receive my soul at last!
insight: Think of a sailor in a small boat as the swell rises, making for the one harbor he can see; Wesley's prayer is that simple, hide me till the storm of life be past. On a day when the waves are high, you need no strategy, only a place to fly to.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: Jesu, Lover of my soul (1740), st. 2
text:
Other refuge have I none,
Hangs my helpless soul on thee;
Leave, ah! leave me not alone,
Still support and comfort me:
All my trust on thee is stayed,
All my help from thee I bring;
Cover my defenceless head
With the shadow of thy wing.
insight: What would you list as your refuges if you wrote them down: savings, health, a good name, a friend who always picks up? Wesley has crossed them all off and hangs his helpless soul on Christ alone, and that is a safe place to hang yours as well.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: Jesu, Lover of my soul (1740), st. 4
text:
Plenteous grace with thee is found,
Grace to cover all my sin,
Let the healing streams abound;
Make and keep me pure within:
Thou of life the fountain art,
Freely let me take of thee,
Spring thou up within my heart,
Rise to all eternity.
insight: Both verbs count in make and keep me pure, because the grace that covers sin also springs up within to change the heart. Take freely from that fountain again for the sin that clings to you, and expect cleansing along with pardon.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: And can it be, that I should gain (1738), st. 2
text:
'Tis mystery all! The Immortal dies!
Who can explore his strange design?
In vain the first-born seraph tries
To sound the depths of love divine!
'Tis mercy all! let earth adore,
Let angel-minds inquire no more.
insight: Worship what you cannot explain. Wesley pictures the first-born seraph trying and failing to sound the depths of divine love, so your bewilderment before the cross puts you in good company, and wonder is a fitting reply.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: And can it be, that I should gain (1738), st. 4
insight: Imagine waking in a dark cell to find it blazing with light and the chains already on the floor; Wesley paints conversion like Peter's release in Acts 12. Grace moves first, and your part is the one Wesley names: to rise, go forth, and follow.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: And can it be, that I should gain (1738), st. 5
text:
No condemnation now I dread,
Jesus, and all in him, is mine!
Alive in him, my living Head,
And clothed in righteousness divine,
Bold I approach the eternal throne,
And claim the crown, through Christ my own.
insight: Courtrooms end with a verdict, and Wesley's no condemnation, borrowed from Romans 8, means the verdict on him has been read and it is acquittal. You may approach the eternal throne boldly, clothed in Christ's righteousness with your own record set aside.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: Love Divine, all loves excelling (1747), st. 1
text:
LOVE Divine, all loves excelling,
Joy of heaven, to earth come down!
Fix in us thy humble dwelling,
All thy faithful mercies crown;
Jesu, thou art all compassion,
Pure, unbounded love thou art;
Visit us with thy salvation,
Enter every trembling heart.
insight: Visitors leave by evening, so Wesley asks love divine to fix in us thy humble dwelling and stay. If your heart trembles, take comfort, since the trembling heart is exactly the one named as the place he means to enter.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: Love Divine, all loves excelling (1747), st. 3
text:
Finish then thy new creation,
Pure and spotless let us be;
Let us see thy great salvation,
Perfectly restored in thee;
Changed from glory into glory,
Till in heaven we take our place,
Till we cast our crowns before thee,
Lost in wonder, love, and praise!
insight: Hand the unfinished work of your holiness back to the one who began it. Wesley prays finish then thy new creation, trusting God to carry you from glory into glory until you cast your crown before him, lost in wonder, love, and praise.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: Rejoice, the Lord is King (1744), st. 1
text:
REJOICE, the Lord is King!
Your Lord and King adore,
Mortals, give thanks, and sing,
And triumph evermore;
Lift up your heart, lift up your voice,
Rejoice, again I say, rejoice.
insight: Paul wrote rejoice, again I say, rejoice to the Philippians while in chains, and Wesley sets that doubled command to music for a King who reigns now. When joy feels far off, you can obey the command first and trust the feeling to follow.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: Rejoice, the Lord is King (1744), st. 3
text:
His kingdom cannot fail,
He rules o'er earth and heaven;
The keys of death and hell
Are to our Jesus given:
Lift up your heart, lift up your voice,
Rejoice, again I say, rejoice.
insight: Wesley takes the keys of death and hell from Revelation 1:18, where the risen Christ says he was dead and is alive for evermore. Your own death and grave are under his hand, so you may face them in the hope that the one who holds those keys has already walked out of the tomb.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

text:
SOLDIERS of Christ, arise,
And put your armour on,
Strong in the strength which God supplies
Through his eternal Son;
Strong in the Lord of hosts,
And in his mighty power,
Who in the strength of Jesus trusts
Is more than conqueror.
insight: Wesley calls Christ's soldiers to arise and arm themselves, and then places all their strength outside them, in 'the strength which God supplies / Through his eternal Son'. If you feel short of courage, you are the soldier the hymn has in mind, and trusting in the strength of Jesus is how you become 'more than conqueror'.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

text:
Stand then in his great might,
With all his strength endued;
But take, to arm you for the fight,
The panoply of God;
That, having all things done,
And all your conflicts passed,
Ye may o'ercome through Christ alone,
And stand entire at last.
insight: Wesley tells Christ's soldiers to stand in his great might and take 'the panoply of God', the whole armour of Ephesians 6, so that when all their conflicts are passed they may 'o'ercome through Christ alone' and stand entire at last. In whatever fight of faith you face, his strength will keep you to the end, so arm yourself with it and hold your ground.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

text:
HARK the herald-angels sing
"Glory to the new-born King,
Peace on earth, and mercy mild;
God and sinners reconciled."
insight: George Whitefield altered Wesley's first line in 1753, trading hark how all the welkin rings for the herald-angels we sing now, yet God and sinners reconciled is Wesley's own. Next time you sing it half-awake in December, stop at that line and hear it describe you.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

text:
COME, thou long-expected Jesus,
Born to set thy people free,
From our fears and sins release us,
Let us find our rest in thee.
Israel's strength and consolation,
Hope of all the earth thou art;
Dear Desire of every nation,
Joy of every longing heart.
insight: Impatience with waiting is older than you are: Israel longed for this deliverer for centuries before the child came. Wesley turns that long ache into a prayer, so bring your own unanswered longing to the one he calls joy of every longing heart.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

text:
Born thy people to deliver,
Born a child and yet a king,
Born to reign in us for ever,
Now thy gracious kingdom bring:
By thine own eternal Spirit
Rule in all our hearts alone;
By thine all-sufficient merit
Raise us to thy glorious throne.
insight: Three lines open with 'Born': born his people to deliver, born a child and yet a king, born to reign in us for ever. The one who lay in a manger came to rule, so ask him to reign in your heart by his Spirit through the ordinary choices of your week.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: Come, O thou Traveller unknown (1742), st. 1
text:
COME, O thou Traveller unknown,
Whom still I hold, but cannot see!
My company before is gone,
And I am left alone with thee;
With thee all night I mean to stay,
And wrestle till the break of day.
insight: Jacob at the Jabbok, alone after sending his company across, wrestled a stranger until dawn, and Wesley makes that night his picture of prayer. When you pray without seeing anything, you may hold on as Jacob did and refuse to let go until morning.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: Depth of mercy! can there be (1740), st. 1
text:
DEPTH of mercy! can there be
Mercy still reserved for me?
Can my God his wrath forbear?
Me, the chief of sinners, spare?
I have long withstood his grace,
Long provoked him to his face,
Would not hearken to his calls,
Grieved him by a thousand falls.
insight: Shame asks the question Wesley asks, whether mercy could be left for someone who has long withstood grace and provoked God to his face. If you have fallen a thousand times, you are the kind of person this hymn was written for, and mercy runs deeper than your record.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: Jesu, thy blood and righteousness (1740), st. 1
text:
JESU, thy blood and righteousness
My beauty are, my glorious dress;
Midst flaming worlds in these arrayed,
With joy shall I lift up my head.
insight: Imputed righteousness is the theological term for what this line pictures: Christ's blood and righteousness worn as a glorious dress the sinner did not sew. Amid flaming worlds you can lift up your head, because you are wearing his clothes.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: Jesu, thy blood and righteousness (1740), st. 2
text:
Bold shall I stand in thy great day,
For who aught to my charge shall lay?
Fully absolved through these I am,
From sin and fear, from guilt and shame,
insight: Zinzendorf's hymn, in John Wesley's translation, borrows Paul's question from Romans 8:33, 'who aught to my charge shall lay?', and answers it with being 'fully absolved' through Christ's blood and righteousness. On the great day your boldness can rest on that absolution, even when your own conscience accuses you.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

text:
ARISE, my soul, arise,
Thy Saviour's sacrifice!
All the names that love could find,
All the forms that love could take,
Jesus in himself hath joined,
Thee, my soul, his own to make.
insight: Wesley gathers all the names that love could find and all the forms that love could take into Jesus himself, the Saviour whose sacrifice the soul is called to rise and see. Whether you need a shepherd, a physician, an advocate or a friend, you can come to him, because every one of those names meets in one person.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

ref: O For a heart to praise my God (1742), st. 1
text:
O FOR a heart to praise my God,
A heart from sin set free!
A heart that always feels thy blood
So freely spilt for me!
insight: Pray for a heart that feels. Wesley asks for more than good behavior; he wants a heart that always feels the blood so freely spilt, and you can ask the same whenever your devotion has gone numb and dutiful.

witness.work: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists (1780; 1889 ed.)

text:
New every morning is the love
Our wakening and uprising prove;
Through sleep and darkness safely brought,
Restored to life, and power, and thought.
insight: John Keble published The Christian Year in 1827, and this morning hymn draws its thought from Lamentations 3. Each time you wake, restored to life and power and thought after the helplessness of sleep, you hold fresh evidence that God's compassion has not failed.

text:
New mercies, each returning day,
Hover around us while we pray;
New perils past, new sins forgiven,
New thoughts of God, new hopes of Heaven.
insight: How many new things can you count before breakfast? Keble names five, fresh mercies, perils past, sins forgiven, thoughts of God, hopes of heaven, and none of them waits on how well you managed yesterday.

text:
The trivial round, the common task,
Would furnish all we ought to ask;
Room to deny ourselves; a road
To bring us daily nearer God.
insight: Dishes, commutes, the same report due every Friday: Keble calls it the trivial round and says it furnishes all we ought to ask, room to deny ourselves and a road nearer God. You need no different life to grow in holiness, only eyes for the road under your feet.

text:
Only, O Lord, in Thy dear love
Fit us for perfect Rest above;
And help us, this and every day,
To live more nearly as we pray.
insight: Close the gap between the words you pray and the life you live this afternoon. Keble's request is small and searching, to live more nearly as we pray, so pick one line from your morning prayer and try to live it before dark.

text:
Old friends, old scenes will lovelier be,
As more of Heaven in each we see:
Some softening gleam of love and prayer
Shall dawn on every cross and care.
insight: Some imagine holiness drains the color from ordinary life, as if heaven-minded people must grow bored with earth. Keble expects the opposite, old friends and old scenes growing lovelier as more of heaven shows in each, so look again at the familiar faces around your table.

text:
Sun of my soul! Thou Saviour dear,
It is not night if Thou be near:
Oh, may no earth-born cloud arise
To hide Thee from Thy servant’s eyes!
insight: Keble calls Christ the 'Sun of my soul' and draws the conclusion that follows from it: 'It is not night if Thou be near.' Whatever the hour, pray as he does that no earth-born cloud may rise between you and the Saviour, because his nearness is your daylight.

text:
When the soft dews of kindly sleep
My wearied eyelids gently steep,
Be my last thought, how sweet to rest
For ever on my Saviour’s breast.
insight: Where does your mind go in the last minute before sleep: the inbox, the argument, the worries of tomorrow? Keble asks that his last thought be how sweet to rest for ever on the Saviour's breast, and each night gives you a small rehearsal of that final rest.

text:
Abide with me from morn till eve,
For without Thee I cannot live:
Abide with me when night is nigh,
For without Thee I dare not die.
insight: Cannot live and dare not die bracket Keble's prayer, one for the day and one for the night that is coming. Both are plain facts about you, so ask Christ to abide with you from morn till eve and trust him for the dark as well.

text:
Watch by the sick: enrich the poor
With blessings from Thy boundless store:
Be every mourner’s sleep to-night,
Like infants’ slumbers, pure and light.
insight: Name the sick, the poor and the grieving you know as you pray tonight. Keble moves straight from his own rest to theirs, asking that every mourner's sleep be light as an infant's, and intercession like that is one way you love people you cannot visit.

text:
Oh! by Thine own sad burthen, borne
So meekly up the hill of scorn,
Teach Thou Thy Priests their daily cross
To bear as Thine, nor count it loss!
insight: Keble was an ordained clergyman when he wrote this prayer for his fellow priests, asking that they bear their daily cross as Christ bore his up the hill of scorn. Whatever your calling, you can ask for that same meekness when your load feels like loss.

text: THERE is a book, who runs may read,
insight: Keble's opening line borrows from Habakkuk 2:2, where the Lord has a vision written plainly on tablets so that whoever reads it may run with it. God does not bury what he means you to know, so on a rushed morning you can open his word expecting it to be plain enough to read.

text: Two worlds are ours: ’tis only Sin
insight: Distance seems like the obstacle between earth and heaven, yet Keble names sin as the only thing that bars the way between the two worlds God has made ours. When heaven feels far off, you may need confession more than a map.

text:
AWAKE—again the Gospel-trump is blown—
From year to year it swells with louder tone,
insight: Listen for the trumpet. Keble hears the gospel call swelling louder from year to year each Advent, and every year that passes brings Christ's return nearer, so live your week as someone who has heard it blown.

text: Flows out the echoing lay beyond the starry choir;
insight: Sound pours outward in Keble's line, an echoing song flowing beyond the starry choir before any village carol begins. When you sing at Christmas, you are adding your voice to music that was already full and overflowing.

text:
OH! day of days! shall hearts set free
No “minstrel rapture” find for thee?
Thou art this Sun of other days,
They shine by giving back thy rays:
insight: Can a heart set free from death keep silent on the day Christ rose? Keble asks it plainly and then calls Easter the Sun whose rays every other day gives back, so each ordinary joy you have this week is reflected Easter light.

text: WHEN God of old came down from Heaven,
insight: Sinai was the first great descent, fire and smoke on a mountain Israel dared not touch, and Keble begins there to prepare for Pentecost. The same God now comes down to dwell in his people by the Spirit, so you carry his presence into rooms Israel could only have feared.

text:
CREATOR, Saviour, strengthening Guide,
Now on Thy mercy’s ocean wide
Far out of sight we seem to glide.
insight: Three titles, Creator, Saviour and strengthening Guide, address one God whose mercy is an ocean too wide to see across. When you feel far out of sight of land, you are afloat on that mercy, and you can trust Father, Son and Spirit without charting the whole sea.

text:
Commit whatever grieves thee
At heart, and all thy ways,
To Him who never leaves thee,
On whom creation stays.
Who freest courses maketh
For clouds, and air, and wind,
And care who ever taketh
A path for thee to find.
insight: Gerhardt tells the grieving heart to commit both its sorrow 'and all thy ways' to the one who never leaves and on whom creation stays. Hand him the grief you have carried alone along with the plans you are making, since he who finds courses for clouds, air and wind can find a path for you.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)

text:
The Lord thou must repose on
If thou wouldst prosper sure,
His work must ever gaze on
If thine is to endure.
By anxious care and grieving,
By self-consuming pain,
God is not mov'd to giving;
By pray'r must thou obtain.
insight: Worry can feel like responsibility, as if lying awake over a problem did some good. Gerhardt says anxious care and self-consuming pain do not move God to giving, while prayer obtains what worry never could, so turn your worrying tonight into asking.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)

ref: Oh! bleeding head, and wounded (1656), st. 1
text:
Oh! bleeding head, and wounded,
And full of pain and scorn,
In mockery surrounded
With cruel crown of thorn!
Oh Head! before adornèd
With grace and majesty,
Insulted now and scornèd,
All hail I bid to Thee!
insight: The head once adorned with grace and majesty is crowned with thorns and surrounded with mockery, and Gerhardt answers the soldiers' mocking hail with a true one: 'All hail I bid to Thee!' You can honor Christ as King where he looks most defeated, since the scorn he bore was borne for you.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)
witness.path: gutenberg/pg30362.txt#TO THE COUNTENANCE OF THE LORD JESUS.

ref: Oh! bleeding head, and wounded (1656), st. 2
text:
They spit upon and jeer Thee,
Thou noble countenance!
Though mighty worlds shall fear Thee,
And flee before Thy glance.
How hath Thy colour faded,
The light too of Thine eye!
Say who to pale hath made it?
None shone so brilliantly.
insight: Grief is the right response to Gerhardt's question, who made that brilliant face so pale? Stay with the answer before hurrying to Easter: your sins had a part in it, and the one before whom worlds will flee bore it without fleeing.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)
witness.path: gutenberg/pg30362.txt#TO THE COUNTENANCE OF THE LORD JESUS.

ref: A Lamb bears all its guilt away (1647), st. 1
text:
A Lamb bears all its guilt away
The world thus to deliver,
All sins of sinners patiently
It bears and murmurs never.
It goes, and weak and sick is made
An off'ring on the altar laid,
All pleasure it forsaketh,
Submits to shame, and scorn, and wrath,
To anguish, wounds, stripes, cross, and death,
This cup with gladness taketh.
insight: Gerhardt's Lamb bears 'all sins of sinners' patiently and goes as an offering laid on the altar, submitting to shame, scorn, wrath and death, as Isaiah 53 foretold of the servant. That wrath fell on the Lamb in the sinner's place, so bring your guilt to him and trust that what he carried for you has been carried away.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)
witness.path: gutenberg/pg30362.txt#A LAMB BEARS ALL THE GUILT AWAY.

ref: Awake, my heart! be singing (1647), st. 1
text:
Awake, my heart! be singing,
Praise to thy Maker bringing,
Of every good the Giver,
Who men protecteth ever.
insight: Give thanks before you check anything else in the morning. Gerhardt wakes his heart to sing to the Giver of every good who protects men ever, and that small habit can set the tone of your whole day.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)

ref: Awake, my heart! be singing (1647), st. 2
text:
As shades of night spread over
Earth as a pall did cover,
Then Satan sought to have me,
But God was near to save me.
insight: Fear of the dark is older than electric light, and Gerhardt admits that when night spread over the earth like a pall, Satan sought to have him, yet God was near to save. Through every hour you sleep and notice nothing, you are kept by that same nearness, if you trust him.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)

ref: Is God for me? t'oppose me (1653), st. 1
text:
Is God for me? t'oppose me
A thousand may uprise;
When I to pray'r arouse me,
He'll chase mine enemies.
And doth the Head befriend me,
Am I belov'd by God?
Let foes then rise to rend me,
The wild opposing brood!
insight: Romans 8:31 supplies Gerhardt's opening line, and his answer is that if the Head befriends him and God loves him, a thousand foes may rise against him without doing final harm. Before you size up whatever stands against you, take Paul's answer to heart: for all who are in Christ, God is for them.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)
witness.path: gutenberg/pg30362.txt#A SONG OF CHRISTIAN CONSOLATION AND JOY.

ref: Why should sorrow ever grieve me (1653), st. 1
text:
Why should sorrow ever grieve me?
Christ is near,
What can here
E'er of Him deprive me?
Who can rob me of my heaven
That God's Son,
As mine own,
To my faith hath given?
insight: Gerhardt asks, 'Why should sorrow ever grieve me?', and answers that Christ is near and that no one can rob the believer of the heaven God's Son has given to faith. Your sorrow is real, yet it cannot take from you what Christ has made your own.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)

ref: Now with joy my heart is bounding (1653), st. 1
text:
Now with joy my heart is bounding,
With delight
Angels bright
Praises forth are sounding.
Hark! hark! how the choirs of Heaven,
Through the sky
Raise the cry,
Christ to you is given!
insight: Overhead the choirs of heaven raise their cry and Gerhardt's heart bounds along with them: Christ to you is given. Those last words are addressed to you, so sing your carols as someone receiving a gift.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)
witness.path: gutenberg/pg30362.txt#NOW WITH JOY MY HEART IS BOUNDING.

ref: Up! up! my heart with gladness (1648), st. 1
text:
Up! up! my heart with gladness,
See what to-day is done!
How after gloom and sadness
Comes forth the glorious Sun!
My Saviour there was laid
Where our bed must be made,
When to the realms of light
Our spirit wings its flight.
insight: Easter morning in Gerhardt's hymn looks at the grave where our bed must be made and finds that the Saviour has lain there first and risen. When you think of your own death, you can picture a bed Christ has already slept in and left.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)
witness.path: gutenberg/pg30362.txt#UP! UP! MY HEART WITH GLADNESS.

ref: O Jesus Christ! my fairest Light (1653), st. 1
text:
O Jesus Christ! my fairest Light,
Who in Thy soul dost love me,
I ne'er can tell it, nor its height
Mete, 'tis so high above me,
Grant that my heart may warm to Thee,
With ardent love ne'er ceasing,
Thee embracing,
And as Thy property,
Cleave to Thee, ever gazing.
insight: Measure fails Gerhardt entirely, mete being the old word for it: he can neither tell nor mete the height of Christ's love, so he asks for a heart that warms and cleaves to him. You need not understand that love before you cling to it.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)

ref: Now spread are evening's shadows (1647), st. 1
text:
Now spread are evening's shadows,
O'er forests, towns, and meadows,
And sleepeth ev'ry eye;
Awake my pow'rs and sing ye,
And pray'r and praises bring ye,
That your Creator please on high!
insight: Spend the last minutes of your day on praise. As shadows spread over forests, towns and meadows and every eye sleeps, Gerhardt calls his own powers awake to please their Creator, and you can close your evening with that same small act.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)

ref: Go forth, my heart, and seek delight (1653), st. 1
text:
Go forth, my heart, and seek delight
In this summer time so bright,
The bounties God displayeth,
The garden's splendour go and see,
Behold how God for me and thee
Them gorgeously arrayeth.
insight: Five years after the Thirty Years' War ended, Gerhardt sent his heart out into a summer garden to find God's kindness in the flowers. After whatever winter you have come through, go outside and take one bright bloom as evidence of the Father's care for you.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)

ref: Jesus! Thou, my dearest Brother (1653), st. 1
text:
Jesus! Thou, my dearest Brother,
Who dost well to me intend,
Thou mine Anchor, Mast, and Rudder,
And my truest Bosom-Friend.
To Thee, ere was earth or heaven,
Had the race of man been given;
Thou, e'en me, poor guest of earth,
Chosen hadst before my birth.
insight: Gerhardt traces Christ's friendship back past his own birth to a gift made ere was earth or heaven, when the race of man was given to the Son. If you trust Christ, his care for you did not begin when you started to need it, so let that eternal choice hold you on the days you feel least wanted.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)

ref: O Lord! I sing with mouth and heart (1653), st. 1
text:
O Lord! I sing with mouth and heart,
Joy of my soul! to Thee
To earth Thy knowledge I impart,
As it is known to me.
insight: Gerhardt joins mouth and heart in one song and promises to tell the earth about God only as far as God is known to him. Before you speak of Christ to a friend, ask what you have tasted of his kindness, and begin your witness from that honest place.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)
witness.path: gutenberg/pg30362.txt#O LORD! I SING WITH MOUTH AND HEART.

text:
The golden morning,
Joy her adorning,
With splendour near us
Draweth, to cheer us
With her heart-refreshing and lovely light.
My head and members
Lay wrapt all in slumbers,
But now awaking,
And sleep from me shaking,
Heaven's bless'd sunshine doth gladden my sight.
insight: Picture a sleeper shaking off the blankets as golden light crosses the room, and a man whose first waking thought is gladness. Tomorrow when your alarm sounds, greet the sunshine as a gift from heaven before you reach for anything else.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)

ref: Shall I not my God be praising (1653), st. 1
text:
Shall I not my God be praising,
And in Him not joyful be?
For in all His works amazing,
See I not His care for me?
Is it not pure love that filleth,
And His faithful heart o'erflows,
When He ever cares for those,
Who do only what He willeth?
All things run their course below,
God's love doth for ever flow.
insight: Gerhardt asks questions whose answers are obvious: see I not His care for me? Can you name one ordinary thing from yesterday, a meal or a safe drive home, that ran its course under your Father's love?

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)
witness.path: gutenberg/pg30362.txt#SHALL I NOT MY GOD BE PRAISING?

ref: Immanuel! to Thee we sing (1653), st. 1
text:
Immanuel! to Thee we sing,
The Fount of life, of grace the Spring,
Than fairest lily fairer far,
Lord of all Lords, the morning Star!
Hallelujah!
insight: If worship has gone stale for you, watch Gerhardt pile title on title, Fount, Spring, lily, Star, Lord of Lords, until the only word left is Hallelujah. Boredom with Jesus often means you have stopped naming him, so try one of these titles on your commute.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)

ref: Now at the manger here I stand (1653), st. 1
text:
Now at the manger here I stand,
My Jesus, Life from Heaven!
I stand, and bring Thee in my hand
What Thou to me hast given.
Take it, it is my mind and wit,
Heart, soul, and all I have, take it,
And deign to let it please Thee!
insight: Some picture Christmas as the moment you must bring Jesus something impressive, yet Gerhardt carries to the manger only the mind, heart, and soul God first gave him. Hand back the ordinary self you woke up with; it is the gift he asked for.

witness.work: Paul Gerhardt's Spiritual Songs, tr. John Kelly (1867)

ref: Rock of ages cleft for me (1776), st. 1
text:
Rock of ages cleft for me,
Let me hide myself in Thee;
Let the water and blood,
From thy riven side which flow'd,
Be of sin the double cure,
Cleanse me from its guilt and power.
insight: Double cure is Toplady's way of saying sin wounds you twice, with guilt that condemns and power that enslaves, and the water and blood from Christ's side answer both. When you have trusted him and are forgiven yet feel the old habit tugging, ask for the second half of the cure too.

ref: Rock of ages cleft for me (1776), st. 2
text:
Not the labors of my hands
Can fulfil Thy laws demands;
Could my zeal no respite know,
Could my tears for ever flow,
All for sin could not atone,
Thou must save, and Thou alone,
insight: Stop trying to pay for your sins in tears and zeal; Toplady ran that arithmetic and found that no amount of either could atone. Bring the failure you keep rehearsing to Christ, since he must save, and he alone.

ref: Rock of ages cleft for me (1776), st. 3
insight: Each line pairs a lack with a supply: an empty hand with the cross, nakedness with dress, helplessness with grace, filth with the fountain. Name your own lack to Christ tonight in the same plain way, and ask him for what answers it.

ref: Rock of ages cleft for me (1776), st. 4
text:
While I draw this fleeting breath,
When my eyelids close in death,
When I soar thro' tracts unknown,
See Thee on Thy judgment throne,
Rock of ages, cleft for me,
Let me hide myself in thee.
insight: Fear of dying is met by the same prayer that opened the hymn, hide me in thee, because the refuge you lean on at breakfast is the one that holds at your last breath. Pray that line on an ordinary afternoon so it is familiar when you need it most.

ref: Take my life, and let it be (1874), st. 1
text:
Take my life, and let it be
Consecrated, Lord, to Thee.
Take my moments and my days;
Let them flow in ceaseless praise.
insight: Havergal wrote these couplets in 1874, and they begin with moments and days, the smallest units a life is spent in. Offer God the next hour you have, the meeting or the dishes, and you will have prayed her first stanza honestly.

ref: Take my life, and let it be (1874), st. 2
text:
Take my hands, and let them move
At the impulse of Thy love.
Take my feet, and let them be
Swift and 'beautiful' for Thee.
insight: Consecration, in Havergal's sense, means your hands and feet moving at the impulse of love, so the reason behind a motion changes before the motion does. When you walk to your next errand, ask whose love set your feet going.

ref: Take my life, and let it be (1874), st. 3
text:
Take my voice, and let me sing
Always, only, for my King.
Take my lips and let them be
Filled with messages from Thee.
insight: Whose message do your lips carry on an average weekday? Havergal asks that her voice sing always, only, for her King, and that her lips be filled with messages from him; you might ask the same before your next conversation.

ref: Take my life, and let it be (1874), st. 4
text:
