Take my silver and my gold;
Not a mite would I withhold.
Take my intellect, and use
Every power as Thou shalt choose.
insight: Many believers happily consecrate their feelings while keeping money and mind for themselves, and Havergal refuses that split by naming silver, gold, and intellect together. Look at your bank statement and your reading list, since both belong on the altar.

ref: Take my life, and let it be (1874), st. 5
insight: Havergal calls her heart a royal throne and says it is already Christ's own, so giving up her will means letting the rightful King take the seat that belongs to him. Before your next real decision, ask whose will you are consulting.

ref: Take my life, and let it be (1874), st. 6
text:
Take my love; my Lord, I pour
At Thy feet its treasure-store.
Take myself, and I will be
Ever, only, ALL for Thee.
insight: Havergal's last couplet gathers every earlier gift, moments, hands, voice, silver, will, into one offering of herself, and prints ALL in capitals. If you are in Christ, the giver belongs on the altar along with the gifts, so offer him yourself, whole, in your next prayer.

text:
I fear no foe, with Thee at hand to bless;
Ills have no weight, and tears no bitterness.
Where is death's sting? Where, grave, thy victory?
I triumph still, if Thou abide with me.
insight: Lyte meets the grave with Paul's questions from 1 Corinthians 15, where is death's sting, where its victory, and every boast in these lines hangs on the gift named in the last one, if Thou abide with me. When you fear what is coming, ask Christ to stay with you, because ills lose their weight when he is at hand.

witness.work: Abide With Me (1847), Open Hymnal Project edition

insight: Lyte calls earth's shadows vain because heaven's morning breaks through them, and it is the cross held before his eyes that points him to the skies. When the gloom of a hard season closes in, look to the crucified Christ as the one who points you beyond it.

witness.work: Abide With Me (1847), Open Hymnal Project edition

text:
I need Thy presence every passing hour.
What but Thy grace can foil the tempter's power?
Who, like Thyself, my guide and stay can be?
Through cloud and sunshine, Lord, abide with me.
insight: Which hour of your day feels least in need of God? Lyte asks for his presence every passing hour, through cloud and sunshine, because the tempter rarely waits for a crisis before he comes calling.

witness.work: Abide With Me (1847), Open Hymnal Project edition

text:
The soul that on Jesus has leaned for repose,
I will not, I will not desert to its foes;
That soul, though all hell should endeavor to shake,
I'll never, no never, no never forsake.
insight: Repetition carries the weight of the promise, I will not, I will not, and no never, no never, because God speaks in the first person and wants his word to outlast every doubt you raise. Your only task is to lean; the refusing to forsake belongs to him.

witness.work: How Firm A Foundation (1787), Open Hymnal Project edition

text:
Even down to old age all My people shall prove
My sovereign, eternal, unchangeable love;
And when hoary hairs shall their temples adorn,
Like lambs they shall still in My bosom be borne.
insight: Aging can frighten you with the thought of becoming a burden, yet God promises that when hoary hairs come his people will be borne like lambs in his bosom. Being carried near the end is exactly how unchangeable love planned to finish.

witness.work: How Firm A Foundation (1787), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: O Sacred Head, Now Wounded (1153), st. 6
text:
What language shall I borrow to thank Thee, dearest friend,
For this Thy dying sorrow, Thy pity without end?
O make me Thine forever, and should I fainting be,
Lord, let me never, never outlive my love to Thee.
voice: Bernard of Clairvaux (tr. James Waddell Alexander)
insight: The singer knows that no words of his own are equal to Christ's dying sorrow, so he asks what language he could borrow, and then turns his thanks into a request: make me Thine forever. When your gratitude to Christ feels too small, ask him to keep you his and to keep your love for him alive.

witness.voice: Bernard of Clairvaux (tr. James Waddell Alexander)
witness.work: O Sacred Head, Now Wounded (1153), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: O Sacred Head, Now Wounded (1153), st. 7
text:
My Shepherd, now receive me; my Guardian, own me Thine.
Great blessings Thou didst give me, O source of gifts divine.
Thy lips have often fed me with words of truth and love;
Thy Spirit oft hath led me to heavenly joys above.
voice: Bernard of Clairvaux (tr. James Waddell Alexander)
insight: The singer asks the Shepherd to own him as his, then recalls how often those lips have fed him with words of truth and love. You may make the same request of Christ, and then open the Bible expecting to be fed by the Shepherd who claims you.

witness.voice: Bernard of Clairvaux (tr. James Waddell Alexander)
witness.work: O Sacred Head, Now Wounded (1153), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: O Sacred Head, Now Wounded (1153), st. 11
text:
Be Thou my consolation, my shield when I must die;
Remind me of Thy passion when my last hour draws nigh.
Mine eyes shall then behold Thee, upon Thy cross shall dwell,
My heart by faith enfolds Thee. Who dieth thus dies well.
voice: Bernard of Clairvaux (tr. James Waddell Alexander)
insight: The hymn measures a good death by where the eyes rest, on Christ upon his cross, and by a heart that enfolds him by faith. If you are afraid of dying badly, take comfort that both the sight and the faith are gifts Christ gives to those who ask him to be their shield.

witness.voice: Bernard of Clairvaux (tr. James Waddell Alexander)
witness.work: O Sacred Head, Now Wounded (1153), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: All My Heart This Night Rejoices (1656), st. 6
text:
Ye who pine in weary sadness, Weep no more, For the door
Now is found of gladness. Cling to Him for He will guide you
Where no cross, Pain or loss, Can again betide you.
insight: Tired of a sadness that will not lift, you are the one Gerhardt addresses: weep no more, for the door of gladness is found. Cling to Christ on the heavy morning, since he guides you toward a place no cross, pain, or loss can reach.

witness.work: All My Heart This Night Rejoices (1656), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: All My Heart This Night Rejoices (1656), st. 9
text:
Blessed Savior, let me find Thee! Keep Thou me Close to Thee,
Cast me not behind Thee! Life of life, my heart Thou stillest,
Calm I rest On Thy breast, All this void Thou fillest.
insight: Children in a crowd press close so they will not be left behind, and Gerhardt prays the same way: cast me not behind thee. When you feel the void in your chest this afternoon, ask the Life of life to fill it and keep you near.

witness.work: All My Heart This Night Rejoices (1656), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: All My Heart This Night Rejoices (1656), st. 7
text:
Hither come, ye heavy hearted, Who for sin Deep within,
Long and sore have smarted; For the poison'd wounds you're feeling
Help is near, One is here Mighty for their healing!
insight: Comfort that skips the diagnosis heals nothing, so Gerhardt names the poisoned wounds of sin before announcing that help is near. You need not pretend your sin is a scratch; the One mighty for healing came for wounds that have long and sorely smarted.

witness.work: All My Heart This Night Rejoices (1656), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: All My Heart This Night Rejoices (1656), st. 8
text:
Hither come, ye poor and wretched; Know His will Is to fill
Every hand outstretched; Here are riches without measure,
Here forget All regret, Fill your hearts with treasure.
insight: Gerhardt calls the poor and wretched to come, and says God's will is to fill every hand held out to him with riches without measure. Hold out your empty hand to Christ this evening as it is, and let his treasure displace your regret.

witness.work: All My Heart This Night Rejoices (1656), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: Awake, My Soul, And With The Sun (1674), st. 9
text:
Direct, control, suggest, this day,
All I design, or do, or say,
That all my powers, with all their might,
In Thy sole glory may unite.
insight: Thomas Ken wrote his morning hymn for the scholars of Winchester College, and its ninth verse hands the whole day to God before breakfast. Before your first task, pray his three verbs, direct, control, suggest, over all you will design, do, and say.

witness.work: Awake, My Soul, And With The Sun (1674), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: Awake, My Soul, And With The Sun (1674), st. 11
insight: Ken's four lines, sung by many congregations as the Doxology, trace every blessing to one source and call creatures below and the heavenly host above to praise Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. Pick one good thing from your week and praise the Triune God by name for it.

witness.work: Awake, My Soul, And With The Sun (1674), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: Awake, My Soul, And With The Sun (1674), st. 6
text:
All praise to Thee, Who safe has kept
And hast refreshed me while I slept
Grant, Lord, when I from death shall wake
I may of endless light partake.
insight: Ken begins his morning by thanking God for keeping him safe and refreshing him through sleep, and then treats waking as a picture of rising from death into endless light. When you wake tomorrow, thank God that he kept you through the night, and let that small mercy strengthen your hope of the resurrection.

witness.work: Awake, My Soul, And With The Sun (1674), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: Awake, My Soul, And With The Sun (1674), st. 8
text:
Lord, I my vows to Thee renew;
Disperse my sins as morning dew.
Guard my first springs of thought and will,
And with Thyself my spirit fill.
insight: Sunlight burns morning dew off the grass without a trace, and Ken asks God to disperse his sins just that completely. Pray it over yesterday's failures when you wake, then ask him to guard the first springs of your thought and will.

witness.work: Awake, My Soul, And With The Sun (1674), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: All Praise To Thee, My God, This Night (1674), st. 6
text:
O when shall I, in endless day,
For ever chase dark sleep away,
And hymns divine with angels sing,
All praise to thee, eternal King?
insight: Does bedtime feel like the day giving up on you? Ken turns it toward an endless day with no need for sleep, where, if you belong to him, you will sing with angels to the eternal King, and lying down becomes a small rehearsal of hope.

witness.work: All Praise To Thee, My God, This Night (1674), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: I Know That My Redeemer Lives (1775), st. 6
insight: 'Loves me to the end' sits between two lines of titles: the kind, wise Friend is also Prophet, Priest, and King, and his reign guarantees that love will not run out. Because he lives, Medley resolves to sing; make that resolve yours on the day you least feel like it.

witness.work: I Know That My Redeemer Lives (1775), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: I Know That My Redeemer Lives (1775), st. 7
insight: Breathe slowly once and credit that breath to a living Christ, as Medley does. The One who grants your next breath is preparing a mansion for you and lives to bring you safely there, so death is a road he has already paved.

witness.work: I Know That My Redeemer Lives (1775), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: I Know That My Redeemer Lives (1775), st. 8
text:
He lives, all glory to His Name!
He lives, my Jesus, still the same.
Oh, the sweet joy this sentence gives,
I know that my Redeemer lives!
insight: Medley's joy comes from a sentence about someone else, I know that my Redeemer lives, and Jesus is the same whether the singer feels it or not. On an afternoon when joy is missing, say that sentence because it is true, and rest on the living Redeemer whether or not the feeling follows.

witness.work: I Know That My Redeemer Lives (1775), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: Angels From the Realms of Glory (1816), st. 7
text:
All creation, join in praising
God, the Father, Spirit, Son,
Evermore your voices raising
To th'eternal Three in One.
insight: Shepherds, angels, sages, and saints have filled this carol, and now the whole created order is handed a hymnbook to sing to the eternal Three in One. Hear the birds on your walk as part of that choir, and add your own voice.

witness.work: Angels From the Realms of Glory (1816), Open Hymnal Project edition

text:
Yet she on earth hath union
With God the Three in One,
And mystic sweet communion
With those whose rest is won,
With all her sons and daughters
Who, by the Master's hand
Led through the deathly waters,
Repose in Eden land.
insight: Grief can make the dead feel utterly gone, yet Stone sings of mystic sweet communion with those whose rest is won. When you miss a believer who has died, remember that you and they are held in one union with God the Three in One.

witness.work: The Church's One Foundation (1866), Open Hymnal Project edition

text:
O happy ones and holy!
Lord, give us grace that we
Like them, the meek and lowly,
On high may dwell with Thee:
There, past the border mountains,
Where in sweet vales the Bride
With Thee by living fountains
Forever shall abide!
insight: Stone calls the saints at rest happy ones and holy in one breath, so holiness and gladness arrive together, and he prays for grace to join them as the meek and lowly. If holiness has looked joyless to you, ask God for that grace, and let lowliness become the road into their happiness.

witness.work: The Church's One Foundation (1866), Open Hymnal Project edition

text:
From earth's wide bounds, from ocean's farthest coast,
Through gates of pearl streams in the countless host,
And singing to Father, Son and Holy Ghost:
insight: Crowds stream in from every coastline through gates of pearl, a countless host singing one song to Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. Your small congregation on a rainy Sunday is one tributary feeding that river.

witness.work: For All The Saints (1864), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: We Give Thee But Thine Own (1864), st. 6
text:
And we believe Thy Word,
Though dim our faith may be;
Whate'er for Thine we do, O Lord,
We do it unto Thee.
insight: How lets a dim faith and a real belief stand side by side, and he teaches that whatever is done for Christ's people is done unto Christ himself. Do the kind thing for a fellow believer even while your faith trembles, since the Lord receives the service without waiting for your certainty to grow.

witness.work: We Give Thee But Thine Own (1864), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: Blest Be The Tie That Binds (1782), st. 6
text:
From sorrow, toil and pain,
And sin, we shall be free,
And perfect love and friendship reign
Through all eternity.
insight: Freedom, as Fawcett pictures it, is a life where sorrow, toil, pain, and sin are gone and perfect love and friendship reign. Every good friendship you enjoy in the church is a foretaste, so call one of those friends this week and thank God for them.

witness.work: Blest Be The Tie That Binds (1782), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: To Shepherds As They Watched By Night (1543), st. 6
text:
Ye shall and must at last prevail;
God's own ye are, ye cannot fail.
To God forever sing your praise
With joy and patience all your days.
insight: By its last verse Luther's carol has widened from the shepherds to everyone who receives the news: God's own ye are, ye cannot fail. If you belong to Christ, those words are addressed to you, so let your praise carry the patience of someone whose final victory God has secured.

witness.work: To Shepherds As They Watched By Night (1543), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: Look Down, O Lord, From Heaven Behold (1524), st. 6
insight: Luther is paraphrasing Psalm 12, whose last verse sees the wicked walking on every side when the vilest are exalted, and he turns that complaint into a prayer to lean on God's word. When corruption seems to be winning, even among God's people, read Psalm 12 and pray its promise that the Lord keeps his pure words.

witness.work: Look Down, O Lord, From Heaven Behold (1524), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: For The Beauty Of The Earth (1864), st. 8
text:
For each perfect gift of Thine,
To our race so freely given,
Graces human and divine,
Flowers of earth and buds of Heaven.
insight: Pierpoint's pairing, flowers of earth and buds of Heaven, sets a garden bloom beside a grace of the Spirit, both from one generous hand. Thank God for the tomato on your windowsill and the patience he gave you in the same prayer.

witness.work: For The Beauty Of The Earth (1864), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: Sing, O Sing, This Blessed Morn (1865), st. 6
text:
God comes down that man may rise, Lifted far above the skies
He is Son of Man, that we Sons of God in Him may be;
insight: Incarnation, compressed into one line, means God comes down that man may rise: the Son became Son of Man so you could become a child of God in him. Call God Father when you pray tonight, knowing what it cost to give you that right.

witness.work: Sing, O Sing, This Blessed Morn (1865), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: Sing, O Sing, This Blessed Morn (1865), st. 11
insight: Wordsworth's carol ends by giving glory to each Person in turn, the Father, the Son in whom we live, and the Spirit, and then naming them Godhead One and Persons Three. When you thank God for Christ's birth, give that thanks also to the Father who sent him and the Spirit who unites you to him.

witness.work: Sing, O Sing, This Blessed Morn (1865), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: Sing, O Sing, This Blessed Morn (1865), st. 7
text:
Human flesh is now become Christ's abode, the Godhead's home;
Royal Palace, sacred shrine For the Majesty Divine;
insight: Wordsworth calls human flesh a royal palace and sacred shrine because the Son of God took it up as his home in the incarnation. Your own body, tired or aging, is the kind of flesh Christ wore and will raise, so care for it and use it with honor.

witness.work: Sing, O Sing, This Blessed Morn (1865), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: The Winds and Billows Loudly Roar (1865), st. 7
text:
O never, never when distressed,
To doubtful means resort;
Christ's Bark, when on the billow's crest,
Is safe as in the port.
insight: Panic whispers that a storm changes everything, but Wordsworth answers that Christ's bark on the billow's crest is as safe as in the port. When distress tempts you toward a doubtful shortcut, stay in the boat.

witness.work: The Winds and Billows Loudly Roar (1865), Open Hymnal Project edition

text:
Word of the ever-living God!
Will of His glorious Son!
Without Thee, how could earth be trod?
Or Heaven itself be won?
insight: Barton addresses scripture as the Word of the ever-living God and the will of his glorious Son, needed for treading earth as much as for winning heaven. Open the Bible for your ordinary decisions too, a purchase or a hard email, and ask what the Son's will is for that step.

witness.work: Lamp of Our Feet (1826), Open Hymnal Project edition

text:
Our shield and buckler in the fight!
Vict'ry's triumphant palm!
Comfort in grief! in weakness, might!
In sickness, Gilead's balm.
insight: Soldiers and physicians both get their tools in Barton's four lines, shield and buckler set beside Gilead's balm. Whatever trouble you carry into tomorrow, a fight or a fever, bring it to the same book.

witness.work: Lamp of Our Feet (1826), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: Lord Jesus Think On Me (430), st. 6
text:
Lord Jesus, think on me
That, when the flood is past,
I may th'eternal brightness see
And share Thy joy at last.
voice: Synesius of Cyrene (tr. Allen William Chatfield)
insight: Four plain words, Lord Jesus, think on me, open the stanza, asking only to be remembered by Christ when the flood of death has passed. You may pray them in a hospital corridor when longer prayers will not come.

witness.voice: Synesius of Cyrene (tr. Allen William Chatfield)
witness.work: Lord Jesus Think On Me (430), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: Lord Jesus Think On Me (430), st. 7
text:
Lord Jesus, think on me
That I may sing above
To Father, Spirit, and to Thee
The strains of praise and love.
voice: Synesius of Cyrene (tr. Allen William Chatfield)
insight: Lord Jesus, think on me opens the prayer again, and this time the singer names his reason: that he may sing to Father, Spirit, and Son the strains of praise and love. When you ask Jesus to remember you, ask with the same goal, that your whole life would lead into praise of the Triune God.

witness.voice: Synesius of Cyrene (tr. Allen William Chatfield)
witness.work: Lord Jesus Think On Me (430), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: The People That in Darkness Sat (1781), st. 7
text:
Lord Jesus, reign in us, we pray,
And make us Thine alone,
Who with the Father ever art
And Holy Spirit, one.
insight: Is there a corner of your heart you would prefer Christ ruled from far away? Morison's prayer asks him to reign in us and make us his alone, and the King invited inside is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

witness.work: The People That in Darkness Sat (1781), Open Hymnal Project edition

text:
At last the march shall end; The wearied ones shall rest;
The pilgrims find their Father's house, Jerusalem the bless'd.
insight: Weariness from a long obedience is exactly what Plumptre addresses: the march shall end and the wearied ones shall rest. Keep walking toward your Father's house, a real home with a door, waiting at the end of your road.

witness.work: Rejoice, O Pilgrim Throng (1865), Open Hymnal Project edition

text:
Then on, ye pure in heart! Rejoice, give thanks and sing!
Your festal banner wave on high, The cross of Christ your King.
insight: Nobody qualifies to march by earning a clean heart first; Plumptre's pure in heart wave a banner that is the cross of Christ their King, the very thing that made them clean. Sing with them now, however unready you feel.

witness.work: Rejoice, O Pilgrim Throng (1865), Open Hymnal Project edition

text:
Yes onward, onward still With hymn, and chant and song,
Through gate, and porch and columned aisle, The hallowed pathways throng.
insight: Plumptre's pilgrims never move in silence: through every gate and aisle they go with hymn, chant and song, so their worship is a journey made singing. Sing with God's people on the Lord's Day as fellow travellers heading the same way, whatever the building looks like.

witness.work: Rejoice, O Pilgrim Throng (1865), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: O Love, How Deep, How Broad, How High (1500), st. 7
insight: Three times in four lines the hymn says for us, fastening resurrection, ascension, and Pentecost to the people they were done for. You can read your hardest week inside that pattern, guided, strengthened, and cheered by the Spirit Christ sent.

witness.work: O Love, How Deep, How Broad, How High (1500), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: O Love, How Deep, How Broad, How High (1500), st. 8
text:
All honor, laud, and glory be,
O Jesus, virgin-born to Thee!
All glory, as is ever meet
To Father and to Paraclete.
insight: The doxology names Jesus by his birth from the virgin and gives him the same glory it gives the Father and the Paraclete, as is always fitting. When you praise Jesus, you praise the child of Mary and the eternal Son together, since he is one Person worthy of worship with the other two.

witness.work: O Love, How Deep, How Broad, How High (1500), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: 'Take Up Thy Cross', the Savior Said (1833), st. 6
text:
To Thee, great Lord, the One in Three,
All praise forevermore ascend:
O grant us in our home to see
The heavenly life that knows no end.
insight: The hymn closes by lifting all praise to the One in Three and asking for one thing, to see the heavenly life that knows no end. Let your prayers tonight end the same way, with praise to Father, Son, and Spirit and a plain request to be brought safely home.

witness.work: 'Take Up Thy Cross', the Savior Said (1833), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: The Advent of Our God (1736), st. 6
text:
All glory to the Son
Who comes to set us free,
With Father, Spirit, ever One,
Through all eternity.
insight: Liberation is the reason given for the Son's coming: he comes to set us free, and he shares one being with Father and Spirit through all eternity. Thank Christ by name for a freedom you have tasted, then widen the thanks to the whole Trinity.

witness.work: The Advent of Our God (1736), Open Hymnal Project edition

ref: Hark, the Voice of Jesus Calling (1868), st. 6
insight: Refuse the excuse March names, there is nothing I can do, and reply with Isaiah's words, send me, send me. Take the small task Jesus puts in front of you tomorrow gladly, and answer quickly when he calls.

witness.work: Hark, the Voice of Jesus Calling (1868), Open Hymnal Project edition
